title: Getting Started
body: Get productive with MatchBox MatchBox brings BoxLang to environments where a JVM runtime is not the right fit: native applications, browsers, WASI hosts, serverless functions, and embedded devices. Start with the CLI, then select a target based on the capabilities your application needs. 1 Install MatchBox Use MVM or the direct macOS/Linux or Windows installer, or download a full CLI executable or Docker image. See installation and releases and downloads . 2 Run BoxLang Start with a script or the interactive REPL. The CLI and standalone programs do not require Java. 3 Choose a target Use the native CLI for local execution, then package for native, browser WebAssembly ( --target js ), WASI, or ESP32 as appropriate. Install Get the MatchBox CLI for your operating system and verify it works. Your first application Write a small BoxLang program, run it, and package a native executable. Agentic Development Set up a coding agent with the project context and validation loop it needs. BoxLang AI Understand how AI features in an application differ from AI-assisted development. Choose your path Native application: Start with native builds . Browser module: Read JavaScript and WebAssembly . WASI host or container: See WASM containers for what works in MatchBox 0.11.0 and the known issues. Embedded device: Follow the ESP32 guide . Web application: Explore the webroot server or application server . MatchBox and the BoxLang JVM runtime share language concepts, but they are distinct runtimes. Check compatibility and target differences before relying on JVM libraries or host-specific APIs.

title: MatchBox Playground
body: MatchBox Playground Run BoxLang in your browser with MatchBox compiled to WebAssembly. The page ships six demos (hello, data pipelines, Fibonacci, classes, a Mandelbrot set and the Game of Life), an editor and a stateful REPL. Code runs on your device and is never sent to a server. Limits: runs stop after 5 seconds, with 128 MiB of memory and 64 KiB for source and output. Files, network, the DOM, JVM APIs and the JIT are not available in the browser build. See differences from BoxLang and JavaScript and WebAssembly . Share and embed Copy link puts your code in the link itself, after the # , so it is never sent to a server. Anyone who opens it gets the code in their own browser and presses Run themselves. Links hold about 8 KB of compressed source. Share gives you an <iframe> for your own page, with an optional read only mode: <iframe src="https://matchbox.boxlang.io/playground/embed/#code=...&ro=true" width="600" height="400" allow="fullscreen"></iframe> Full screen expands the editor and console to the whole window. Clear empties the editor and the console, and keeps session variables.

title: Releases and Downloads
body: Releases and downloads MatchBox publishes eight full CLI binaries and a Linux multiarchitecture Docker image. See installation for supported platforms and MVM commands, or Docker for image usage. Stable and snapshot versions The root Cargo.toml holds the base version. A push to master releases that version, creates a stable Git tag such as v0.11.0 , and finalizes the changelog. Stable tags are never overwritten. After publication succeeds, CI commits the finalized changelog to master , advances develop to the next minor version, and dispatches its snapshot build. For example, releasing 0.11.0 advances development to 0.12.0 . Build GitHub release tag Build identity example Stable v0.11.0 0.11.0+42 Development snapshot snapshot 0.12.0-snapshot+133 The +<build-number> suffix identifies the CI build. The CLI's --version output also reports its source commit and build date. GitHub release titles and Docker image version labels include the build number; Git tags and Docker tags omit it. Download locations GitHub Releases and S3 publish the same platform filenames, plus version.json and SHA256SUMS . S3 download directories are: https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/<version>/ https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/latest/ https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/snapshot/ Examples for Linux x64: https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/0.11.0/matchbox-linux-x64 https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/latest/matchbox-linux-x64 https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/snapshot/matchbox-linux-x64 https://downloads.ortussolutions.com/ortussolutions/matchbox/0.12.0-snapshot/matchbox-linux-x64 Stable version directories are immutable. The latest and snapshot channels, rolling GitHub snapshot assets, and version-keyed snapshot directories are refreshed. A path such as 0.12.0-snapshot/ is not an immutable build pin, and the build number is not a separate download directory. Use a stable version or Docker image digest for reproducible deployments. Metadata and verification version.json records the base version, full build version, build ID, source revision, channel, release tag, and SHA-256 checksum for each binary. SHA256SUMS covers all eight binaries and version.json . Download metadata/checksums from the same release or directory as the executable and verify the checksum before executing it. Linux sha256sum , macOS shasum -a 256 , and Windows PowerShell Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 can calculate the binary's digest. MVM uses these checksums before replacing installations and compares build identity to refresh changed snapshots. It retains one rolling snapshot slot, not an archive of every historical snapshot build. Published artifacts versus source capabilities Slim and standalone server executables are no longer published. Their source and custom build options remain available. Browser JavaScript/WASM distribution is deferred; this does not remove local browser packaging or other deployment targets. ESP32 runner publication remains disabled pending toolchain/dependency fixes; see the ESP32 guide for local builds.

title: What is MatchBox?
body: What is MatchBox? MatchBox is an independent Rust implementation of the BoxLang language and runtime. It brings BoxLang to native binaries, browser and server-side WebAssembly, and embedded targets without requiring a JVM for its core runtime. BoxLang is a software productivity platform for building, modernizing, and running applications, with developers and AI agents working together. MatchBox is a pillar of that platform for workloads that need a portable runtime or a target beyond the JVM. A runtime for more places MatchBox includes a compiler, bytecode virtual machine, command-line tools, and target-specific runners. Depending on the build and host, it can run .bxs scripts, package native applications, compile for JavaScript/WebAssembly in the browser, produce WASI modules and components (with known issues in 0.11.0 ), build ESP32 applications, and serve web applications. The same language does not mean identical host APIs. Each target has its own capabilities and constraints; review compatibility and target differences before relying on JVM libraries or platform-specific features. How it fits with BoxLang MatchBox and the JVM runtime are distinct implementations. Shared language concepts make it possible to write portable application logic, but JVM libraries, Java interop, web services, I/O, and deployment features must be checked against the specific MatchBox target. MatchBox does not promise that every BoxLang module or JVM API is available. Choose a next step Install MatchBox . Build your first application . Learn about Agentic Development or BoxLang AI . Browse the deployment targets .

title: Installation
body: Install MatchBox MatchBox publishes one full CLI per supported operating system and architecture, with the VM, compiler, REPL, built-in webroot server, and embedded cross-platform runners. Running ordinary BoxLang code does not require a JVM. Install with MVM MatchBox Version Manager (MVM) installs stable versions side by side and manages a rolling snapshot installation. Linux and macOS curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox-quick-installer/main/install/install.sh | bash Windows PowerShell irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox-quick-installer/main/install/install.ps1 | iex Review the installer before executing it, then follow its shell/PATH instructions and open a new terminal if needed. Select a MatchBox version mvm install latest mvm use latest matchbox --version For development builds: mvm install snapshot mvm use snapshot mvm current Running mvm install snapshot again refreshes the installation when its build ID or revision changes. Unchanged builds are skipped unless you pass --force . MVM keeps the snapshot slot, saves version.json , and displays the actual version, build ID, and source revision in version listings and current . MVM verifies the binary's SHA-256 checksum before replacing an installation. A failed verification leaves the existing installation intact. Verification uses Linux sha256sum , macOS shasum , or Windows PowerShell Get-FileHash . Historical releases without version.json cannot be newly installed with verified-download MVM. Use latest for the latest stable release, snapshot for the rolling development build, or a stable version such as 0.11.0 . Versioned snapshot names are not MVM install selectors. See releases and downloads for channels and build identity. Direct CLI installation The direct MatchBox installer prompts for stable or snapshot and installs a single CLI outside MVM's version management. Unlike MVM, these scripts do not currently verify published checksums. Linux and macOS curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox/master/install/install.sh | bash Windows PowerShell iex (Invoke-RestMethod -Uri https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox/master/install/install.ps1) These commands download and execute an installer. Review the shell installer or PowerShell installer before running it if you prefer. Follow its PATH instructions and open a new terminal if needed. Verify the installation matchbox --version matchbox --help matchbox --version prints three lines ( -v does the same). Example output: matchbox version 0.11.0 commit: 37be346 built on: 2026-10-17 The last command starts the REPL. Try println("Hello from MatchBox!"); , then type exit or press Ctrl+D to leave. See the CLI reference for every command and option. Published distributions Distribution Intended use Full CLI ( matchbox ) Development, compilation, REPL, built-in webroot serving, and bundled target runners. Docker The same released CLI packaged for Linux amd64 and arm64 . Slim and standalone server binaries are no longer published. Custom build options and the server crate remain available from source . Platform CLI architectures Linux x64 , x86 , arm64 , armv7 macOS x64 , arm64 Windows x64 , arm64 Manual downloads are individual executables named matchbox-<os>-<arch> ( .exe on Windows), not release archives. Download the appropriate binary from GitHub Releases or S3 , rename it to matchbox or matchbox.exe , and add its directory to PATH. On Linux/macOS, make it executable with chmod +x matchbox . Verify its checksum against the same release's SHA256SUMS before running it. For Docker, see the Docker guide . For repeatable builds, pin a stable version or image digest rather than a moving snapshot or latest tag. Do I need Rust? Not to run the prebuilt CLI or ordinary standalone applications. Rust is required to build MatchBox from source or compile Native Fusion code. --target js needs the wasm-bindgen command line tool (version 0.2.114) but not Rust; see JavaScript and WebAssembly . ESP32 builds have their own toolchain requirements; see the ESP32 guide .

title: Your First Application
body: Your first MatchBox application This walkthrough uses the MatchBox CLI and a single BoxLang script. If MatchBox is not installed yet, start with Installation . Write a script Create hello.bxs : function greet(name) { return "Hello, #name#!"; } println(greet("world")); Run it matchbox hello.bxs Expected output: Hello, world! MatchBox parses, compiles, and executes the file. The .bxs extension is used for BoxLang scripts. Build a standalone native executable matchbox --target native hello.bxs ./hello Native binary produced: hello Hello, world! On Windows, run hello.exe . The output is specific to its operating system and architecture. The executable includes the MatchBox runner (4.5 MiB on Linux x86_64 for MatchBox 0.11.0, see native builds ), so the destination does not need Java or a separate MatchBox install. Native Fusion or host integrations may introduce their own platform requirements. Compile portable bytecode matchbox --build hello.bxs matchbox hello.bxb Compiled to hello.bxb Hello, world! A .bxb file contains compiled bytecode, not a standalone runtime. Its destination still needs a compatible MatchBox runner. Keep compiler and runtime versions aligned. To omit embedded source text: matchbox --build --strip-source hello.bxs Errors retain file and line information, but removing source reduces diagnostic context. It is not encryption or intellectual-property protection. Explore interactively Start the REPL by running matchbox without a filename. It reads one line at a time and prints the value of an expression after => . Type exit or quit , or press Ctrl+D, to leave. bx> x = 1 + 2 => 3 bx> println(x) 3 Continue with language essentials , browse the CLI reference , or choose a deployment target .

title: Language Essentials
body: Language essentials MatchBox runs BoxLang source on its own Rust VM. It covers the core of the language and a large function library, and it leaves some features out. Every snippet below was run on MatchBox 0.11.0, and the ones with a Run button run in your browser. Before moving a JVM application, read BoxLang compatibility . It lists what is missing and the bugs to avoid. For the language in depth, use the language reference . To learn by doing, start with the course . Variables, strings and operators name = "MatchBox"; active = true; count = 3; println( "Hello, #name#!" ); println( "Built with " & name ); println( count * 2 + 1 ); println( "abc" contains "b" ); println( n ?: "n is null" ); Output: Hello, MatchBox! Built with MatchBox 7 true n is null Variables are dynamically typed. & joins strings, #expression# interpolates inside a double-quoted string, and ?: supplies a value when the left side is null. See operators . Arrays and structs targets = [ "native", "browser", "embedded" ]; println( targets[ 1 ] ); targets.append( "wasi" ); println( targets.len() ); project = { name: "Hello", ready: true }; println( project.NAME ); lengths = arrayMap( targets, ( target ) => len( target ) ); println( serializeJSON( lengths ) ); { name, ready } = project; println( name & " " & ready ); println( serializeJSON( [ 0, ...targets ] ) ); Output: native 4 Hello [6,7,8,4] Hello true [0,"native","browser","embedded","wasi"] Arrays are 1-indexed and struct keys are case-insensitive. Destructuring and spread are covered in destructuring, spread and ranges . MatchBox also has a set type . Control flow and functions for ( target in [ "native", "browser" ] ) { if ( target == "native" ) { println( "Build an executable" ); } else { println( "Explore " & target ); } } switch ( "b" ) { case "a": println( "A" ); break; case "b": case "c": println( "B or C" ); break; default: println( "other" ); } function greet( name = "world" ) { return "Hello, " & name; } double = ( number ) => number * 2; println( greet() ); println( greet( name = "Ada" ) ); println( double( 21 ) ); Output: Build an executable Explore browser B or C Hello, world Hello, Ada 42 Also supported: while , do ... while , break , continue , ranges ( for ( i in 1..3 ) ), closures and arrow functions. Labeled continue , lock and thread statements are not supported. A closure inside a function cannot see that function's variables, so use a loop there. See scopes . Classes class Product accessors="true" { property name; property price; function init() { return this; } } product = new Product(); product.setName( "Widget" ); println( product.getName() ); Output: Widget init must end with return this , and a class extends another with extends="Parent" , not the keyword form. super is not available. See classes . Errors and asynchronous work try { throw( type = "MyError", message = "boom" ); } catch ( any e ) { println( e.type & ": " & e.message ); } finally { println( "done" ); } future = runAsync( () => { sleep( 100 ); return "finished"; } ); println( future.get() ); Output: MyError: boom done finished The type in catch ( SomeType e ) is ignored, so catch any and test e.type . See error handling and async and futures . In the browser, futures take turns on one thread. Function library MatchBox ships built-in functions for strings, arrays, structs, dates, JSON, regular expressions, XML, hashing and more. The function reference lists each one. Some groups are optional parts of the build: Group Needs the build feature In the browser Files and directories bif-io (default) No http() bif-http (default) Not tested, see HTTP Hashing and encryption bif-crypto (default) No ( hash is not defined) Terminal helpers bif-cli (default) No ( cliClear is not defined) Java interop bif-jni (default) No Zip and tar bif-zip Not tested Queries and datasources bif-datasource ; qoq for query of queries No See Building MatchBox for the feature table. The default CLI also removes functions it thinks your script does not use; --no-shaking turns that off. A member call such as a.sort( "numeric" ) can fail with BIF arraysort not found. until you do. Other parts of the language Templates (.bxm) : a few tags work, <bx:loop> does not. Modules : add functions and classes with --module . Queries and data . Java interop : experimental. Native Fusion : call Rust from BoxLang.

title: Build and Run
body: Build and run an application MatchBox supports a quick interpreter loop and multiple deployment targets. Start by running a source file, then select a build based on the target host. Run a BoxLang script function greet(name) { return "Hello, #name#!"; } println(greet("world")); matchbox hello.bxs Use the REPL Run matchbox without a filename to start an interactive session. The prompt is bx> , each line is evaluated on its own (there is no multi-line mode, history or tab completion), and exit , quit or Ctrl+D leaves it. Build for a target matchbox --build hello.bxs # portable bytecode: Compiled to hello.bxb matchbox --target native hello.bxs # native executable: Native binary produced: hello matchbox --target js hello.bxs # ES module + WebAssembly runtime for browsers The --target wasm and --target wasi values exist but do not produce a usable module in MatchBox 0.11.0; see the CLI reference . The targets available also depend on how your MatchBox was built; --target <rust-triple> needs a CLI built with cross-compile . See the full CLI reference and the target guides . A successful compilation does not validate execution on a different host.

title: Agentic Development
body: Agentic Development with MatchBox Agentic development is the practice of working with an AI coding agent that can inspect a project, make changes, and run its checks. MatchBox is one pillar of the BoxLang software productivity platform; the agent still needs clear project constraints and a way to validate its work. For BoxLang's broader approach to agentic development, see the official Agentic Development guide . Give the agent project context Add an AGENTS.md at the root of an application repository. State which MatchBox targets the application supports, how it is built and tested, and which capabilities are intentionally unavailable. Keep the guidance close to the code and update it when the project changes. The MatchBox repository includes focused skills under .agents/skills/ , including runner-development for ESP32 runner work. Skills add task-specific workflows; they do not replace checking the actual application and current MatchBox source. Keep the feedback loop executable An agent should run the same checks a developer would run and report what it could not validate. For an application, document the relevant commands, for example: matchbox --version matchbox tests/smoke.bxs matchbox --target native app.bxs The right checks depend on the target. Browser output, WASI components, and ESP32 firmware need their own runtime or toolchain validation. A successful local script run does not prove an artifact works on every target. Prefer bounded tasks Start with a behavior, target, and acceptance check. Ask the agent to inspect nearby code and relevant skills before changing files; have it show the exact commands and results afterward. Keep secrets out of prompts and test with safe local fixtures. Prompt Plan a focused MatchBox change with executable checks Copy Inspect this repository's AGENTS.md and the relevant .agents/skills before changing code. Identify the MatchBox target and existing tests for this behavior. Make the smallest change that satisfies the request, run the focused checks, and report the exact commands, results, and any target-specific behavior you could not verify. Do not claim support for a target you did not test. Separate development AI from application AI An agent helping write an application is not the same feature as an AI capability running inside that application. For the latter, see BoxLang AI . MatchBox is not a blanket guarantee that BoxLang JVM AI libraries or integrations are available; check the specific runtime and target first in compatibility and target differences .

title: BoxLang AI
body: BoxLang AI BoxLang AI is about adding AI capabilities to an application: connecting providers, composing prompts, using tools and agents, and integrating capabilities such as memory or retrieval. That is different from Agentic Development , where an AI coding agent helps a developer create the application. Start with the official BoxLang AI documentation for the current feature set and supported integrations. MatchBox compatibility is target-specific MatchBox is an independent Rust runtime with its own host and target boundaries. Do not assume that a BoxLang AI module, JVM provider SDK, network client, or storage integration supported by the JVM runtime also works in MatchBox. Confirm the module's requirements and the MatchBox target's supported APIs before designing around it. For native MatchBox applications, begin with the HTTP request guide and verify the providers your application needs. Browser and embedded targets have different I/O and resource constraints; successful native behavior is not proof of browser or ESP32 support. Design for the deployment target Keep provider credentials in server-side configuration, never in browser bundles or firmware images. Use bounded timeouts, avoid logging secrets or prompts containing sensitive data, and test failure paths such as unavailable providers and malformed responses. Treat model output as untrusted input when it can influence tools or application state. For capabilities that are not documented for MatchBox, use the JVM BoxLang runtime or validate a minimal prototype on the intended MatchBox target before committing to the integration.

body: Member functions A member call such as "abc".ucase() or items.map( fn ) is resolved by a fixed table in the VM ( resolve_member_method ). Each entry maps (type, member name) to a function and calls it with the value as the first argument. Names are matched without regard to case. A function that has no entry for a type cannot be called as a member on that type, even when the global function exists. Struct values also run any function stored under the member name in the struct itself, before the table is consulted. title: App server example
body: MatchBox App Server Example This example demonstrates the routed MatchBox app server API built around web.server() and ColdBox-style handlers: function( event, rc, prc ) { ... } App-server scripts should import the namespace explicitly: import boxlang.web; It is a different product from the static/BXM webroot server. Use this app server when you want to build: JSON APIs lightweight microservices middleware pipelines signed webhook receivers server-rendered endpoints with explicit template rendering apps that need explicit static asset mounts inside a routed server This example is for the native matchbox_server binary. ESP32 firmware does not run web.server() scripts; it serves files from an app/ directory instead. See Building for ESP32 . The Web server guide lists the whole app-server API. For a websocket-focused example, see websocket_counter . Project Structure app.bxs : Main routed application. public/site.css : Static asset served through app middleware. views/home.bxm : Template rendered by event.setView() . Key Concepts 1. The Handler Shape Each route handler receives three arguments: event : A native request/response object with ColdBox-style helpers. rc : The public request collection. Route params, query params, form fields, and top-level JSON object keys are merged here. prc : The private request collection for passing internal state across middleware and handlers. 2. Middleware Middleware uses a fourth next argument: app.use( function( event, rc, prc, next ) { prc.requestStarted = true; next.run(); } ); Middleware can mutate rc , prc , session , headers, cookies, status codes, and response bodies. 3. Templates Routes can render templates explicitly: event.setView( "views/home.bxm", { "title": "MatchBox" } ); Templates receive: event rc prc session viewArgs 4. Static Files Middleware Static assets can be mounted explicitly inside the app server: app.use( app.middleware.buildStaticFiles( "/assets", "public" ) ); This serves files from the public directory at /assets/... . The directory is resolved relative to the app script root, missing files fall through to the normal app routing path, and traversal outside the mounted directory is blocked. 5. Webhook Builder Webhook endpoints can be declared with a fluent builder. There is no env scope; read secrets from the process environment with getSystemSetting( name, [default] ) : app.webhook( app.buildWebhook() .path( "/webhooks/stripe" ) .secret( getSystemSetting( "STRIPE_SECRET" ) ) .signatureHeader( "stripe-signature" ) .prefix( "sha256=" ) .timestampHeader( "stripe-timestamp" ) .toleranceSeconds( 300 ) .replayHeader( "stripe-event-id" ) .replayTtlSeconds( 300 ), function( event, rc, prc ) { event.renderText( "ok" ); } ); Running the Example The --app flag belongs to the matchbox_server binary, which you build from the MatchBox source tree. matchbox app.bxs cannot run this script. From the project root: cargo run -p matchbox_server -- --app docs/examples/app_server/app.bxs The address comes from app.listen( 8090 ) in the script, which binds 127.0.0.1 . To listen on all interfaces pass a struct: app.listen( { "host": "0.0.0.0", "port": 8090 } ) . Then visit: http://localhost:8090/ http://localhost:8090/api/hello/MatchBox http://localhost:8090/assets/site.css The script is compiled once, but its top level runs again on every request. Reload / to see the visit count in session.visitCount rise: session data is kept by the MBX_SESSION_ID cookie, while a plain variable at the top of the script would reset on each request. Because this app registers middleware with app.use() , an unknown URL such as /missing currently returns 500 instead of 404 in v0.11.0. What The Example Covers app-level middleware route groups cookies in-memory session state JSON responses static asset serving with app.middleware.buildStaticFiles() template rendering with setView() signed webhook route registration for websockets, see the dedicated websocket counter example

title: Arrays and structs
body: Arrays and structs An array is an ordered list. A struct is a set of named values, like an object or a dictionary. Between them they cover most of the data you will handle. Arrays Array positions start at 1 , not 0. This surprises people coming from JavaScript or Rust, so it is worth a run. colors = [ "red", "green", "blue" ]; println( colors[ 1 ] ); println( colors.len() ); colors.append( "violet" ); println( colors.toList( ", " ) ); colors[ 2 ] = "lime"; println( colors.toList( ", " ) ); println( colors[ 1 ] & " to " & colors[ colors.len() ] ); Output: red 3 red, green, blue, violet red, lime, blue, violet red to violet toList turns an array into a delimited string, which is handy for printing. append , prepend , pop and shift add and remove items. Sorting changes the array in place: scores = [ 30, 4, 100, 12 ]; arraySort( scores, "numeric" ); println( scores.toList( "," ) ); Output: 4,12,30,100 Structs person = { name: "Ada", city: "London" }; println( person.name ); println( person[ "city" ] ); person.age = 36; println( structCount( person ) ); println( person.keyExists( "age" ) ); println( person.keyExists( "email" ) ); structDelete( person, "city" ); println( structCount( person ) ); Output: Ada London 3 true false 2 Reach a value with a dot or with brackets. Brackets let you use a key that is stored in a variable. Assigning to a new key adds it. Nesting Arrays and structs nest freely, which is how most real data looks. person = { name: "Ada", langs: [ "BoxLang", "Rust" ] }; println( person.langs[ 2 ] ); people = [ { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "Linus", age: 28 } ]; for ( p in people ) { println( p.name & " is " & p.age ); } Output: Rust Ada is 36 Linus is 28 Loops for ( n in [ 10, 20, 30 ] ) { println( n ); } for ( i = 1; i <= 3; i++ ) { println( "round " & i ); } total = 0; for ( n in 1..4 ) { total += n; } println( total ); count = 0; while ( count < 3 ) { count += 1; } println( count ); for ( key, value in { a: 1, b: 2 } ) { println( key & "=" & value ); } Output: 10 20 30 round 1 round 2 round 3 10 3 a=1 b=2 1..4 is a range. for ( key, value in struct ) walks a struct. Do not rely on the order of struct keys. Try it Add a println inside the people loop that only prints people older than 30. You will need an if , which lesson 7 covers in depth, but you can guess the shape.

title: Async and futures
body: Async and futures The async lesson introduces futures. This page lists what is available and what breaks. Snippets with a Run button ran in the browser playground and on the CLI with the same output. Futures runAsync( fn ) and futureNew( fn ) start a function and return a future. get() waits for the result. f = runAsync( () => 6 * 7 ); println( f.get() ); g = futureNew( () => "hi" ); println( g.get() ); slow = runAsync( () => { sleep( 30 ); return "slow"; } ); fast = runAsync( () => "fast" ); println( slow.get() & " " & fast.get() ); println( runAsync( () => 4 ).then( v => v * 2 ).get() ); println( serializeJSON( asyncAllApply( [ 1, 2, 3 ], v => v * 2 ) ) ); Output: 42 hi slow fast 8 [2,4,6] Future member functions that work: get , then , exceptionally , onError , getOrDefault . asyncAllApply( items, fn ) maps in parallel and returns an array. asyncAll and asyncAny are not available: calling them fails with Can only call functions. Errors An error inside the callback is stored in the future and raised again by get() . exceptionally and getOrDefault turn it into a value. f = runAsync( () => { throw( message = "bad" ); } ); try { f.get(); } catch ( any e ) { println( "caught" ); } g = runAsync( () => { throw( message = "bad2" ); } ).exceptionally( err => "recovered" ); println( g.get() ); h = runAsync( () => { throw( message = "bad3" ); } ); println( h.getOrDefault( "fallback" ) ); Output: caught recovered fallback On the CLI each failed task also writes an [Async Task Error] block with the source line to the error stream. The browser The playground runs on one thread. Futures take turns instead of running in parallel, sleep yields to the other tasks, and the playground stops a run after five seconds. On a native build the same code can use more threads. Threads and executors threadNew( fn ) , threadJoin( thread ) and executorNew() are available. In testing, threadJoin returned before the thread's println output appeared, in the CLI and in the playground, so do not use printed order to judge whether a join waited. Bugs to avoid Callbacks that use the enclosing function's variables A callback created inside a function cannot see that function's parameters or locals. For runAsync this makes the task fail: function work( id ) { return runAsync( () => id * 10 ); } println( work( 1 ).get() ); Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Operands must be two numbers. The same happens for [ 1, 2, 3 ].map( n => runAsync( () => n * n ) ) and for a loop variable, as in for ( n in [ 1, 2, 3 ] ) { runAsync( () => n * n ); } . In the playground the map line panics with Attempted to access collected object instead of reporting an error. Plain variables assigned at the top level of the script are visible to the callback. This is the closure problem described in scopes . Workaround: asyncAllApply hands each item to the callback as a parameter, which does work: asyncAllApply( [ 1, 2, 3 ], n => n * n ) returns [ 1, 4, 9 ] . Chained then A second then on a future that is itself the result of then uses the original value instead of the previous result: a = runAsync( () => 2 ).then( v => v + 1 ).then( v => v + 100 ).get(); println( a ); Output: 102 The result should be 103. BoxLang 1.13 returns the chained value (it printed 20 for the equivalent 1 , + 1 , * 10 chain). Do the whole computation in one callback. Other gaps f.complete( value ) , f.isDone() and f.isError() do not exist on futures ( Method ... not found ). orTimeout( 1000 ) on a task that finishes in 10 milliseconds failed with Future timed out in the playground, and completeOnTimeout( 5, 100 ) on a finished future returned the timeout value. Treat the timeout functions as unreliable.

title: AWS Lambda
body: AWS Lambda MatchBox runs on Lambda's provided.al2023 custom runtime. The package is a bootstrap executable plus your .bx files. On each invocation the runtime loads a BoxLang class and calls its run method with the event. See the single-file Lambda example for a complete project. Handler contract class { function run( event, context, response ) { response.statusCode = 200; response.body = { "message": "Hello" }; } } Argument Contents event The invocation event JSON converted to BoxLang structs, arrays and simple values. context The Lambda context object, below. response A struct with statusCode (200), headers , cookies (empty array), body (empty string) and isBase64Encoded . Change it in place, or return a value. The runtime builds the HTTP-style result from the response: If run returns a struct that has any of statusCode , headers , cookies , body or isBase64Encoded , that struct is the response. If run returns any other value except null , it replaces response.body . A string body is sent as is. Binary data is Base64-encoded and isBase64Encoded is set to true . Any other value is serialized as JSON. headers starts as Content-Type: application/json and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * . If you assign a new headers struct, those defaults are not added , so the CORS header is gone too. An empty headers struct at the end gets the two defaults back. Context Method Returns getAwsRequestId() The request id from the Runtime API. local-request in a local invoke. getFunctionName() , getFunctionVersion() , getInvokedFunctionArn() From AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME , AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION and the invocation headers. getMemoryLimitInMB() From AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE . getLogGroupName() , getLogStreamName() From AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME and AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME . getRemainingTimeInMillis() Time to the invocation deadline. A local invoke always reports 30000. getLogger().log( message, [level="INFO"] ) Writes [LEVEL] message to standard output. getClientContext() , getIdentity() An empty struct. Routing to classes The class that runs is chosen from the request path: The path comes from requestContext.http.path , else rawPath (when requestContext.domainName exists), else requestContext.resourcePath , else path . The first path segment is converted to PascalCase, splitting on characters that are not letters or digits: /hello-world/x becomes HelloWorld.bx . If that file exists in the package root or in src/main/bx/ , it handles the request. Otherwise, and for / or an event with no path, Lambda.bx handles it. Lambda.bx is looked up in the package root, then in src/main/bx/ . Without it the runtime stops at startup with Lambda.bx not found . Application.bx lifecycle An Application.bx in the package root or in src/main/bx/ is optional. On every invocation the runtime creates a new VM, runs Application.bx , constructs it and calls its hooks. Nothing is cached between invocations, so onApplicationStart runs every time and the startup cost is paid per request. Hook When Arguments onApplicationStart() Before the handler class is loaded. none onRequestStart( path, event, context ) Before run . path is the file path of the handler class. onRequestEnd( path, event, context ) After run , also after a failure. onError( error, "", event, context ) When run throws. error is the error text. Hooks you do not define are skipped. After a failure the runtime posts { "errorMessage": ..., "errorType": "MatchBoxLambdaError" } to the Runtime API error endpoint. Local invoke matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json matchbox lambda invoke ./my-project --event event.json The argument is a .bx file or a project directory. The command runs the same code as Lambda, prints the response as JSON, and uses the local defaults above for the context. Deploy matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \ --function matchbox-hello \ --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 \ --public \ --bootstrap /path/to/bootstrap Put the path to the file or project right after deploy , before any flag. The command takes the first argument that does not start with -- as the path. Flag Meaning --function <name> Required. Function name. --bootstrap <file> Required. A Linux executable for the chosen architecture. It is stored in the zip as bootstrap . --role <arn> Execution role. Required when the function does not exist yet. --arch arm64\|x86_64 Architecture for a new function and for the bootstrap you supply. Default arm64 . --out <file> Where to write the zip. Default target/lambda/<function>.zip . --memory <MB> Memory size, applied with update-function-configuration . --timeout <seconds> Timeout, applied with update-function-configuration . --profile <name> , --region <region> Passed to every aws call. --public Create or update a Function URL with auth type NONE . Anyone can call it. Adds the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions for principal * . --url Create or update a Function URL with AWS_IAM auth. Callers must sign requests. Use at most one of --public and --url . Without either, no Function URL is touched. The URL is printed when one is configured. The command writes the zip, checks for the function with lambda get-function , then either runs update-function-code or, when it does not exist, create-function with --runtime provided.al2023 --handler bootstrap . --memory and --timeout are applied afterwards when given. Memory and timeout are numbers up to 65535. --bootstrap is required in v0.11.0, and the deploy command does not add a bootstrap for you. Package layout The zip stores files without compression. bootstrap has mode 0755. Input Contents of the zip A single .bx file The file as Lambda.bx , every other .bx file in the same directory (not subdirectories), boxlang.json and boxlang_modules/ from that directory. A project directory with src/main/bx/ The whole src/main/bx/ tree at the zip root, src/resources/boxlang.json or boxlang.json , and src/resources/boxlang_modules/ or boxlang_modules/ . A project directory without it The .bx files in the directory root plus the same boxlang.json and boxlang_modules/ rules. Only files ending in .bx are picked up outside boxlang_modules/ . Building the bootstrap The bootstrap binary is the matchbox_lambda_runner crate. The release workflow does not publish it. Build it from the MatchBox source tree: cargo build --release -p matchbox_lambda_runner # result: target/release/matchbox_lambda_runner For a different architecture add --target with the matching Rust target, such as aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu for arm64 , and the linker that target needs. Pass the resulting file to --bootstrap . At start the binary reads these variables: Variable Use AWS_LAMBDA_RUNTIME_API Required. Host and port of the Runtime API. LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT Directory with the package. Default /var/task . AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME , AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_VERSION , AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE , AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_GROUP_NAME , AWS_LAMBDA_LOG_STREAM_NAME Filled into the context. It then loops: fetch the next invocation, run it, post the response or the error. AWS account setup These steps prepare an AWS account and machine for matchbox lambda deploy . 1. Install AWS CLI v2 matchbox lambda deploy shells out to the aws CLI, so install AWS CLI version 2 and verify it is on your PATH . On macOS, the official installer is: curl -o /tmp/AWSCLIV2.pkg https://awscli.amazonaws.com/AWSCLIV2.pkg sudo installer -pkg /tmp/AWSCLIV2.pkg -target / aws --version Expected shape: aws-cli/2.x.x ... AWS CLI v1 and v2 both use the aws command name. If aws --version shows v1, upgrade or fix your PATH before testing deploys. 2. Configure Credentials Recommended: use IAM Identity Center / SSO if your AWS account supports it. aws configure sso --profile matchbox-dev aws sso login --profile matchbox-dev The wizard asks for: SSO start URL SSO region AWS account permission set / role default region output format Use json for output format. If you are using access keys instead of SSO: aws configure --profile matchbox-dev This writes config under: ~/.aws/config ~/.aws/credentials Do not use root account credentials. 3. Pick a Lambda region Choose a region that supports Lambda Function URLs. For example: export AWS_PROFILE=matchbox-dev export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 Or pass them to the deploy command: matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 \ ... 4. Verify your identity Run: aws sts get-caller-identity \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 You should see JSON with: { "UserId": "...", "Account": "123456789012", "Arn": "..." } Keep the Account value handy. 5. Create a Lambda execution role Creating a function requires an existing Lambda execution role ARN. The deploy command does not create IAM roles. Create a trust policy: cat > /tmp/matchbox-lambda-trust-policy.json <<'JSON' { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] } JSON Create the role: aws iam create-role \ --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \ --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/matchbox-lambda-trust-policy.json \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Attach the basic CloudWatch Logs policy: aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Get the role ARN: aws iam get-role \ --role-name matchbox-lambda-execution \ --query 'Role.Arn' \ --output text \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 Save that ARN. It will look like: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution IAM role propagation can take a few seconds. If Lambda create fails with a role-assumption error immediately after creating the role, wait briefly and retry. 6. Permissions your AWS principal needs The AWS profile you use for deploys needs permissions roughly equivalent to: lambda:GetFunction lambda:CreateFunction lambda:UpdateFunctionCode lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig lambda:GetFunctionUrlConfig lambda:AddPermission iam:PassRole for the execution role ARN If you create the role yourself with the commands above, your principal also needs: iam:CreateRole iam:AttachRolePolicy iam:GetRole Manual AWS CLI equivalents matchbox lambda deploy runs AWS CLI calls like these: aws lambda create-function \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --runtime provided.al2023 \ --handler bootstrap \ --architectures arm64 \ --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \ --zip-file fileb://target/lambda/matchbox-hello.zip \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 aws lambda update-function-code \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --zip-file --function-url-auth-type NONE \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 aws lambda get-function-url-config \ --function-name matchbox-hello \ --query FunctionUrl \ --output text \ --profile title: Basic BoxLang project
body: Basic BoxLang Project This example shows a minimal multi-file BoxLang project with a script entry point and model classes split across separate files - the most common project structure for a BoxLang application. Project Layout basic_project/ ├── main.bxs ← entry point (run this) └── models/ ├── ISpeakable.bxs ← interface definition ├── Animal.bxs ← base class └── Dog.bxs ← class that implements ISpeakable Running Run the project directly with the MatchBox interpreter from this directory: matchbox main.bxs Expected output: === MatchBox Basic Project === --- Descriptions --- I am Whiskers and I make the sound 'Meow' I am Rex and I make the sound 'Woof' --- Speak --- Meow! Rex barks: Woof! Woof! --- Dog Only --- Rex fetches the ball! Rex fetches the frisbee! --- Roster --- Whiskers - Cat Rex - Dog All done! Compile to Bytecode Compile to a portable .bxb bytecode file for faster repeated execution: matchbox --build main.bxs matchbox main.bxb Compile to a Native Binary Produce a single self-contained executable with no runtime to install. The file is the MatchBox runner plus your bytecode, about 4.7 MB on x86_64 Linux for this project in v0.11.0. Measure the file you produce: matchbox --target native main.bxs ./main Key Concepts Concept Where to look Class definition models/Animal.bxs Interface models/ISpeakable.bxs , implemented with implements="ISpeakable" in models/Dog.bxs Multi-file imports main.bxs ( import models.Animal ) Struct literals main.bxs (roster array) For-in loop main.bxs (roster iteration) How Multi-File Imports Work MatchBox resolves imports using dot-separated paths relative to the directory where matchbox is invoked. import models.Animal maps to models/Animal.bxs relative to the current working directory. Always run matchbox main.bxs from the basic_project/ directory so that the models.* imports resolve correctly.

title: BoxLang and Alpine.js
body: BoxLang + Alpine.js Example This example demonstrates how to define an Alpine.js Data Component using 100% BoxLang code. How it works Direct Access : The BoxLang script uses js.Alpine.data() to register a component. Normalization : The BoxLang struct returned by the component function becomes the JavaScript object that Alpine uses as the component's data. Closures : The increment , decrement and isEven functions in the struct are wrapped as JS functions that Alpine can call. Calls from HTML : The buttons in index.html call count = increment(count, step) . The BoxLang function receives the current values and returns the new count, which Alpine assigns. Write the component function with the function( initialValue = 0 ) { ... } form. An arrow function with a default parameter, ( initialValue = 0 ) => { ... } , does not parse in v0.11.0. Building the Example You must compile the BoxLang script into a JavaScript/WASM bundle using the MatchBox CLI. The build runs the wasm-bindgen command-line tool, so install wasm-bindgen-cli (or set the WASM_BINDGEN variable to its path) first: cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli matchbox --target js counter.bxs This produces: counter.js : The ES module entry point. index.html imports its ready and registerComponent exports. counter.wasm : The WASM binary containing the BoxLang VM and your compiled code (about 1.9 MB in v0.11.0). counter.d.ts and counter_bg.wasm.d.ts : TypeScript declarations. Running the Example Since browsers block WASM loading from file:// URIs, you must serve this folder using a local web server: # Using Python python3 -m http.server 8000 # Using Node.js (npx) npx serve . Then open http://localhost:8000 in your browser.

title: BoxLang Compatibility
body: BoxLang compatibility MatchBox is an independent runtime written in Rust. It reads BoxLang source but it is not the JVM runtime packaged differently, and it does not match BoxLang everywhere. This page lists what was run against MatchBox 0.11.0, and compares it with BoxLang 1.13 on the JVM where the behavior differs. How to read it: Each row was checked by running a snippet on the 0.11.0 CLI or in the playground , not by reading the roadmap. "BoxLang" means BoxLang 1.13 run from its jar. Fixes for several items below are in progress as GitHub issues and pull requests. None of them is in a released version. Check the release notes before relying on a fix. Feature matrix S means supported, P partial, U unsupported. Language Feature Status What was run Details Variables, #interpolation# , & S "Hello #name#" Language essentials Arrays, structs, ranges in for S for ( i in 1..3 ) Ranges if , switch , for , while , do , break , continue S Each ran Labeled continue outer; U Parse error: unexpected token in expression: : Rewrite with a flag Functions, defaults, named args, closures, arrows S ( a, b ) => a + b , greet( greeting = "Hi", name = "Bob" ) Closures over a function's own variables U adder( 5 )( 10 ) printed 10null Known issue 8 below Typed parameters ( numeric n ) P Accepted, not enforced: typed( "abc" ) returns abc . BoxLang throws. required parameters P Parsed, not enforced Known issue 13 below Functions called before they are defined U Can only call functions. BoxLang hoists them. Define functions first try , catch , finally , throw , rethrow P Work, but the type in catch ( Type e ) is ignored Error handling include , param name = value , assert S Each ran param name="q" default="d" U Parse error Use param q = "d"; Word operators eq neq gt gte lt lte is contains and or xor eqv S Each ran Operators Word operators not , mod , ne , imp U Parse error. y = 7 mod 3; silently stores 7 Known issue 16 below ??= U Parse error x = x ?: 3 Elvis ?: , safe navigation ?. , ternary, castAs , instanceOf S Each ran Operators Bitwise b& b\| b^ b~ b<< b>> b>>> S Each ran Set literal set{} , setNew , setOf , set operators P Work; add() does not deduplicate Sets Destructuring { a, b } = s and [ x, y ] = arr S Ran Destructuring Destructuring with ...rest , or after var U rest is silently null; var { a } = is a parse error Spread in arrays, structs and calls P Work; a duplicate key crashes the VM Spread lock and thread as script statements U Parse error: expected ':' or '=' in struct literal Use threadNew() Scopes variables , server , arguments P See the scopes page Scopes Scopes local , request , application U local.x = 1 fails with Member assignment only supported on structs... Known issue 17 below url , form , cookie , session , cgi P Only when serving templates with --serve Scopes Classes Feature Status What was run Details Inline class Name { } in a script S Ran Classes File-based class ( models/Pet.bx ), import , new models.Pet() S I am rex init , this , variables , onMissingMethod S Ran new C() when init has no return this U Returns null Known issue 1 below extends="P" , implements="I" , accessors="true" attributes S Ran class Dog extends Animal , class Dog implements Shape U Parse error: expected =, found identifier Known issue 14 below super U Variable 'super' not found in class or global scope. Known issue 5 below Parent init() when the child has none U Not called Known issue 6 below property name; with accessors P getName() and setName() work; setters return null Classes property name default="x" , property name="n" U Parse error Known issue 15 below private P Parsed, not enforced static function P Callable on an instance only. S::make() is a parse error. Data, libraries and templates Feature Status What was run Details JSON ( serializeJSON , deserializeJSON ) S Round trip ran Function reference Regular expressions ( reFind , reReplace ) S reFind( "[0-9]+", "ab123" ) is 3 Dates ( createDateTime , dateAdd , dateDiff , dateFormat ) P Ran; mask dialect and arity differ Known issues 3, 4 and 7 below File I/O ( fileWrite , fileRead , fileExists , fileDelete ) S Ran on the CLI XML ( xmlParse ), hashing, UUIDs, numberFormat S Ran Futures, runAsync , then , exceptionally P Ran; see the async page Async Queries ( queryNew , queryExecute , datasources) P Needs the bif-datasource build feature; PostgreSQL only; not in the browser Queries Query of queries U by default QoQ support is not enabled in this build unless built with qoq .bxm templates: set , output , if / else , script P Ran; set and output inside if lose the rest of the page Templates .bxm tags loop , switch , try , include , throw , import U Stubs Known issue 20 below CFML files and tags ( .cfm , .cfc , <cfoutput> ) U .cfm gives a parse error; <cfoutput> is printed as text Modules ( --module , ModuleConfig.bx ) S Ran Modules Java interop P ArrayList.add / size work, get( 0 ) fails Java interop Native Fusion (Rust modules) S See the example Native Fusion Capabilities by target Capability Native CLI or binary Browser Java interop Experimental. Needs a JDK on the host ( bif-jni , in the default features). Not available Queries and datasources Needs bif-datasource . qoq for query of queries. Neither is a default feature. queryNew is not defined Web scopes and .bxm templates With --serve Templates do not run in the playground File I/O Yes fileWrite is not defined See the build guides for the other targets: native builds , JavaScript and WASM and ESP32 . Known issues in 0.11.0 Every item was reproduced on the 0.11.0 CLI. Where a GitHub issue or pull request exists, it is linked. A linked pull request is work in progress, not a release. 1. new C() returns null when init() has no return this class C { function init() { x = 1; } function getX() { return 1; } } c = new C(); println( isNull( c ) ); println( c.getX() ); true Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Method getX not found on null. BoxLang returns the new instance whatever init returns. Workaround: end every init with return this; . Tracked in issue #76 , with a fix in PR #84 . 2. variables.n++ as a statement fails class K { function init() { variables.n = 0; return this; } function bump() { variables.n++; return variables.n; } } println( new K().bump() ); Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Fused increment only supported on structs and instances for now BoxLang prints 1 . Workarounds that run: variables.n += 1; , this.n++; and x = variables.n++; . ++variables.n is a parse error. Tracked in issue #77 , with a fix in PR #85 . 3. dateFormat, timeFormat and dateTimeFormat masks The masks follow Java DateTimeFormatter patterns, so mm is minutes and MM is the month. CFML-style mmm , mmmm , tt , nn , ddd and dddd are not translated. d = createDateTime( 2024, 3, 5, 14, 7, 9, 0 ); println( dateFormat( d, "yyyy-mm-dd" ) ); println( dateFormat( d, "yyyy-MM-dd" ) ); println( dateFormat( d, "MMM" ) ); println( dateFormat( d, "mmm" ) ); println( timeFormat( d, "hh:mm:ss a" ) ); println( timeFormat( d, "hh:mm:ss tt" ) ); Output: 2024-07-05 2024-03-05 Mar mmm 02:07:09 PM 02:07:09 tt BoxLang also prints 2024-07-05 for yyyy-mm-dd , but it throws Too many pattern letters: m for mmm and Unknown pattern letter: t for tt , where MatchBox prints the letters back without an error. Use Java masks: yyyy-MM-dd , MMM , HH:mm:ss , hh:mm:ss a , EEE . Tracked in issue #78 ; PR #87 mirrors BoxLang's behavior. 4. createDateTime needs all seven arguments d = createDateTime( 2024, 3, 5 ); Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: createDateTime() expects at least 7 arguments BoxLang accepts fewer and returns {ts '2024-03-05 00:00:00'} . Pass year, month, day, hour, minute, second and millisecond, or use createDate( 2024, 3, 5 ) . PR #87 relaxes the requirement. 5. The super keyword is not supported Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Variable 'super' not found in class or global scope. super.init() and super.method() both fail. BoxLang supports them. Repeat the parent's setup in the child, or move shared code into a method both classes call. Tracked in issue #82 . 6. Inherited init() is not called when the child has none With class Animal setting this.sound in init() and class Dog extends="Animal" defining no init() , new Dog().sound is null. BoxLang runs the parent's init . Define init() in the child and set the fields there. Tracked in issue #83 . 7. Named time zones use a fixed offset summer = createDateTime( 2024, 7, 1, 12, 0, 0, 0, "America/New_York" ); winter = createDateTime( 2024, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, 0, "America/New_York" ); println( dateTimeFormat( summer, "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm" ) ); println( dateTimeFormat( winter, "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm" ) ); Output: 2024-07-01 16:00 2024-01-01 16:00 Both lines print 16:00 , so the summer offset was applied to January too. The winter line should be 17:00 , and BoxLang prints 17:00 . Named zones come from a fixed-offset table and ignore daylight saving. Create the date in "UTC" , which keeps 12:00 as 12:00 , and add the offset yourself with dateAdd . Tracked in issue #86 . 8. Closures do not capture variables of the enclosing function function adder( n ) { return x => x + n; } println( adder( 5 )( 10 ) ); Output: 10null BoxLang prints 15 . The same happens for callbacks passed to map , each and runAsync inside a function: the function's parameters and locals read as null. Variables assigned at the top level of the script are visible. Inside a function, use a for loop instead of a callback. See scopes . 9. Starting futures inside map panics r = [ 1, 2, 3 ].map( n => runAsync( () => n * n ) ); println( r.len() ); In the playground this panics with Attempted to access collected object . On the CLI it prints 3 and then fails with Operands must be two numbers. from the tasks. BoxLang returns three futures. This is the capture bug above. Use asyncAllApply( [ 1, 2, 3 ], n => n * n ) , which returns [1,4,9] . 10. Member map and each callbacks get no index [ 10, 20 ].each( ( v, i ) => println( "each " & v & " " & i ) ); arrayEach( [ 10, 20 ], ( v, i ) => println( "arrayEach " & v & " " & i ) ); Output: each 10 null each 20 null arrayEach 10 1 arrayEach 20 2 The member form passes null as the index, and so do .map and arrayFilter . arrayEach and arrayMap pass it. BoxLang passes the index to each , map and filter . Use the function form of arrayEach and arrayMap , or count in a for loop. 11. slice( 2 ) returns an empty array a = [ 10, 20, 30, 40 ]; println( serializeJSON( arraySlice( a, 2 ) ) ); println( serializeJSON( arraySlice( a, 2, 2 ) ) ); println( serializeJSON( arraySlice( a, 2, 3 ) ) ); Output: [] [20] [20,30] The third argument is treated as an end position. BoxLang treats it as a length and returns [20,30,40] for slice( 2 ) and [20,30] for slice( 2, 2 ) . To get "from position 2 to the end", pass arrayLen( a ) as the third argument. 12. Tree shaking drops functions that are only called as members The CLI removes BIFs it thinks a program does not use. A call such as a.sort( "numeric" ) or a.first() is not seen as a use, so the CLI fails with BIF arraysort not found. or BIF arrayfirst not found. : a = [ 3, 1, 2 ]; println( serializeJSON( a.sort( "numeric" ) ) ); println( a.first() ); Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: BIF arraysort not found. Run it with --no-shaking and it prints [1,2,3] and 3 . It also prints them in the playground. arraySort( a, "numeric" ) works either way. The same happens to .slice() , .reject() on a set, and datasourceRegister() , which --keep datasourceRegister rescues. Use --no-shaking or --keep name1,name2 when you build, or call the function form. 13. A missing required argument does not throw function f( required x ) { return "ok"; } println( f() ); Output: ok BoxLang throws Required argument [x] is missing for function [f] . Validate arguments yourself with isNull( x ) . 14. class Dog extends Animal and implements are parse errors Parse Error: error: expected =, found identifier 2 | class Dog extends Animal { function speak(){ return "woof"; } } Only the attribute form parses: class Dog extends="Animal" implements="Shape" { } . See classes . 15. property with attributes is a parse error property name default="x"; fails with unexpected token in expression: default , and property name="n"; fails the same way. property string name; parses but does not define name , so its accessor fails. Only property name; works with accessors="true" . Set defaults in init() . 16. Missing operators and statements Code Result BoxLang x = 7 mod 3; No error, x is 7 1 not true Parse error Works x ??= 3; Parse error Parse error in 1.13 too outer: for ... with continue outer; Parse error Works lock name="x" { } Parse error Works thread name="t" { } Parse error Works The mod row is the one that can ship a wrong answer. Search ported code for mod . 17. The local , request and application scopes do not exist Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Member assignment only supported on structs, instances, JS objects, and native objects local.x = 1; , request.x = 1; and application.x = 1; all fail, in scripts and in served templates. BoxLang accepts them. Use var , a top-level variable, the session scope under --serve , or server . Also, at the top level of a script variables.k = 1; println( k ); prints null: write and read through the same spelling. 18. ...rest destructuring leaves rest null [ a, ...rest ] = [ 1, 2, 3 ]; and { p, ...others } = { p: 1, q: 2 }; run without error and leave rest and others null. BoxLang gives [ 2, 3 ] and { q : 2 } . Use arraySlice( a, 2, arrayLen( a ) ) . 19. Java interop passes numbers as doubles Exception in thread "Thread-4" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: argument type mismatch Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Invocation of get failed: Java exception was thrown That is list.get( 0 ) on an ArrayList : every number is sent to Java as a java.lang.Double , so int parameters are not matched. StringBuilder.append( "x" ) fails the same way, and static-only classes such as Math cannot be used. BoxLang runs all three. See Java interop . 20. <bx:loop> and other .bxm tags are stubs <bx:loop array="#[ 1, 2 ]#" item="i">...</bx:loop> compiles to an endless loop and never finishes. <bx:switch> , <bx:try> , <bx:include> , <bx:import> and <bx:throw> are stubs as well. Write loops, switches and includes inside <bx:script> . Tracked in issue #93 . Details are on the templates page . Also found while testing These are not tracked in the issues above. Problem Output Page The type in catch ( B e ) is ignored; the first catch block runs for any error Throwing type A into catch ( B e ) runs the B block Error handling set.add() , append() and addAll() do not deduplicate setOf( 1, 2 ).add( 2 ) makes size() 3 Sets A struct literal that spreads a struct and sets one of its keys crashes the VM { ...s, x: 9 } where s has x : CLI exits 134, playground panics Spread A second then() is applied to the first result's input runAsync( () => 2 ).then( v => v + 1 ).then( v => v + 100 ).get() is 102, not 103 Async for ( i in 1..<1 ) runs twice Prints i=1 then i=0 Ranges arguments holds declared parameters only, and arguments[ 1 ] is null g( 1, 2 ) with no declared parameters: arguments.len() is 0 Scopes 1 + "x" returns 1x BoxLang throws Can't cast [x] to a Number Operators ModuleConfig.bx written as class { } loses its settings Can only instantiate classes. warning Modules Libraries, APIs and integrations JVM libraries, Java APIs and BoxLang modules built for the JVM do not run in MatchBox. A MatchBox module is a different thing: a folder with ModuleConfig.bx , optional BoxLang functions and an optional Rust crate. See modules . Native http() differs from BoxLang's HTTP client. Porting checklist Run the program on the target you ship, not only in the playground. Search for the rows marked U above, especially mod , not , super , local. , request. and application. . End every init with return this; . Test builds with and without --no-shaking if you use member calls. Report differences in MatchBox GitHub Issues . Review the MatchBox changelog when evaluating a release.
