title: Build and ship
body: Build and ship Up to now you have run source files. MatchBox can also build them into something you can ship. This lesson uses a terminal, because a browser tab cannot create files. Start with this script, saved as hello.bxs . Run it here first to be sure it works. function greet( name ) { return "Hello, #name#!"; } println( greet( "world" ) ); Output: Hello, world! A native executable matchbox --target native hello.bxs ./hello MatchBox prints Native binary produced: hello . The result is one self-contained file that contains the runtime and your compiled program. You can copy it to another machine of the same operating system and architecture and run it with no MatchBox and no JVM installed. Build on each platform you want to support, and test the result there. Bytecode matchbox --build hello.bxs matchbox hello.bxb This compiles to a .bxb file instead. Add --strip-source to leave the source text out of the file. Unlike a native executable, a .bxb needs a compatible MatchBox on the machine that runs it. Where else can it run? The same script can be built for other places. Each has its own guide: Target Guide Native executable Native builds Browser and JavaScript JavaScript and WebAssembly Containers Docker image and WASM container AWS Lambda AWS Lambda Microcontrollers ESP32 Targets differ in what they can reach. A browser build has no files or sockets, for example, and a microcontroller has far less memory. Check the guide for the target you pick. Try it Build your own script as a native executable, run it, and check that it prints the same thing as matchbox yourscript.bxs .

title: Building for ESP32
body: Building for ESP32 matchbox --target esp32 cross-compiles the MatchBox ESP32 runner, flashes it, and writes your application to a flash partition. The standard runner is a small web application server: it starts Wi-Fi, listens for HTTP, and runs BoxLang files in response to requests. What the runner executes The runner executes only two things: the Application class (its onApplicationStart method) and the route files in the embedded app. It has no loader for a standalone script, so a file that only calls println and sleep is compiled but the device does not run it. Routes come from an app/ directory next to your entry script, not from web.server() calls. The entry script is still required on the command line. It is compiled and checked, but the routes are built from the files in app/ . my-device/ ├── main.bxs entry script passed to matchbox ├── Application.bx optional, runs onApplicationStart at boot ├── box.json optional build settings └── app/ ├── index.bxm GET / ├── status.get.bxs GET /status ├── print.post.bxs POST /print └── printer/ └── [id].bxm GET /printer/:id Route rules: Only .bxm (template) and .bxs (script) files under app/ become routes. index maps to the directory path. Other names map to a path segment, so app/about.bxm is /about . A method suffix before the extension sets the method: get , post , put , patch , delete , head or options . The default is GET . [name] in a file or directory name captures that segment as name . A route matches when the segment count is equal and each literal segment is equal. If several routes match, the first one in alphabetical path order wins. Application.bx is found next to the entry script or in src/main/bx/ . Each request runs the route file in a shared VM and responds as follows: Route file Response .bxm The captured output as text/html; charset=utf-8 . .bxs that writes output The captured output as text/html; charset=utf-8 . .bxs that writes nothing Its result value serialized as application/json . Error while running 500 with Embedded route execution failed: <error> . No route 404 with Embedded route not found . Inside a route the scopes are strings only: Scope Contents url Query parameters, then route parameters (a route parameter overwrites a query parameter of the same name). form Fields of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body. Other body types are not read. request Empty struct. cgi request_method , path_info and request_uri . Not available: sessions, cookies, static files, event.setView() , app.listen() , webhooks and WebSockets. Compile-time checks on the entry script reject app.listen() , event.setView() / event.renderTemplate() , app.middleware.buildStaticFiles() , webhook helpers, cookie helpers and session helpers. Prerequisites You need these on the development machine: Rust ESP32 toolchain , installed with espup : cargo install espup espup install ESP-IDF , a real checkout activated in your shell. MatchBox builds with ESP_IDF_TOOLS_INSTALL_DIR=fromenv so it uses the tools of the activated environment instead of downloading its own. espflash for flashing. ldproxy , the linker wrapper used by the runner: cargo install ldproxy A C toolchain, Python, CMake and Ninja, as required by ESP-IDF. A MatchBox source checkout. A build with --esp32-web compiles the runner from crates/matchbox-esp32-runner in the source tree the CLI was built from. Activate ESP-IDF and switch the Rust toolchain in the shell you run MatchBox from: source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp Do not layer other ESP export scripts on top of that shell. Without these variables the runner build fails. Check your setup matchbox esp32-doctor The command prints [ok] , [warning] or [fail] for each of: IDF_PATH , idf.py , RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN , cargo , cmake , ninja , ldproxy , espflash , LIBCLANG_PATH , ESP_IDF_ESPUP_CLANG_SYMLINK , the bundled esp32 , esp32s3 and esp32c3 stubs, a .cargo/config.toml in the current directory that forces an ESP target, and serial devices under /dev . It ends with a summary line and exits normally; read the [fail] lines. WSL users Attach the USB device to the Linux instance with usbipd-win , from a Windows Administrator PowerShell: usbipd list usbipd attach --busid <BUSID> --auto-attach Build and flash matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --full-flash Flag Meaning --target esp32 Build for ESP32. --esp32-web Build the routed web runner and embed the app/ routes. Required for the app/ model. Without it a web.server() call in the entry script is rejected at compile time. --chip <name> esp32 , esp32s2 , esp32s3 , esp32c3 , esp32c6 or esp32h2 . esp32c3 , esp32c6 and esp32h2 build for riscv32imc-esp-espidf ; the others for the matching Xtensa target. Any other value, and an omitted flag, builds for esp32 while still passing your text to espflash , so check the spelling. --full-flash Build the runner, flash the firmware with the project partition table, and write the app. Implies flashing. --flash Fast deploy: skip the firmware build and write only the app to flash. --watch Watch mode, see below. Implies flashing. --output <file> Where to write the firmware ELF. Default: the entry script with an .elf extension. A --esp32-web build always compiles the runner locally with cargo build --release --no-default-features --features embedded-web (adding psram when enabled). The route table is compiled into that firmware, and the runner falls back to it when the storage partition holds no valid app. Use --full-flash for the first flash, after changing chip, box.json or MatchBox, and whenever a fast deploy does not change what the device serves. A fast deploy compiles the routes, then writes a 4-byte little-endian length followed by the serialized route table with espflash write-bin and resets the board. Run it from the shell where espflash can open the serial port. Serial port permissions On Linux the build can succeed while flashing fails because your user cannot open the serial device (for example /dev/ttyACM0 ): groups sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER # or the serial group of your distribution, such as uucp Log out and back in before retrying. Do not rerun the whole matchbox ... --full-flash command with sudo ; that repeats the build as root. Build as your user, then flash the ELF with espflash (see Manual flash ). Watch mode matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --watch The first deploy is a full flash. The CLI detects the serial port with espflash board-info , falling back to /dev/ttyACM0 , /dev/ttyUSB0 , /dev/ttyACM1 or /dev/ttyUSB1 , and prints the device output by reading the port with stty and cat . When the entry script file is saved, it stops the reader, recompiles, rediscovers app/ , fast-deploys (three attempts) and restarts the reader. Only saves of the entry script itself trigger a redeploy. Saving a file under app/ does not; touch the entry script afterwards. Watch mode works on Unix-style systems that have stty and cat . Partitions The project partition table ( crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/partitions.csv , passed to espflash ) assumes 8 MB of flash ( CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_8MB ). Name Type Size nvs data, nvs 0x4000 otadata data, ota 0x2000 phy_init data, phy 0x1000 factory app 3 MiB coredump data, coredump 64 KiB storage data, subtype 0x81 0x2F0000 (about 2.9 MiB) The runner finds the storage partition by subtype, memory-maps it, and reads the app from it. Core dumps are written to flash ( CONFIG_ESP_COREDUMP_ENABLE_TO_FLASH ). Runner internals The runner starts a FreeRTOS task named matchbox-runner with a 24 KiB stack ( 24576 bytes) on core 0. A project with a native/ directory builds a Native Fusion runner instead, whose VM task has a 48 KiB stack. The HTTP server task stack is 6144 bytes. The background fiber thread has 8192 bytes. Request handling takes a garbage collection before and after each route. Standard BIFs such as println write to the serial console. HTTP server limits Setting Value max_sessions 2 max_open_sockets 2 max_uri_handlers 20 Methods routed to your files GET , POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE , HEAD , OPTIONS Port 80 unless webPort or MATCHBOX_ESP32_WEB_PORT is set at build time Built-in endpoints These paths are served by the runner and cannot be used by routes: Path Response /__matchbox HTML page with hostname, IP, features and route count. /__matchbox/ping pong as text. /__matchbox/status JSON with hostname , ip , features , heap , diagnostics , partitions and routes . /__matchbox/photo/<id> The captured photo with that id ( image/jpeg ), or 404 . /generate_204 , /gen_204 , /hotspot-detect.html , /library/test/success.html , /connecttest.txt , /ncsi.txt 302 redirect to http://192.168.4.1/ , for captive-portal checks when the device runs as an access point. Configuration Wi-Fi and port The runner's own Wi-Fi connection and its HTTP port are fixed when the firmware is built. Provide them in one of two ways: box.json in the directory where you run matchbox : { "esp32": { "board": "xiao-esp32s3-sense", "psram": true, "webPort": 80, "wifi": { "ssid": "my-network", "password": "my-password", "hostname": "my-device" } } } Environment variables set before running matchbox : Variable Equivalent Meaning MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID wifi.ssid Station network name. MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD wifi.password Station password. MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_HOSTNAME wifi.hostname Device hostname. Default matchbox-esp32 . MATCHBOX_ESP32_WEB_PORT webPort HTTP port. MATCHBOX_ESP32_BOARD board xiao-esp32s3-sense selects the XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense PSRAM settings. MATCHBOX_ESP32_PSRAM psram Setting the variable to any value enables PSRAM. These values are read when the runner is compiled, so they apply to --full-flash builds, not to a fast deploy. box.json values are exported by the CLI for that build. Keep real credentials out of version control. Alternatively connect from BoxLang in Application.bx . onApplicationStart runs before the runner opens its own connection, and a connection made there is reused: class { function onApplicationStart() { esp32WifiStation( "my-network", "my-password", "my-device" ); } } application.esp32.wifi.ssid , .password , .hostname and application.esp32.web.port are filled in before onApplicationStart and can be read in routes. Changing them does not reconnect Wi-Fi or move the HTTP port: the runner only prints them to the boot log. Features compiled into the runner Cargo feature Provides platform-web HTTP routing. Enabled by embedded-web . platform-mdns mDNS announcement. platform-bluetooth BLE (NimBLE), required by the printer functions. platform-printer Printer helpers, depends on bluetooth. platform-camera , platform-pins , platform-sdcard Listed in the crate's default set. psram PSRAM support. The CLI builds the web runner with --no-default-features --features embedded-web , so the BLE and printer functions below are in the firmware only when the runner is built with the platform-bluetooth feature, for example by running cargo build in the runner crate yourself. ESP32 functions Wi-Fi Function Returns esp32WifiStation( ssid, password, [hostname] ) Connects as a station. Returns { mode: "station", ip } . esp32WifiAccessPoint( ssid, [password], [channel=1] ) Starts an access point. Returns { mode: "accessPoint", ip } . esp32WifiStatus() { mode, ip } , with mode "off" and an empty ip when not connected. USB HID These functions make the board act as a USB keyboard and mouse through the ESP-IDF TinyUSB driver. Calls that need the device install the driver first with the product name MatchBox HID ; call esp32RegisterAsHID() first to choose another name. Commands go through a queue of eight, and each function returns true once the command is queued. An error is raised if the driver cannot be installed or the host has not mounted the device. Function Purpose esp32RegisterAsHID( [productName] ) Install the USB HID driver. esp32USBHidReady() true when the driver is installed and the host has mounted the device. esp32USBMouseMove( dx, dy ) Move the pointer. Each value from -128 to 127. esp32USBMouseClick( button ) Press and release. 1 left, 2 right, 3 middle; values 1 to 7 are accepted. esp32USBMouseDown( button ) , esp32USBMouseUp( button ) Hold and release a button. esp32USBMouseScroll( x, y ) Scroll. Each value from -128 to 127. esp32USBKeyboardPress( keycode ) , esp32USBKeyboardRelease( keycode ) Press and release a key by USB HID usage code, 0 to 255. esp32USBKeyboardReleaseAll() Release all keys. Each name also exists in the spellings esp32UsbMouseMove and esp32usbmousemove . Camera The camera functions are compiled in only for the esp32s3 chip, and use the pin presets of the XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense. Function Purpose esp32CameraCapture() Capture a JPEG and keep it in memory. Returns { id, format, imageUrl, bytes, width, height, version } . esp32CameraCaptureBitmap() Capture and convert to a monochrome bitmap { width, height, bytesPerRow, bytes } . esp32PhotoInfo( photo ) The capture struct for a stored photo. esp32PhotoUrl( photo ) /__matchbox/photo/<id>?v=<version> . esp32PhotoFree( [photo] ) Release a stored photo. esp32BitmapFromJpeg( bytes ) Convert JPEG bytes to the monochrome bitmap struct. photo is the struct returned by esp32CameraCapture() or its numeric id . BLE printer Available only in a runner built with platform-bluetooth (see above). The functions send TSPL commands over a BLE characteristic; the default characteristic is 00002af1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb . Function Purpose esp32BluetoothConnect( options ) Connect. options accepts address , addressType , namePrefix , characteristicUuid and timeoutMs (default 5000). Returns { handleId, deviceName, deviceId, writeMode, characteristicUuid } . esp32BluetoothDisconnect( handle ) Disconnect. esp32BluetoothWrite( address, characteristicUuid, payload ) Write bytes or text to a characteristic. esp32PrintTspl( payload ) Send TSPL to a printer. esp32PrintTsplTo( address, payload ) Send TSPL to a printer at an address. esp32PrinterPrintTspl( handle, payload ) Send TSPL over an open connection. esp32PrintHelloBoxLang() Print a test label. esp32PrinterCaptureBitmap( handle ) , esp32CaptureAndPrint() , esp32CaptureBitmapAndPrintTo( address, ... ) Capture a camera frame and print it. Also require the camera ( esp32s3 ). handle is the connection struct or its handleId . Troubleshooting Missing ldproxy If the runner build fails with linker ldproxy not found : cargo install ldproxy Stale build artifacts After changing ESP-IDF version, chip or shell environment, remove the runner build output and retry: rm -rf crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/target rm -rf target/esp32_stubs Manual flash If the ELF builds but the CLI cannot open the serial device, flash it with espflash : espflash flash \ --chip esp32s3 \ --port /dev/ttyACM0 \ --partition-table crates/matchbox-esp32-runner/partitions.csv \ main.elf

title: Building MatchBox from source
body: Building MatchBox from Source This guide covers how to clone, configure, and build custom versions of MatchBox. The facts here were checked against MatchBox 0.11.0 on Linux x86_64 with Rust 1.97. Cloning the Repository git clone https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox.git cd matchbox Prerequisites To build MatchBox, you need the Rust toolchain : Rust 1.85 or newer (the crates use the 2024 edition). Runner stubs build.rs builds a runner stub for the host on every build, and also tries to build two WebAssembly stubs. A missing target does not fail the build; the matching --target then fails at run time with runner stub for target '...' is not embedded . Rust target Needed for wasm32-wasip1 The wasi stub used by --target wasm and --target wasi . Both targets are currently broken, see the CLI reference . wasm32-unknown-unknown The web stub used by --target js . wasm32-wasip2 --target wasi-http , built on demand the first time it is used. rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 wasm32-unknown-unknown Web & WASM build wasm-bindgen CLI at exactly version 0.2.114, matching the pinned crate: cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version 0.2.114 . --target js runs it. Set WASM_BINDGEN to its path if it is not on PATH . ESP32 build (optional) Toolchain : Espressif Rust Toolchain (Xtensa), installed with espup install ESP-IDF : a full ESP-IDF environment activated with source <esp-idf>/export.sh Shell : export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp before building ESP32 artifacts Linker wrapper : cargo install ldproxy Flashing tool : espflash 3.3.0 or newer matchbox esp32-doctor checks these. Crate Overview The Cargo workspace has nine members. Two more crates live in the repository but are not workspace members. Crate Path Description matchbox / The CLI. Its build.rs builds the runner stubs and embeds them into the binary. matchbox_vm crates/matchbox-vm The execution engine: bytecode, fibers, the built-in functions, the JIT. matchbox_compiler crates/matchbox-compiler Parses BoxLang and BXM templates and emits bytecode. matchbox-macros crates/matchbox-macros Procedural macros for BIF registration and Native Fusion. matchbox_server crates/matchbox-server The web server behind --serve . Also a standalone matchbox_server binary with --app . matchbox_lambda_runner crates/matchbox-lambda-runner The AWS Lambda runtime, packaging and lambda deploy support. matchbox_wasi_http_runner crates/matchbox-wasi-http-runner The wasm32-wasip2 component that --target wasi-http fills with a webroot. matchbox_tui crates/matchbox-tui Terminal UI classes, registered when the bif-tui feature is on. matchbox_utility crates/matchbox-utility The shared --verbose logging switch. matchbox-embedded crates/matchbox-embedded Route manifests for embedded web apps on ESP32. matchbox_runner crates/matchbox-runner The runner stub. It has its own [workspace] , so it is built by build.rs and not as a workspace member. matchbox-esp32-runner crates/matchbox-esp32-runner The ESP32 firmware runner. Listed under exclude in the root Cargo.toml . The stub is the VM plus a loader that finds bytecode appended to its own file. Measured sizes for the 0.11.0 sources on Linux x86_64 with default CLI features: Stub file Bytes runner_stub_x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 4,751,936 runner_stub_wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm 2,647,829 runner_stub_wasip1.wasm 2,110,700 A --target native executable for a three-line script was 4,752,169 bytes, the stub plus 217 bytes of bytecode and a 16 byte footer. Sizes change with the features, the Rust version and the release, so measure your own output. Cargo features matchbox (root crate): Feature Default What it does bif-io yes File system functions ( fileRead , directoryList , and others). bif-http yes The http function, using reqwest with rustls. bif-crypto yes Hashing and encryption functions. bif-cli yes Terminal helpers such as cliGetArgs , cliExit and cliClear . bif-jni yes Java interoperability through a host JVM. jit yes The Cranelift JIT in the interpreter. See JIT . server yes --serve and --target wasi-http . Pulls in matchbox_server and tokio . bif-zip no Zip, tar and compression functions. bif-datasource no PostgreSQL datasources, configured in matchbox.toml . bif-tui no Registers the matchbox_tui native classes. qoq no Query of queries, in the VM and compiler. debugger no Compiles the VM's debug API ( start_debug_chunk , debug_step_source_line , and others) for embedders. The CLI has no flag that uses it. cross-compile no Makes build.rs also build runner stubs for the other targets and embed them. Release CLIs use it. The matchbox_compiler crate has two features: bxm (default) and qoq . bxm is declared but nothing in the code is gated on it, so BXM template parsing is always available. The server feature does not add a BXM transpiler. The matchbox_vm crate has no default features. It adds js (the browser host bridge) and js-host-abi to the list above. The root crate has no js feature. Which features reach the stubs build.rs forwards only bif-io , bif-http , bif-zip , bif-crypto and bif-cli to the runner stubs, and adds js to the web stub. A --target native executable therefore has no JIT, no JNI and no datasources, whatever the CLI itself was built with. Feature flags such as bif-datasource apply to matchbox app.bxs only. Build Examples 1. Local CLI (default) cargo build --release 2. CLI with cross-platform runners Builds runner stubs for Linux (x86_64, i686, aarch64, armv7), Windows (x86_64 and aarch64 MSVC, x86_64 GNU) and macOS (x86_64, aarch64), where the toolchain for each is available. On a Linux host the macOS stubs are skipped unless they already exist in stubs/ . cargo build --release --features cross-compile 3. Slimmer CLIs The matchbox_server crate always enables jit , bif-jni , bif-datasource , bif-zip , bif-crypto , bif-cli , bif-http and bif-io on matchbox_vm . Enabling the root server feature therefore turns all of them back on. cargo tree -e features shows cranelift-jit , jni , postgres and axum in the dependency tree for --no-default-features --features server,bif-io,bif-http . To leave the server, JIT, JNI and datasources out, do not enable server : cargo build --release --no-default-features --features bif-io,bif-http cargo tree for that command shows none of cranelift-jit , jni , postgres or axum . With this build --serve fails with Server feature not enabled in this build. To drop only the JIT, keep every default feature except jit and server : cargo build --release --no-default-features --features bif-io,bif-jni,bif-crypto,bif-cli,bif-http The JIT cannot be switched off while server is on. These two recipes were checked by inspecting the resolved dependency tree, not by building them. 4. Browser runtime for source strings The root matchbox crate cannot be used for this. It depends unconditionally on matchbox_lambda_runner , which pulls in zip , xz2 and the C library lzma-sys . cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --lib --no-default-features --features matchbox_vm/js failed here while compiling lzma-sys ( 'stdlib.h' file not found ). The root crate also has no js feature, so the --features js command from earlier versions of this page does not exist. Build a small crate that depends on matchbox_compiler and matchbox_vm instead, as the playground does (next section). For a ready-made browser module of your own program, use matchbox --target js . 5. ESP32 stub (directly) source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp cd crates/matchbox-esp32-runner cargo build --release --target xtensa-esp32s3-espidf --target esp32 expects the same environment to be active. Run MatchBox from that activated shell. The build script only builds ESP32 stubs when the esp toolchain is installed, and only rebuilds existing ones when MATCHBOX_REBUILD_EMBEDDED_STUBS is 1 , true or yes . It builds stubs for esp32 , esp32s3 and esp32c3 ; other chips fall back to a local build. The playground build The in-browser playground (published at /playground/ ) does not build the root crate. Its playground-runtime crate depends on matchbox_compiler and matchbox_vm with default-features = false , so it has no BIF libraries, no JIT and no JavaScript host bridge, and runs programs with the synchronous interpret_sync entry point. It is built with bash tools/build-runtime.sh , which compiles for wasm32-unknown-unknown and runs wasm-bindgen 0.2.114 , using RUSTFLAGS='--cfg getrandom_backend="wasm_js"' and a 128 MiB memory cap. Release builds CI publishes one full CLI per supported OS/architecture using --features cross-compile , plus Linux amd64 / arm64 Docker images built from those same binaries. Custom source builds do not create additional published distribution variants. Pushes to master publish the base version in Cargo.toml . After publication succeeds, CI advances develop to the next minor version and starts its snapshots. See releases and downloads for tags, channels, metadata, and checksum verification. Understanding build.rs build.rs in the root directory runs on every cargo build . It: Records the Git commit and build date for --version . MATCHBOX_BUILD_VERSION overrides the version string. Builds crates/matchbox-runner for the host and for the WebAssembly targets, into the stubs/ directory. A stub is rebuilt when a runner or VM source file is newer than it. With cross-compile , builds the other desktop stubs. Writes src/stubs.rs , a table of include_bytes! entries for every stub that exists. This file is regenerated by each build, so a local build leaves it modified in the working tree. Embedded stubs let matchbox package standalone targets without downloading a runtime. Not every target has a stub: ESP32 deployments need the local toolchain above. Optimization profiles The release profile in Cargo.toml is tuned for size: [profile.release] opt-level = "z" # Optimize for size lto = true # Link Time Optimization codegen-units = 1 # Maximum optimization panic = "abort" # Smallest error handling strip = true # Remove symbols For heavy server workloads you can set opt-level = 3 locally to trade binary size for speed.

title: Classes
body: Classes The classes lesson teaches the basics. This page lists what works and what does not in 0.11.0. Snippets with a Run button ran in the browser playground. Where a class can live Inline in a .bxs script, as in the snippets below. In a .bx file whose name is the class name. The header is class { ... } and the file name supplies the name. // models/Pet.bx class { function init( name ) { this.name = name; return this; } function speak() { return "I am " & this.name; } } // main.bxs import models.Pet; p = new Pet( "rex" ); println( p.speak() ); q = new models.Pet( "tom" ); println( q.speak() ); On the CLI this prints I am rex and I am tom . The playground has no file system, so file-based classes only work from the CLI or a build. Constructor, this and variables class Counter { function init( start = 0 ) { variables.n = start; this.label = "ctr"; return this; } function inc() { variables.n = variables.n + 1; return this; } function get() { return variables.n; } } c = new Counter( 1 ).inc().inc(); println( c.get() ); println( c.label ); println( isNull( c.n ) ); println( c instanceOf "Counter" ); println( new Counter( start = 7 ).get() ); Output: 3 ctr true true 7 this.x is public. variables.x is stored on the instance but is not visible from outside. init must return this new C() returns the value init() returns. Without return this , you get null. class C { function init() { x = 1; } function getX() { return 1; } } c = new C(); println( isNull( c ) ); println( c.getX() ); true Error: VM Runtime Error: ExpressionException: Method getX not found on null. BoxLang returns the instance regardless. This is issue #76 , with a fix in PR #84 . Until a release includes it, end every init with return this . Inheritance and interfaces The header takes attributes: extends="Parent" , implements="Interface" and accessors="true" . The BoxLang-style words class Dog extends Animal and class Dog implements Shape are parse errors ( expected =, found identifier ). interface Shape { function area(); } class Square implements="Shape" { function init( side ) { this.side = side; return this; } function area() { return this.side * this.side; } } class Animal { function init() { this.sound = "..."; return this; } function speak() { return this.sound; } function hello() { return "hi " & who(); } function who() { return "animal"; } } class Cat extends="Animal" { function init() { this.sound = "meow"; return this; } } class Dog extends="Animal" { function who() { return "dog"; } } println( new Square( 3 ).area() ); println( new Cat().speak() ); println( new Dog().hello() ); Output: 9 meow hi dog Not supported Feature MatchBox 0.11.0 BoxLang 1.13 super.method() and super.init() Variable 'super' not found in class or global scope. ( issue #82 ) Works. Inherited init() when the child has none Not called. new Dog().sound is null for the Dog above, which has no init . ( issue #83 ) Called. class Dog extends Animal Parse error Not tested. Use extends="Animal" . private Parsed, not enforced. new A().secret() runs. Enforced. S::make() Parse error: expected ), found :: Works. static { } blocks Parse error: unexpected token in expression: static Not tested. For super , the workaround is to repeat the parent's assignments in the child, or to call a helper method that both classes share. For the inherited init , define init in the child. Static functions static function parses and runs, but you call it on an instance: class S { static function make() { return 1; } function init() { return this; } } println( new S().make() ); This prints 1 . S.make() fails with Method make not found and S::make() is a parse error. Properties and accessors Use the bare form property name; . With accessors="true" the class gets getName() and setName() . class Person accessors="true" { property name; property age; function init() { return this; } } p = new Person(); p.setName( "Ann" ); p.setAge( 5 ); println( p.getName() & " " & p.getAge() ); println( isNull( p.name ) ); Output: Ann 5 true property name default="x"; is a parse error ( unexpected token in expression: default ), and so is property name="n"; . property string name; parses but does not create name : setName() then fails with Variable 'name' not found in class or global scope. Setters return null, so p.setName( "Ann" ).setAge( 5 ) fails with Method setAge not found . BoxLang setters return the instance. Call them as separate statements. The property is not readable as p.name from outside. BoxLang allows it. Other behavior class Ghost { function init() { return this; } function onMissingMethod( name, args ) { return "missing:" & name; } } println( new Ghost().anything() ); function typed( numeric n ) { return n; } println( typed( "abc" ) ); Output: missing:anything abc onMissingMethod works. Type hints on parameters are not enforced: typed( "abc" ) returns abc . A missing required argument does not throw: function f( required x ) { return "ok"; } f() returns ok . BoxLang throws Required argument [x] is missing for function [f] . println( instance ) prints <instance of Name> ; a toString() method is not used. You can add keys to an instance ( s.dyn = 5 ), but structKeyExists( s, "dyn" ) is false . @Name annotations parse in front of a function inside a class. At the top of a script, @Foo("bar") function f() {} is a parse error.

title: Classes and objects
body: Classes and objects A class bundles data with the functions that work on it. You create an object from a class with new . A first class class Counter { function init( start = 0 ) { variables.count = start; return this; } function increment() { variables.count = variables.count + 1; return this; } function get() { return variables.count; } } c = new Counter( 5 ); c.increment(); c.increment(); println( c.get() ); Output: 7 init is the constructor . It runs when you call new Counter( 5 ) . Always end init with return this . In MatchBox 0.11.0 a constructor without it gives you null instead of an object. variables.count is private state, stored inside the object. Code outside the class reaches it only through the methods. this is the object itself. Chaining Because increment returns this , calls can be chained: class Counter { function init( start = 0 ) { variables.count = start; return this; } function increment() { variables.count = variables.count + 1; return this; } function get() { return variables.count; } } println( new Counter().increment().increment().increment().get() ); Output: 3 Public data Values you store on this are public. That is simple, but it means anyone can change them. class Account { function init( owner, balance = 0 ) { this.owner = owner; variables.balance = balance; return this; } function deposit( amount ) { variables.balance = variables.balance + amount; return this; } function withdraw( amount ) { if ( amount > variables.balance ) { throw( type = "Funds", message = "Insufficient funds" ); } variables.balance = variables.balance - amount; return this; } function getBalance() { return variables.balance; } } account = new Account( "Ada", 100 ); account.deposit( 50 ).withdraw( 30 ); println( account.owner & " has " & account.getBalance() ); try { account.withdraw( 500 ); } catch ( Funds e ) { println( "Refused: " & e.message ); } Output: Ada has 120 Refused: Insufficient funds Here the owner is public on this , while the balance is private, so the only way to change it is through deposit and withdraw , which enforce the rules. The try and catch at the bottom are the subject of the next lesson. A class that holds a collection class Stack { function init() { variables.items = []; return this; } function push( value ) { variables.items.append( value ); return this; } function pop() { return variables.items.pop(); } function size() { return variables.items.len(); } } s = new Stack().push( 1 ).push( 2 ).push( 3 ); println( s.pop() ); println( s.size() ); Output: 3 2 Going further Inheritance, interfaces and the other class features are covered, along with where MatchBox differs from BoxLang on the JVM, in differences from BoxLang . Check there before relying on them: some forms of inheritance syntax are not supported yet. Try it Add a reset() method to Counter that sets the count back to zero and returns this .

title: CLI Reference
body: MatchBox CLI This page was checked against the matchbox CLI at version 0.11.0 (source src/lib.rs , plus runs of a release build on Linux x86_64). matchbox --help prints the same option list in short form. The CLI parses its arguments by hand, not with an argument-parsing library. That has consequences, described under Argument handling , that you should know before passing flags to your own scripts. matchbox [options] [file.bxs|file.bxm|file.bxb|directory] [script arguments] matchbox esp32-doctor matchbox lambda invoke <path> --event <event.json> matchbox lambda deploy <path> --function <name> --bootstrap <path> [options] Common commands Command Purpose matchbox Start the REPL . matchbox app.bxs Compile in memory and run a script. matchbox app.bxm Run a template file. matchbox app.bxb Run precompiled bytecode. matchbox src/ Run a directory, see Directories . matchbox --build app.bxs Write bytecode to app.bxb . matchbox --target native app.bxs Write a standalone executable for the current host. matchbox --target js app.bxs Write an ES module plus a .wasm file for browsers. matchbox --serve --webroot www Serve a directory over HTTP. matchbox --version Print the version, commit and build date. Options Option Takes a value Meaning -h , --help no Print usage and exit. -v , --version no Print version information and exit. --verbose no Print [LOG] lines on stderr. Only the --target js packaging step emits them in 0.11.0. --build no Compile to bytecode instead of running. --target <value> yes Package for a target, see Targets . Requires a file or directory, except wasi-http . --output <path> yes Output file path for --build , --target builds and wasi-http . --keep <a,b,c> yes Comma-separated list of standard library (prelude) functions that tree-shaking must keep. --no-shaking no Include the whole standard library prelude instead of only the functions the program uses. --no-std-lib no Leave the standard library prelude out entirely. --strip-source no Remove embedded source text from the compiled output. Errors still report file and line. --module <dir> yes Load a module directory. Repeatable. See Configuration . --serve no Start the built-in web server. Requires a build with the server feature, which is on by default. --host <address> yes Server bind address. Default 127.0.0.1 . Read only with --serve . --port <number> yes Server port. Default 8080 . Read only with --serve . --webroot <path> yes Server root, and the input of --target wasi-http . Default . . --chip <name> yes ESP32 chip: esp32 (default), esp32s2 , esp32s3 , esp32c3 , esp32c6 , esp32h2 . --flash no ESP32: flash the device after building. --full-flash no ESP32: flash the full firmware, not only the bytecode. Implies --flash . --watch no ESP32: rebuild and flash on file changes. Implies --flash , and the first build is a full flash. --esp32-web no ESP32: build the embedded routed web runtime. --fast-deploy no Deprecated. --flash is already a bytecode-only flash for ESP32. The ESP32 flags are covered in the ESP32 guide . Examples matchbox --build hello.bxs Compiled to hello.bxb matchbox --build --strip-source hello.bxs --output small.bxb Compiled to small.bxb For the three-line hello.bxs used in the quick start , the bytecode file is 217 bytes, or 137 bytes with --strip-source . --build does not create missing directories. matchbox --build hello.bxs --output out/x.bxb fails with Error: No such file or directory (os error 2) when out/ does not exist. Tree-shaking only affects the prelude, which is the part of the standard library written in BoxLang. A script that calls uCase and listLen compiled to 240 bytes by default and 23,014 bytes with --no-shaking . Targets --target selects which runner stub MatchBox appends your bytecode to, or which packaging path to use. Value Output Printed line Status in 0.11.0 native <name> ( <name>.exe on Windows) Native binary produced: hello Works. Marked executable on Unix. a Rust triple, for example aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu same as native Native binary produced: hello Works only if that stub is embedded. Release CLIs are built with --features cross-compile . See below. js <name>.js , <name>.wasm , <name>.d.ts , <name>_bg.wasm.d.ts Standalone JS module produced: ./hello.js Works. Needs wasm-bindgen 0.2.114 on PATH , or set WASM_BINDGEN . wasm <name>.wasm WASM binary produced: hello.wasm Broken, see the known issue below. wasi <name>.wasm none Fails, see the known issue below. wasi-http <webroot>.wasm , or --output WASI HTTP component produced: site.wasm Produces a component. Not run here. See below. esp32 <name>.elf , or flashes with --flash See the ESP32 guide . Any other value is treated as a Rust triple and looked up in the embedded stubs. If it is not embedded, the CLI stops with: Error: runner stub for target 'aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu' is not embedded A .bxb input is always run, never packaged: matchbox --target native hello.bxb runs hello.bxb and writes no executable. Compile from .bxs or .bxm source to package. Native and cross-compiled output --target native copies the runner stub for the current host, appends the serialized bytecode, an 8-byte length and the 8-byte marker BOXLANG\x01 , then writes the result. matchbox --target native hello.bxs ./hello Native binary produced: hello Hello, world! --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu produced the same executable on an x86_64 Linux build because that triple is the host. Other triples require a CLI built with the cross-compile Cargo feature, which makes build.rs build and embed more runner stubs. The list of triples is on the native builds page. A native executable does not parse MatchBox flags. Everything on its command line goes to the script, including -v and --help . Runner stub sizes, measured on 0.11.0 for Linux x86_64 with the default features: the native stub is 4,751,936 bytes (4.5 MiB) and hello.bxs produced a 4,752,169 byte executable. Details are on the native builds page. JavaScript output matchbox --target js hello.bxs Standalone JS module produced: ./hello.js The run wrote hello.js (50,747 bytes), hello.wasm (1,937,302 bytes) and the two .d.ts files. The bytecode is embedded in hello.js as base64. --output dist/hello.js creates dist/ and uses hello as the file stem. Without wasm-bindgen the command stops with wasm-bindgen not found. Install wasm-bindgen-cli or set WASM_BINDGEN. See JavaScript and WebAssembly . WASI targets Known issue: `wasm` and `wasi` in 0.11.0 Both container targets were run on a build with the wasm32-wasip1 stub embedded. --target wasi fails with WASI stub is missing the BOXLANG_EMBED sentinel. Rebuild the runner stub: cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 -p matchbox_runner . The runner crate contains no such sentinel, so rebuilding the stub does not help. --target wasm prints WASM binary produced: hello.wasm and writes the stub followed by 236 extra bytes. Node 22 refuses to compile that file: CompileError: WebAssembly.compile(): unknown section code #0xea . The appended custom section is written without a section header, so the module is invalid. The unmodified stub does run. Under Node's WASI implementation with the current directory preopened, it ran app.bxb and printed Hello, world! ; with no app.bxb it exits 1 with No embedded bytecode or app.bxb found . The runner looks for bytecode appended to its own file, which a WASI host cannot read, and then falls back to app.bxb . A workaround that produced a working module: put an empty native/ directory next to the script. That switches --target wasi to the Native Fusion path, which compiles a standalone module with the bytecode inside it. matchbox --target wasi hello.bxs --output out/hello.wasm printed WASI Fusion binary produced: out/hello.wasm , wrote 8,669,526 bytes after about 50 seconds, and the file printed Hello, world! under Node's WASI. This path needs a Rust toolchain with the wasm32-wasip1 target and the MatchBox source tree the CLI was built from, and the output directory must already exist. No wasmtime was available, so nothing was run in a standalone WASI runtime. For the browser, use --target js . If a build without the wasm32-wasip1 target installed is used, --target wasm and --target wasi both fail earlier with runner stub for target 'wasi' is not embedded . WASI HTTP --target wasi-http does not take a script. It packages a webroot into the prebuilt matchbox_wasi_http_runner component: matchbox --target wasi-http --webroot www --output site.wasm WASI HTTP component produced: site.wasm The run produced a 6,503,104 byte file from a one-page webroot. It was not executed. The webroot payload is limited to 4,194,292 bytes; larger roots fail with WASI HTTP webroot payload (... bytes) exceeds the embed capacity (4194292 bytes). The command needs the server feature and the wasm32-wasip2 Rust target. It reads target/wasm32-wasip2/release/matchbox_wasi_http_runner.wasm under the source checkout the CLI was compiled from and runs cargo build there if the file is missing, so it works from a source build, not from a downloaded binary. Running code Files Extension Behaviour .bxs and other source files Parsed and compiled in memory, then run. .bxm Parsed as a template, then run. .bxb Deserialized and run. Module discovery is skipped. Directories If the argument is a directory, MatchBox runs the first of index.bxs , main.bxs or Application.bx that exists in it, in that order. With none of them the command fails with No entry point found in directory . matchbox app from index Script arguments Everything after the file name is passed to the script. Read it with cliGetArgs() , which returns { options, positionals } . matchbox args.bxs first second --name=bob --flag Known issue: first argument dropped in interpreted runs cliGetArgs() always skips the first element of the argument list, because a compiled executable passes its own path first. An interpreted run passes only the script arguments, so the first one is lost. With the command above, args.bxs printing cliGetArgs().positionals sees one positional ( second ). The same script built with --target native and run as ./args first second --name=bob --flag sees both. Until this is fixed, pass a placeholder as the first argument when running with matchbox . REPL matchbox with no file starts a REPL: BoxLang REPL (Rust) Type 'exit' or 'quit' to exit. bx> x = 1 + 2 => 3 bx> println(x) 3 bx> exit The REPL reads one line at a time from standard input. It has no multi-line mode, history or tab completion. exit , quit or end of input (Ctrl+D) leaves it. Combining --build or --target with no file is an error: No filename provided for build/target . Argument handling The CLI looks for flags with args.contains(...) over the whole command line, including your script's arguments: -h , --help , -v and --version are matched anywhere. matchbox app.bxs -v prints the version and does not run app.bxs . Likewise --build , --verbose , --serve and the other flags are honoured wherever they appear. The file is the first argument that does not start with -- and is not the value of --target , --keep , --output , --module or --chip . The words native , wasm , wasi , wasi-http , js and esp32 are also never taken as the file. Unknown --flags are ignored without a message. A single-dash flag other than -h and -v is not recognised as a flag: matchbox -x app.bxs treats -x as the file name and fails. --port , --host and --webroot values are only read with --serve ( --webroot is also read for wasi-http ). A --port value that is not a number silently becomes 8080 . Native executables skip all of this, see Native and cross-compiled output . To pass -v or -h to a script, build it with --target native and run the executable. Server matchbox --serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --webroot www MatchBox Server listening on http://0.0.0.0:8080 Web root: www Rewrites: Disabled A www/index.bxm containing <bx:output>#1+1#</bx:output> returned 2 from /index.bxm , and www/a.txt was served as a static file. The server is a separate crate, matchbox_server . From the full CLI only --host , --port and --webroot are available. See the web server example . Subcommands esp32-doctor Checks the ESP32 toolchain: IDF_PATH , idf.py , RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN , cargo , cmake , ninja , ldproxy , espflash , LIBCLANG_PATH , ESP_IDF_ESPUP_CLANG_SYMLINK , the three embedded ESP32 stubs and serial devices. Each line starts with [ok] , [warning] or [fail] . It exits 0 even when it reports [fail] lines, so do not use its exit code in scripts. lambda Command Meaning lambda invoke <path> --event <file.json> Run a Lambda.bx file or project locally against an event and print the JSON response. lambda deploy <path> --function <name> --bootstrap <path> Package and deploy with the AWS CLI. Prints Created <name> or Updated <name> , then the function URL if one was requested. lambda deploy options: Option Default Meaning --function <name> required Function name. --bootstrap <path> required Bootstrap binary to include in the zip. --arch <arm64\|x86_64> arm64 Lambda architecture. Anything else fails with unsupported Lambda architecture . --out <zip> target/lambda/<function>.zip Where to write the package. --memory <MB> not set Function memory. Must be a number. --timeout <seconds> not set Function timeout. Must be a number. --role <arn> not set Execution role. --profile <name> , --region <name> not set AWS CLI profile and region. --public off Create a function URL with no authentication. --url off Create a function URL with IAM authentication. Using both --public and --url fails. lambda without invoke or deploy fails with Missing lambda command. Expected 'invoke' or 'deploy'. See the AWS Lambda guide . Environment variables Variable Read by Effect MATCHBOX_DEBUG compiler When set, prints Tree-shaking: included N prelude functions to stdout while compiling. BX_TRACE VM When set, prints a [TRACE] ip=... op=... stack=[...] line to stderr for every instruction. Very verbose. WASM_BINDGEN --target js Path of the wasm-bindgen executable. Default: wasm-bindgen on PATH . MATCHBOX_BUILD_VERSION build.rs Overrides the version string baked into --version . Default: the crate version. MATCHBOX_REBUILD_EMBEDDED_STUBS build.rs 1 , true or yes rebuilds the ESP32 stubs when building the CLI from source. BOXLANG_BYTECODE_PATH generated ESP32 Fusion build.rs Path of the bytecode file to embed. Set by the CLI. MATCHBOX_ESP32_BOARD , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WEB_PORT , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_HOSTNAME ESP32 runner build Compile-time settings. The CLI sets them from the esp32 block of box.json . MATCHBOX_ESP32_PSRAM ESP32 build Any value enables PSRAM, as does "psram": true in box.json . MATCHBOX_EMBEDDED_ROUTE_TABLE ESP32 build Route table path. Set by the CLI. IDF_PATH , RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN , LIBCLANG_PATH , ESP_IDF_ESPUP_CLANG_SYMLINK ESP32 builds, esp32-doctor Toolchain locations, see the ESP32 guide. CARGO Fusion builds Cargo executable used for Native Fusion builds. Default cargo . Scripts can read any environment variable with getSystemSetting("NAME", "default") . Configuration files MatchBox reads matchbox.toml , box.json and the modules/ and boxlang_modules/ directories from the current working directory, not from the script's directory. See Configuration for their contents. Exit codes Code When 0 The script, build or REPL finished normally. Also esp32-doctor in every case. 1 A CLI error such as a missing file, an unknown target, a parse error or a script error that was not caught. Messages begin with Error: on stderr. A native executable prints Runtime Error: instead. n A script that calls cliExit(n) . $ matchbox err.bxs a Error: VM Runtime Error: CustomException: boom > 1 | println("a"); throw("boom"); Files MatchBox writes If the CLI panics, it writes the panic report and a backtrace to panic_debug.txt in the current directory. Native executables built from the runner stub do not install this hook. The JIT compiler, when it compiles a loop or function, prints [JIT] ... status lines to stderr, not stdout. See JIT compilation .

title: Configuration
body: Configuration The MatchBox CLI has no global config file. Behaviour comes from command-line options, environment variables and three project files that it looks for in the current working directory: Path Used for matchbox.toml Module paths and datasources. box.json Module dependencies and the esp32 block. modules/ , boxlang_modules/ Module directories that are scanned automatically. All three are resolved against the directory you run matchbox from, not the directory of the script. Running matchbox /path/to/app.bxs from another directory does not see /path/to/modules . A .bxb file skips module discovery because its modules were resolved when it was compiled. Modules Module discovery runs whenever MatchBox compiles source. It collects module directories from four places, in this order. A later source replaces an earlier entry with the same name. box.json dependencies and devDependencies . A value that starts with . or contains / or \ is a path, relative to the current directory, if it exists. Any other value is ignored and the dependency name is looked up in modules/<name> and then boxlang_modules/<name> . matchbox.toml [modules.<name>] tables. Every subdirectory of modules/ and boxlang_modules/ that contains a ModuleConfig.bx , unless a module with that name was already found. Each --module <dir> option. The module name is the directory's name. Every module must contain a ModuleConfig.bx ; otherwise the build stops with Module '<name>' at '<path>' is missing ModuleConfig.bx . modules/greeter/ ModuleConfig.bx bifs/shout.bxs class ModuleConfig { function configure() { this.settings = { greeting: "Howdy" }; return this.settings; } function onLoad() {} } What MatchBox does with a module: The source of every bifs/*.bxs and bifs/*.bx file is added to the standard library prelude, so the functions inside are callable by name. ModuleConfig.bx is run once at compile time in a separate VM: onLoad() first, then configure() . The returned struct is baked into the program and read back with getModuleSettings("<name>") . If the lifecycle fails, MatchBox prints a warning and the settings are an empty struct. A matchbox/Cargo.toml inside the module marks it as a native module and switches the build to Native Fusion . With the module above in modules/greeter/ , this script run from the project directory printed HI! and Howdy : println(shout("hi")); println(getModuleSettings("greeter").greeting); The same script run from another directory failed with Can only call functions. , because modules/ was not found. With --module ./mymod the settings name is mymod , not greeter , so getModuleSettings("greeter") returned null . matchbox.toml [modules.greeter] path = "mymod" # relative to the working directory, or absolute [datasources.main] driver = "postgresql" # "postgres" is accepted too host = "localhost" # default port = 5432 # default database = "app" username = "app" password = "secret" maxConnections = 10 # default driver , database , username and password are required in each [datasources.*] table. Datasources are registered only when a source file is run (not when it is built) and only by a CLI built with the bif-datasource Cargo feature, which is off by default. The only driver is PostgreSQL; another driver value prints Warning: datasource '<name>' has unknown driver '<driver>', skipping. box.json Module dependencies are read as described above. For ESP32 builds the CLI also reads an esp32 block: { "esp32": { "board": "xiao-esp32s3-sense", "psram": true, "webPort": 8080, "wifi": { "ssid": "my-network", "password": "my-password", "hostname": "matchbox-device" } } } All keys are optional. The CLI passes them to the ESP32 runner build as MATCHBOX_ESP32_BOARD , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WEB_PORT , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID , MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD and MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_HOSTNAME . "psram": true enables PSRAM, as does setting MATCHBOX_ESP32_PSRAM to any value. box.json is only parsed for the esp32 block when the target is esp32 . See the ESP32 guide . Cargo features These apply when you build MatchBox from source. See Building MatchBox for the table of features, their defaults and the slim-build recipes.

title: Destructuring, spread and ranges
body: Destructuring, spread and ranges Snippets with a Run button ran in the browser playground, and the CLI printed the same output. Destructuring Pull values out of a struct or an array in one statement. { name, age } = { name: "Ann", age: 30 }; println( name & " is " & age ); { name: who } = { name: "Bob" }; println( who ); [ first, second ] = [ 10, 20, 30 ]; println( first & "," & second ); { a, b } = { a: 1 }; println( isNull( b ) ); Output: Ann is 30 Bob 10,20 true A struct pattern matches by key. { name: who } renames. A key that is missing from the struct leaves the variable null. Destructuring works inside functions too. Limits Form Result in MatchBox 0.11.0 BoxLang 1.13 on the JVM [ a, ...rest ] = [ 1, 2, 3 ] Parses, but rest is null with no error. rest is [ 2, 3 ] . { p, ...others } = { p: 1, q: 2 } Parses, but others is null with no error. others is { q : 2 } . [ x, y ] = [ 1 ] Fails with Array index out of bounds . y is null. var { a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 } Parse error: expected identifier, found { . Supported. Workaround for the rest of an array: arraySlice( a, 2, arrayLen( a ) ) . Spread ... expands an array into an array literal or a call, and a struct into a struct literal. base = [ 1, 2 ]; println( serializeJSON( [ 0, ...base, 3 ] ) ); println( serializeJSON( [ ...base, ...base ] ) ); defaults = { color: "red" }; println( serializeJSON( { ...defaults, size: 9 } ) ); function add( p, q ) { return p + q; } println( add( ...[ 3, 4 ] ) ); Output: [0,1,2,3] [1,2,1,2] {"color":"red","size":9} 7 Not supported: A rest parameter such as function f( ...nums ) is a parse error ( expected identifier, found ... ). Destructuring in a parameter list, function f( { a, b } ) , is a parse error too. A struct literal that spreads a struct and also sets one of its keys crashes the VM, in either order. { ...defaults, color: "blue" } aborts the CLI with exit code 134 and panics in the playground. To override a key, copy and append: merged = duplicate( defaults ); structAppend( merged, { color: "blue" } ); . Ranges a..b is an inclusive range and a..<b stops before b . Both are meant for for ... in . for ( i in 1..3 ) { println( "up " & i ); } for ( i in 3..1 ) { println( "down " & i ); } for ( i in 1..<4 ) { println( "short " & i ); } n = 3; for ( i in 1..n ) { println( "var " & i ); } total = 0; for ( i in 1..100 ) { total += i; } println( total ); Output: up 1 up 2 up 3 down 3 down 2 down 1 short 1 short 2 short 3 var 1 var 2 var 3 5050 A range stored in a variable prints as 1..5 and arrayLen( r ) returns its size. It is not an array: r.len() and r.toArray() fail with Method ... not found . arrayMap( 1..3, fn ) fails with Invalid access: base must be array or struct . a[ 2..3 ] fails with Array index must be a number . for ( i in 1..<1 ) runs twice, with i set to 1 and then 0. 1..<1 should be empty. Guard it with if ( start < end ) . For a slice of an array use arraySlice . Its third argument is an end position in 0.11.0, not a length: arraySlice( [ 10, 20, 30, 40 ], 2, 3 ) returns [ 20, 30 ] , and arraySlice( a, 2 ) with no third argument returns an empty array. See also operators and sets .

title: Docker image
body: Docker Image MatchBox publishes a general-purpose Docker image to GitHub Container Registry: ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox The image supports Linux amd64 and arm64 . CI packages the same full CLI binaries published in GitHub releases using Dockerfile.release ; the original Dockerfile remains available for local source builds. The image runs the main matchbox CLI as its entrypoint. That makes it useful for CI builds, direct script execution, bytecode compilation, native executable generation, and webroot serving without installing MatchBox on the host. Tags Stable releases publish: Tag Description latest Most recent stable release vX.Y.Z Specific release version, matching the Git tag/Cargo version Develop snapshots publish: Tag Description vX.Y.Z-snapshot Refreshed snapshot image for the next base version develop Latest build from the develop branch snapshot Rolling snapshot alias be Rolling BE/development image alias Pull the stable image: docker pull ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest Pull the current develop image: docker pull ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:develop Basic Usage The container workdir is /app . Mount your project there and pass normal MatchBox arguments: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --help docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --version docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest my_script.bxs Because matchbox is the entrypoint, arguments after the image name are passed directly to MatchBox. Docker selects the matching image architecture automatically; use --platform linux/amd64 or --platform linux/arm64 when selecting it explicitly. The CLI's --version output and the image's org.opencontainers.image.version label include the build number, for example 0.12.0-snapshot+133 . Tags omit the +133 suffix. After a stable release succeeds, CI advances develop to the next minor version and builds its snapshot. See releases and downloads . Build Artifacts Compile bytecode into the mounted project directory: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --build my_script.bxs Build a native Linux artifact: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --target native my_app.bxs Native artifacts produced inside the container target Linux. Use the release binaries or source builds when you need macOS or Windows native artifacts. The image holds only the CLI binary and CA certificates (see Dockerfile.release ). It has no Rust toolchain and no wasm-bindgen , so --target js and Native Fusion builds (a native/ directory) cannot run inside it. --target wasm and --target wasi are not usable in 0.11.0, see WASM container deployment . Webroot Server To serve .bxm templates and static files, bind the server to 0.0.0.0 inside the container and publish the port: docker run --rm \ -p 8080:8080 \ -v "$PWD/www:/app" \ ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest \ --serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --webroot /app Then open http://localhost:8080 . CI Example Use the image in a CI job when you only need the MatchBox CLI: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --build src/main.bxs docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" ghcr.io/ortus-boxlang/matchbox:latest --target native src/main.bxs For production and repeatable CI, pin a stable version tag such as v0.11.0 or an image digest instead of latest . Snapshot tags, including vX.Y.Z-snapshot , are mutable and are not immutable build pins.

title: Error handling
body: Error handling The errors lesson covers the basics. Snippets with a Run button ran in the browser playground and on the CLI with the same output. try, catch, finally try { throw( type = "MyError", message = "boom", detail = "more", errorCode = "E1" ); } catch ( any e ) { println( e.type & " | " & e.message & " | " & e.detail & " | " & e.errorCode ); } finally { println( "finally runs" ); } try { x = 1 / 0; } catch ( any e ) { println( e.type & ": " & e.message ); } try { throw "plain text"; } catch ( any e ) { println( e.message ); } try { try { throw "inner"; } catch ( any e ) { rethrow; } } catch ( any e ) { println( "outer got " & e.message ); } function f() { try { return "from try"; } finally { println( "cleanup" ); } } println( f() ); Output: MyError | boom | more | E1 finally runs ExpressionException: Division by zero plain text outer got inner cleanup from try The caught value is a struct. It holds only what throw was given, plus stackTrace . throw( type = "A" ) gives e.message as null, and structKeyExists( e, "type" ) is false for throw( message = "x" ) . Errors raised by the VM have e.type set to ExpressionException , for example division by zero or calling an undefined function. catch ( e ) without the any keyword is accepted. An uncaught error prints Error: ... with the source line and the CLI exits with status 1. Catch types are ignored The type in catch ( SomeType e ) is parsed and then ignored. The first catch block always runs, whatever was thrown. try { throw( type = "A", message = "m" ); } catch ( B e ) { println( "B" ); } catch ( A e ) { println( "A" ); } This prints B . BoxLang prints A . Two more consequences: A typed catch placed before catch ( any e ) swallows everything. catch ( "Custom.Sub" e ) with a quoted type is a parse error. Workaround: use one catch ( any e ) and branch on e.type , then rethrow what you do not handle. function risky( kind ) { throw( type = kind, message = "failed: " & kind ); } for ( kind in [ "NotFound", "Denied", "Other" ] ) { try { risky( kind ); } catch ( any e ) { if ( e.type == "NotFound" ) { println( "404 " & e.message ); } else if ( e.type == "Denied" ) { println( "403 " & e.message ); } else { println( "unhandled " & e.type ); } } } Output: 404 failed: NotFound 403 failed: Denied unhandled Other Asynchronous errors An error inside a runAsync callback surfaces when you call get() . See async and futures .

title: Errors and control flow
body: Errors and control flow Choosing a path temperature = 22; if ( temperature > 30 ) { println( "hot" ); } else if ( temperature > 15 ) { println( "pleasant" ); } else { println( "cold" ); } day = 3; switch ( day ) { case 1: println( "Monday" ); break; case 3: println( "Wednesday" ); break; default: println( "some other day" ); } Output: pleasant Wednesday switch needs a break at the end of each case, otherwise execution falls through into the next one. Skipping and stopping continue skips to the next round of a loop, and break leaves the loop. for ( i = 1; i <= 6; i++ ) { if ( i == 2 ) { continue; } if ( i == 5 ) { break; } println( i ); } Output: 1 3 4 Handling errors When something goes wrong, code throws an error. If nothing catches it, the script stops. A try block lets you catch the error and carry on. try { println( "before" ); throw "something broke"; println( "never printed" ); } catch ( any e ) { println( "caught: " & e.message ); } finally { println( "always runs" ); } Output: before caught: something broke always runs catch ( any e ) catches every kind of error. finally runs whether or not an error happened, which makes it the right place for cleanup. Built-in errors The runtime throws errors of its own, for example when you divide by zero. try { println( 10 / 0 ); } catch ( any e ) { println( "caught: " & e.message ); } Output: caught: Division by zero Your own error types Give an error a type so callers can catch exactly the problems they know how to handle. function parseAge( text ) { if ( !isNumeric( text ) ) { throw( type = "BadInput", message = "'" & text & "' is not a number" ); } return text + 0; } try { println( parseAge( "36" ) ); println( parseAge( "old" ) ); } catch ( BadInput e ) { println( e.type & ": " & e.message ); } Output: 36 BadInput: 'old' is not a number Try it Change the second call to parseAge( "42" ) and run again. Then add a catch ( any e ) after the BadInput one and throw a different kind of error to see which handler runs.

title: ESP32 Camera Streamer
body: ESP32 camera streamer This example shows a BoxLang script calling native Rust functions for cameraInit() , cameraTake() , and serialWrite() . The script sends ten byte arrays over the serial interface. [!warning] Camera capture is simulated The current Rust implementation does not initialize an ESP32 camera or capture real frames. cameraInit() reports simulated success, and cameraTake() returns a fixed ten-byte sample. Only serialWrite() writes the supplied bytes to UART0. The example is useful for exploring how a Rust runner can register native BIFs for BoxLang code. It is not a working camera firmware project. Build A native/ directory next to the entry script makes MatchBox build a Native Fusion runner for the board. That runner executes the compiled script directly instead of serving routes: source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --chip esp32s3 --full-flash The native code calls esp_idf_sys , so the project needs the ESP toolchain from the ESP32 guide . That guide also covers the routed app model and the real camera functions ( esp32CameraCapture() on esp32s3 ). For a project that serves pages, start from the regular ESP32 example .

title: ESP32 example
body: ESP32 example This example is a small web app for an ESP32 board. The device joins Wi-Fi and serves the files under app/ . esp32/ ├── main.bxs entry script passed to matchbox ├── Application.bx runs onApplicationStart at boot └── app/ ├── index.bxm GET / ├── hello/[name].bxm GET /hello/:name └── echo.post.bxs POST /echo The ESP32 runner does not run standalone scripts. It runs Application.bx and the route files in app/ . main.bxs is only the entry point for the command line. See Building for ESP32 for the full model. Run it Connect the board over USB and note its chip ( esp32 , esp32s3 , esp32c3 , ...). Activate ESP-IDF and the Rust ESP toolchain in your shell: source /path/to/esp-idf/export.sh export RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=esp matchbox esp32-doctor Set your Wi-Fi network for the build, then build and flash from this directory: export MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_SSID="my-network" export MATCHBOX_ESP32_WIFI_PASSWORD="my-password" matchbox main.bxs --target esp32 --esp32-web --chip esp32s3 --full-flash You can put the same values in a box.json in this directory instead; see the guide. Watch the serial output and wait for the line that prints the address of the HTTP server: espflash monitor Open the address in a browser, or use curl: curl http://<device-ip>/ curl http://<device-ip>/hello/ESP32 curl -d "msg=hi" http://<device-ip>/echo curl http://<device-ip>/__matchbox/status /__matchbox/status is served by the runner and reports heap, partitions and the list of routes, which is a quick way to confirm which app is on the device. Change the app Edit a file under app/ and run the same command again with --flash instead of --full-flash to write only the app. If the device keeps serving the old pages, repeat with --full-flash . With --watch in place of --full-flash , saving main.bxs redeploys the app. Saving a file under app/ does not trigger a redeploy on its own.
