title: Functions and callbacks
body: Functions and callbacks Functions function greet( name, greeting = "Hello" ) { return greeting & ", " & name; } println( greet( "Ada" ) ); println( greet( "Ada", "Hi" ) ); println( greet( greeting = "Hey", name = "Linus" ) ); Output: Hello, Ada Hi, Ada Hey, Linus A parameter with = has a default. You can also pass arguments by name , in any order. Functions can call themselves: function factorial( n ) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial( n - 1 ); } println( factorial( 10 ) ); Output: 3628800 Arrow functions An arrow function is a short, nameless function. It is often passed to another function. double = n => n * 2; add = ( a, b ) => a + b; println( double( 4 ) ); println( add( 2, 3 ) ); Output: 8 5 Map, filter and reduce Arrays come with three workhorses. map transforms every item, filter keeps some of them, and reduce folds the array down to one value. words = [ "box", "lang", "match" ]; println( words.map( w => w.ucase() ).toList( " " ) ); println( words.filter( w => w.len() > 3 ).toList( "," ) ); println( words.reduce( ( total, w ) => total + w.len(), 0 ) ); nums = [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 ]; sumOfSquares = nums .filter( n => n % 2 == 0 ) .map( n => n * n ) .reduce( ( a, n ) => a + n, 0 ); println( sumOfSquares ); Output: BOX LANG MATCH lang,match 12 56 each , every and some work the same way. every is true when the callback is true for all items, some when it is true for at least one. println( [ 1, 2, 3 ].every( n => n > 0 ) ); println( [ 1, 2, 3 ].some( n => n > 2 ) ); [ "a", "b" ].each( v => println( "item " & v ) ); Output: true true item a item b Functions as values A function is a value, so you can pass one to another function. function apply( fn, value ) { return fn( value ); } println( apply( s => s.ucase(), "shout" ) ); println( apply( n => n + 1, 41 ) ); Output: SHOUT 42 Known limitation in 0.11.0 An arrow function can read and update variables at the top level of your script. A function that returns another function which uses the outer function's own variables (a counter factory, for example) does not capture those variables correctly yet: they read as null . Until that is fixed, keep state in a class instead. Try it Write an arrow function isLong that returns true for words longer than 4 letters, then use it with filter on the words array.

title: HTTP requests
body: HTTP Requests Native MatchBox includes http() when built with the bif-http feature (enabled by default). Requests run in-process; no curl executable or shell is needed. This also works in standalone native binaries . Make a Request http() returns a future. Call .get() to wait for completion, then deserialize its JSON result: response = jsonDeserialize(http({ url: "https://example.com/", timeout: 10 }).get()); println(response.status); println(response.body); The response contains: Field Meaning status Numeric HTTP status, such as 200 or 404 . body Response text, when not downloading to a file. file_content The same response text as body . file_path Destination path, when downloading to a file instead of returning text. For a JSON API, deserialize response.body separately to obtain the API's data. HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses are returned normally; check status before using the body or downloaded file. Request Options Pass a struct with these case-insensitive keys: Option Default Behavior url Required HTTP or HTTPS URL. method "GET" GET , POST , PUT , or DELETE ; case-insensitive. headers None Struct of header names and values. body None Request body as text. Serialize JSON explicitly when needed. path None Write the response body to this file instead of returning text. timeout 30 Total network request deadline in seconds , including connection, redirects, and response-body reads/downloads. 0 disables this deadline. connectionTimeout 0 Connection deadline in seconds , including DNS, TCP, and TLS setup. 0 means no separate connection deadline; timeout still applies. redirect true Follow at most 10 redirects. false returns the original 3xx response without requesting its target. noProxy false true bypasses system/environment proxies for this request only. Otherwise normal proxy settings apply. ipv4Only false true restricts outgoing connections to IPv4, including connections made after redirects. Otherwise normal IPv4/IPv6 selection applies. Both deadlines accept non-negative finite numbers, including fractional seconds. Negative, non-numeric, infinite, NaN, or out-of-range durations are rejected. The three boolean controls require actual true / false values, not strings or numbers. Explicit null is invalid for these five controls; omit a key to use its default. The total deadline is not an inactivity timeout: receiving another chunk does not restart it. If both deadlines are enabled, whichever expires first ends the request. ipv4Only controls this machine's connections. When using a proxy, the proxy chooses its own upstream route. Combine ipv4Only: true with noProxy: true when you need a direct IPv4 connection. Probe a Private Service With apiKey loaded from your application's configuration: try { response = jsonDeserialize(http({ url: "http://private-agent:8642/api/sessions?limit=1", headers: { Authorization: "Bearer " & apiKey }, timeout: 5, connectionTimeout: 2, redirect: false, noProxy: true, ipv4Only: true }).get()); println("HTTP status: " & response.status); } catch (any error) { println("Probe failed: " & error.message); } Headers stay in-process rather than being passed to a child command's arguments. Avoid logging request structs, credentials, or sensitive response bodies. HTTPS certificate verification remains enabled; these options do not disable TLS checks. Downloads and Failures response = jsonDeserialize(http({ url: "https://example.com/archive.zip", path: "archive.zip.tmp", timeout: 60 }).get()); A download overwrites an existing destination once response headers arrive. An interrupted download can leave a partial file. Use a temporary destination, check the status and any required checksum, and only then move it into place. Invalid control values throw immediately from http() , before a connection is opened or the destination is touched. Transport and file errors reject the future and throw when .get() is called. Timeouts report HTTP request timed out . Transport diagnostics omit the request URL and do not include header values or request bodies. The positional forms remain available with default controls: http(url) , http(url, method) , and http(url, method, path) . Use the struct form to configure headers, body, or request controls. Runtime Compatibility This page describes native MatchBox , not the JVM HTTP client or browser fetch. MatchBox's request struct, future, and JSON result are distinct from JVM BoxLang's fluent HTTP client. The timeout , connectionTimeout , and redirect names follow BoxLang terminology; noProxy and ipv4Only are native MatchBox extensions. Do not assume these examples are drop-in JVM code. Successful HTTP future completion is not implemented for WASM/browser builds. These options do not add WASM HTTP support. See Differences from BoxLang .

title: Install and run
body: Install and run The browser is great for learning, but real projects live on your machine. This lesson installs MatchBox and runs the same script from a terminal. Install with MVM MVM is the MatchBox Version Manager. It installs releases side by side and switches between them. On Linux and macOS: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox-quick-installer/main/install/install.sh | bash On Windows PowerShell: irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ortus-boxlang/matchbox-quick-installer/main/install/install.ps1 | iex Restart your shell, then install and activate the latest MatchBox: mvm install latest mvm use latest matchbox --version The last command prints the version, for example matchbox version 0.11.0 . If matchbox is not found, run mvm doctor . The installation page covers other options. Run a script Save this as hello.bxs . Press Run to try it here first. function greet( name ) { return "Hello, #name#!"; } println( greet( "world" ) ); Output: Hello, world! Then run it from your terminal: matchbox hello.bxs MatchBox parses the file, compiles it to bytecode and runs it, all in one step. Compile to bytecode You can compile once and run the result many times: matchbox --build hello.bxs matchbox hello.bxb A .bxb file holds compiled bytecode. It is not a standalone program, so the machine that runs it needs a MatchBox of a compatible version. Lesson 9 shows how to build something that needs no install at all. Try it Run matchbox --version , then run your own script. If you get stuck, the quick start walks through the same steps.

title: Java interop
body: Java interop Java interop is experimental. It needs a JDK on the host and a native MatchBox build with the bif-jni feature, which is in the default feature set. It does not exist in the browser. The Java interop example shows the intended use. This page records what actually ran on the 0.11.0 CLI, so none of these snippets have a Run button. What works import java:java.util.ArrayList as List; import java:java.util.HashMap; l = new List(); l.add( "x" ); l.add( "y" ); println( l.size() ); println( l.contains( "x" ) ); m = new HashMap(); m.put( "a", "b" ); println( m.get( "a" ) ); 2 true b Instantiating a class with new , either from an import java: or from createObject( "java", "java.util.ArrayList" ) , and calling methods with string arguments works. What fails Code Result list.get( 0 ) Invocation of get failed: Java exception was thrown , with java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: argument type mismatch printed on the error stream. sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.append( "x" ) The same argument type mismatch failure. import java:java.lang.Math; then Math.sqrt( 16 ) Method sqrt not found on null. Static-only classes cannot be called through an import. createObject( "java", "java.lang.Math" ) Constructor with 0 arguments not found on class java.lang.Math . The same happens for java.util.UUID . import java:java.lang.System; then System.getProperty( ... ) Method getProperty not found on null. java.new( "java.lang.StringBuilder", "Hello" ) Parse error: expected identifier, found new . The cause of the first row is that every MatchBox number is passed to Java as a java.lang.Double , so a method that takes an int is not matched. add , contains and map put and get with string arguments work. StringBuilder.append( "x" ) fails even though its argument is a string, so test each method you depend on. BoxLang 1.13 on the JVM runs list.get( 0 ) , Math.sqrt( 16 ) and sb.append( "x" ) without error, so Java code that runs there can fail here. Use a Native Fusion Rust module for numeric work.

title: Java interop example
body: Java Interop Example This example calls Java classes from BoxLang through MatchBox's experimental JNI bridge . Important limitations: Java interop works when you run a script with matchbox main.bxs . Binaries produced with --target native do not include the bridge: the same calls fail at run time with Java interoperability is not enabled in this build. It is not available in WASM builds. A JDK must be installed on the machine that runs the script. The feature is experimental. APIs may change between MatchBox releases. Running From this directory: matchbox main.bxs Expected output: === BoxLang Java Interop === --- StringBuilder --- Hello, World! Length: 13 --- ArrayList --- Size: 3 Contains 'Rust': true List: [BoxLang, MatchBox, Rust] --- HashMap --- language -> BoxLang runtime -> MatchBox Contains 'backend': true Size: 3 Done! The runner stubs that --target native copies into your binary are built without the bif-jni feature. The matchbox command itself has it, so only interpreter mode can reach Java. What It Demonstrates Java class Syntax java.lang.StringBuilder import java:java.lang.StringBuilder as SB java.util.ArrayList import java:java.util.ArrayList as List java.util.HashMap import java:java.util.HashMap Import Syntax // Import with an alias import java:java.util.ArrayList as List; myList = new List() myList.add("item") // Import without an alias (use the bare class name) import java:java.util.HashMap; myMap = new HashMap() myMap.put("key", "value") // Without an import sb = createObject("java", "java.lang.StringBuilder", "Hello") println(sb.toString()) A constructor is chosen by argument count, so new SB("Hello") calls the one-argument constructor. Limitations These results were observed with OpenJDK 21: Call Result Constructing StringBuilder , ArrayList , HashMap Works ArrayList.add , size , contains , toString ; HashMap.put , get , containsKey , size Works ArrayList.get( 0 ) Fails: argument type mismatch StringBuilder.append( "text" ) Fails: argument type mismatch createObject( "java", "java.lang.String", "abc" ) Fails with a ClassCastException --target native binaries Java is not enabled WASM builds Not supported Running without a JDK installed Not supported See differences-from-boxlang.md for the full list of unsupported features across all build targets.

title: JavaScript and WebAssembly
body: JavaScript + WebAssembly MatchBox compiles BoxLang for the browser with --target js . This page was checked against MatchBox 0.11.0, including a run of the generated module in Node 22. Mode Command Status JS module (AOT) --target js Works. Ship a compiled app or library as an ES module. Raw .wasm --target wasm Does not work. See the known issue below. Runtime (source strings) your own crate Needs a small Rust crate, described below. Mode 1: JavaScript ES module (AOT) MatchBox compiles your script to bytecode and writes an ES module that loads a generic MatchBox runtime ( .wasm ) and the bytecode. Prerequisites The wasm-bindgen command line tool, version 0.2.114, must be on PATH , or its location set in WASM_BINDGEN . Without it the command stops with wasm-bindgen not found. Install wasm-bindgen-cli or set WASM_BINDGEN. Compile matchbox --target js my_lib.bxs Standalone JS module produced: ./my_lib.js The command writes four files next to the script, or next to --output : File Contents my_lib.js The ES module. The compiled bytecode is embedded in it as a base64 string. my_lib.wasm The MatchBox runtime. It does not contain your program. For a three-line script it was 1,937,302 bytes, and my_lib.js was 50,747 bytes. my_lib.d.ts , my_lib_bg.wasm.d.ts TypeScript declarations for the runtime. --output dist/my_lib.js creates dist/ and names the files from the stem my_lib . Use in HTML <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head><title>BoxLang App</title></head> <body> <script type="module"> import { greet, calculate } from './my_lib.js'; const result = await greet("Developer"); document.body.textContent = result; </script> </body> </html> Runtime contract The module starts loading as soon as it is imported. It exports: One async function per top-level BoxLang function. Every call returns a promise, so always await it. With function greet(name) and function calculate(a, b) in the script, await greet('Developer') returned Hello, Developer! and await calculate(6, 7) returned 42 in Node 22. ready , a promise that resolves when the runtime and bytecode are loaded. BoxLangVM , run_bytecode , initSync and the default init function from the runtime. In a browser the module also registers window.MatchBox.modules["my_lib"] , window.MatchBox.ready("my_lib") , window.MatchBox.State(moduleName, options) , and fires a matchbox:ready event on window with detail.module set to the module name. This browser contract is the supported path. Importing the module outside a browser worked in Node 22 only after the compiled .wasm was supplied through a global the module checks ( globalThis.__matchboxWasmModule ), so treat non-browser use as unsupported. Exporting functions Functions declared at the top level of the script are exported. The exporter collects every top-level function declaration and does not look at access modifiers. function greet(name) { return "Hello, " & name & "!" } function calculate(a, b) { return a * b } Mode 2: Raw WASM binary Known issue: `--target wasm` does not produce a usable module matchbox --target wasm my_app.bxs prints WASM binary produced: my_app.wasm , but it builds the file from the WASI runner stub (not the browser stub that --target js uses) and appends bytes that are not a valid WebAssembly section. In Node 22, WebAssembly.compile rejects the result with unknown section code #0xea . Use --target js for the browser. Details and a WASI workaround are in the CLI reference . Mode 3: Calling functions and loading bytecode BoxLangVM is exported by every --target js module. It runs bytecode produced by matchbox --build : import { ready, BoxLangVM } from './my_lib.js'; await ready; // runtime is initialised const bytes = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch('./other.bxb')).arrayBuffer()); const vm = new BoxLangVM(); vm.load_bytecode(bytes); // runs the script's top level // call() is async: it returns a Promise const message = await vm.call("greet", ["BoxLang"]); console.log(message); // Hello, BoxLang! load_bytecode(bytes) , call(name, args) (async), pump() and vm_ptr() are the methods on BoxLangVM . There is no load_source method. In Node 22, loading lib.bxb into a new BoxLangVM and awaiting vm.call('greet', ['BoxLang']) returned Hello, BoxLang! . Compiling source strings in the browser The .wasm produced by --target js contains the VM but not the compiler, so it can only run bytecode. To compile and run source text in the browser you need a WebAssembly build that includes matchbox_compiler . The root matchbox crate defines run_boxlang(source) for wasm32 , but the root crate could not be built for wasm32-unknown-unknown in testing (see Building from source ). The supported pattern is the one this site's playground uses: a small cdylib crate that depends on matchbox_compiler and matchbox_vm with default-features = false , parses and compiles each snippet, and runs it with the synchronous interpret_sync . Its source is playground-runtime/ in the documentation repository. JavaScript Interop from BoxLang When BoxLang code is running inside the browser JS target, it can access a browser bridge through the js global: // DOM access title = js.document.title js.document.getElementById("output").innerText = "Updated by BoxLang" // Browser APIs js.alert("Hello!") js.console.log("Logged from BoxLang") // Location url = js.location.href The important current rule is: Plain JS values cross the boundary as BoxLang values: strings, booleans, null, numbers, arrays, and plain objects. Browser host objects stay as JS handles: DOM nodes, document , window , functions, and other browser-native objects. That keeps state/data interop predictable while preserving access to real browser objects. js.* is a browser-only surface. Using it in a native build throws a runtime error. Serving Locally for Development Browsers block WASM file loading over file:// . Serve your project with any local HTTP server: npx serve . # or python3 -m http.server 8080 Then open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. Production Deployment The WASM output files ( *.js + *.wasm ) can be deployed to any static hosting service: CDN : upload to S3, Cloudflare R2, or a similar object store. Vercel / Netlify : drop the files into your project's output directory. Ensure your server sets the correct Content-Type for .wasm files: Content-Type: application/wasm Most modern hosts handle this automatically.

title: JIT compilation
body: JIT Compilation MatchBox includes a multi-tier JIT compiler built on Cranelift . It profiles hot code at runtime and compiles it to native machine code, eliminating interpreter dispatch overhead for the loops and functions that matter most. Where JIT is Available Build target JIT active? Reason Native CLI ( matchbox script.bxs ) Yes Enabled by default in the native CLI binary Native runner stubs (cross-deployed) No Stubs are built without the jit feature to keep their embedded size down WASM (browser / container) No Cranelift does not target WASM; the browser's own JIT runs the WASM module ESP32 / embedded No The matchbox-esp32-runner crate is workspace-excluded and has no Cranelift dependency The JIT is compiled in via the jit Cargo feature, which is included in the default feature set of the matchbox CLI crate. The matchbox_vm library crate keeps jit opt-in (default off) so that consumers (the ESP32 runner, WASM runner, and native runner stubs) remain lean unless they explicitly request it. The Four Tiers The JIT uses a tiered strategy: cheap profiling runs first, and compilation only fires once a site has proven itself hot. Tier 1: Empty loop elimination Trigger: A for loop whose body is empty, after ≥ 10 000 iterations. The entire loop is replaced by a single select instruction: the counter jumps straight to its final value in one native call. No iteration actually occurs. Tier 2: Numeric loop body Trigger: A for loop with a numeric-only body, after ≥ 10 000 cumulative iterations (counter persists across fiber scheduler quanta). The loop body is translated to Cranelift SSA IR. Local variables live in registers throughout; only the final values are written back to the VM's locals array on exit. Inline-cached struct member reads (monomorphic or bi-morphic) are also supported. Tier 3: Array iteration Trigger: A for-in loop over a float-only array, after ≥ 5 000 cumulative iterations. The array data pointer and length are passed directly to the compiled loop, bypassing the iterator protocol entirely. Tier 4: Hot function compilation Trigger: A function body that passes a translatability check, after ≥ 100 calls. The entire function body is compiled to a native fn(locals_ptr, heap_ptr, out_val_ptr) -> status function. Supported operations: Category Opcodes Locals GET_LOCAL , SET_LOCAL , SET_LOCAL_POP Constants Numeric literals Arithmetic ADD , SUB , MUL , DIV , MOD (float and int variants) Comparison == , != , < , <= , > , >= Boolean NOT Control flow JUMP , JUMP_IF_FALSE (forward jumps) Stack POP , DUP Calls CALL (direct calls to other JIT-compiled functions) Strings STRING_CONCAT ( & operator, via jit_concat runtime helper) Return RETURN If any unsupported opcode is present, the function is silently skipped and keeps running in the interpreter with no correctness impact. If a type guard fails at runtime (for example a variable expected to be numeric turns out to be a heap pointer), the compiled frame deopts : execution transfers back to the interpreter at the current bytecode position. Deopts are counted per function, and a function that keeps deopting is recompiled in a more tolerant mode ( crates/matchbox-vm/src/vm/jit.rs , inc_fn_deopt ): Deopts of one function Action 5 Recompile in Mode 1 (polymorphic). Arithmetic keeps its numeric fast path and falls back to a runtime helper when an operand is not a number. 10 (after Mode 1) Recompile in Mode 2 (relaxed). Arithmetic always goes through the helper. Each upgrade drops the compiled code and sets the call counter to 10 below the threshold, so the function is recompiled after 10 more calls. Mode 0 is the first compile. Each step prints a [JIT] Tier-4 function ... deopted N times. Upgrading to Mode ... line to stderr. What Is Not Supported in Tier 4 The following categories cause a function to remain interpreted: Global variables : GET_GLOBAL , SET_GLOBAL , DEFINE_GLOBAL , GET_PRIVATE , SET_PRIVATE I/O : PRINT , PRINTLN Object / collection creation : NEW , ARRAY , STRUCT Property and index access : MEMBER , SET_MEMBER , INC_MEMBER , INDEX , SET_INDEX Dynamic calls : INVOKE , INVOKE_NAMED , CALL_NAMED Loops inside functions : FOR_LOOP_STEP , LOOP , ITER_NEXT Exception handling : PUSH_HANDLER , POP_HANDLER , THROW Multi-word compare-jumps : LOCAL_COMPARE_JUMP , GLOBAL_COMPARE_JUMP , COMPARE_JUMP , LOCAL_JUMP_IF_NE_CONST Miscellaneous : INC , DEC , INC_LOCAL , INC_GLOBAL , SWAP , OVER , JUMP_IF_NULL In practice, Tier 4 is most effective for pure computational functions: numeric kernels, string-building loops, recursive math, and hot helper functions that operate only on their arguments and local variables. Diagnostics The JIT reports through eprintln! , so its [JIT] ... lines ( compiled hot fn , compiled empty loop , compiled generic loop , compiled iter loop , deopt upgrades and compile failures) go to stderr, not stdout. They are not controlled by --verbose . Opting Out To build the CLI without the JIT, leave out jit and also server . The matchbox_server crate enables jit on the VM itself, so with server on the JIT cannot be switched off ( cargo tree -e features shows cranelift-jit for any feature set that includes server ). cargo build --release --no-default-features \ --features "bif-io,bif-jni,bif-crypto,bif-cli,bif-http" This drops --serve and --target wasi-http along with the JIT. The dependency tree for this command contains no cranelift-jit and no axum ; it was inspected, not built. Future Directions JIT in native runner stubs The build.rs feature-forwarding block (the features list at lines 92 to 108) explicitly lists which features are passed to matchbox-runner stub builds. Adding "jit" there would give deployed native runner stubs the same JIT benefits as the CLI's local interpreter. The trade-off is binary size: Cranelift would be linked into every stub, which multiplies across targets in cross-compile mode. When that trade-off becomes acceptable, the change is a one-liner in build.rs : if env::var("CARGO_FEATURE_JIT").is_ok() { features.push("jit"); } Wider Tier-4 opcode coverage The most impactful missing opcodes for real-world functions are globals and property access. Both are achievable with runtime helpers following the same pattern as jit_concat and jit_ic_member_fallback . The main constraint is the deopt story: any operation that can throw or have side effects needs a clean deopt path back to the interpreter. String constant support in Tier-4 Currently, CONSTANT only accepts numeric literals in compiled functions. String constants require the GC heap at JIT-compile time, which isn't available. One path forward: a jit_intern_const helper that lazily allocates the string object on first call and caches its GC id, making string constants safe to use from compiled frames. Tier-4 for embedded loops Functions containing FOR_LOOP_STEP are currently rejected by fn_is_translatable . Supporting them would require the Tier-2 loop compiler to operate within Tier-4's SSA frame, essentially merging the two tiers. The deopt model is the main complexity: a loop inside a compiled function that deopts mid-iteration needs to restore both the function's locals and the loop counter.

title: Learn MatchBox
body: Learn MatchBox MatchBox is the Rust runtime for BoxLang. This course takes you from a first script to a native executable in ten short lessons. You do not need to install anything to start: every code sample has a Run this in your browser button that opens a real MatchBox runtime, compiled to WebAssembly, right under the code. Edit the sample, break it, run it again. Your progress is remembered in this browser, so you can stop and pick up where you left off. Continue where you left off: Welcome to MatchBox What MatchBox is, how it relates to BoxLang, and your first script, run in the browser. Install and run Install MatchBox with MVM, then run and compile a script on your own machine. Values and strings Variables, numbers, strings, interpolation and operators. Arrays and structs Lists and key-value data, and the loops that walk over them. Functions and callbacks Functions, default and named arguments, arrow functions, and map, filter and reduce. Classes and objects Bundle data and behavior together, with a constructor and methods you can chain. Errors and control flow if and switch, break and continue, and handling errors with try, catch and finally. Running work at the same time Futures, runAsync and then, and how the browser build runs them. Build and ship Turn a script into bytecode or a single native executable you can hand to anyone. Where to go next A map of what to explore after the basics, and what to watch out for in this release. Before you start You should know the basics of at least one programming language. You do not need to know BoxLang, CFML or Rust. The lessons that install tools or build files (lessons 2 and 9) show commands for your own terminal, because a browser tab cannot do those. Everything else runs on this page. The playground has limits: a run stops after 5 seconds, source and output are capped at 64 KiB, and there are no files, network or Java. See the playground page for the full list.

title: Modules
body: Modules A module is a folder with a ModuleConfig.bx . It can add BoxLang functions, classes and settings to a script, and optionally a native Rust crate. Modules are loaded by the matchbox command, not by the playground. Everything here was run on the 0.11.0 CLI. Layout greetings/ ModuleConfig.bx bifs/ greet_bifs.bxs functions added to every script models/ Greeter.bxs classes, imported through bxModules matchbox/ Cargo.toml optional native Rust crate ModuleConfig.bx must declare a class named ModuleConfig : class ModuleConfig { function onLoad() { println( "loading" ); } function configure() { return { version: "1.0.0", enabled: true }; } } At compile time MatchBox creates the class, calls onLoad() , then calls configure() and keeps the struct it returns as the module settings. Output from onLoad() appears once, before your script runs. If the file uses the anonymous form class { ... } , as the Rust modules guide in the MatchBox repository shows, the lifecycle fails with Warning: Module 'name': ModuleConfig.bx lifecycle error: ... Can only instantiate classes. and the settings are empty. The bifs/ functions still load. Name the class. Using a module Given bifs/shout.bxs : function shout( s ) { return ucase( s ) & "!"; } and a script t.bxs : println( shout( "hi" ) ); println( serializeJSON( getModuleSettings( "mymod" ) ) ); run it with the module folder: matchbox --module ./mymod t.bxs loading HI! {"enabled":true,"version":"1.0.0"} Every .bxs or .bx file in bifs/ is added to the script, so its functions are callable by name. getModuleSettings( "mymod" ) returns the struct from configure() . The name is the module's folder name. A class in the module is imported through the bxModules prefix: import bxModules.greetings.models.Greeter as Greeter; and then new Greeter() . The greetings module in the MatchBox test suite uses this. A path that does not exist fails with Module 'name': path does not exist , and a folder without ModuleConfig.bx fails with is missing ModuleConfig.bx . How modules are found MatchBox collects modules from these places, and a later source with the same folder name replaces an earlier one. All four were run. Order Source Example 1 dependencies and devDependencies in box.json { "dependencies": { "mymod": "./libs/mymod" } } 2 matchbox.toml [modules.mymod] then path = "./libs/mymod" 3 Folders in the project directory named modules/ and boxlang_modules/ that contain ModuleConfig.bx modules/mymod/ModuleConfig.bx 4 --module <path> , repeatable matchbox --module ./mymod t.bxs A box.json value that starts with . or contains a slash is a path. Any other value is looked up by name in modules/ and then boxlang_modules/ . The Rust modules guide shows [modules] followed by my-utils = "./custom/path" in matchbox.toml . That form is rejected with a TOML parse error. Use the [modules.name] table with a path key. Native modules A module with matchbox/Cargo.toml is treated as having a native Rust part. That is the Native Fusion feature. See the native fusion example and the Rust modules guide in the MatchBox repository for the crate layout.

title: Native Builds
body: Native builds --target native writes a self-contained executable. It copies a prebuilt runner stub, which is the MatchBox VM plus a loader, and appends your compiled bytecode. It does not translate BoxLang into machine code. Build for the current host matchbox --target native my_app.bxs Native binary produced: my_app The output is my_app next to the script ( my_app.exe on Windows) and is marked executable on Unix. --output <path> changes the name. The destination needs neither Java nor a MatchBox install. Run it with ./my_app . If the argument is a .bxb file, MatchBox runs it and writes nothing. Package from .bxs or .bxm source. What is in the executable Measured with MatchBox 0.11.0 (source commit 37be346, built 2026-10-17) on Linux x86_64 with default features: Item Bytes Native runner stub ( stubs/runner_stub_x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu ) 4,751,936 hello.bxs bytecode 217 Resulting hello executable 4,752,169 The executable is the stub, then the bytecode, an 8-byte length and an 8-byte BOXLANG\x01 marker. The stub is built with the size-optimised release profile and only the bif-io , bif-http , bif-crypto and bif-cli libraries (plus bif-zip if the CLI was built with it). The size depends on those features, the Rust version and the MatchBox version, so measure your own output instead of relying on a fixed figure. The stub has no JIT, no JNI and no datasource support, whatever features the CLI was built with. The CLI enables the JIT when it runs a script itself ( matchbox app.bxs ); the stub has none. See JIT compilation and Cargo features . Running a native executable It does not parse MatchBox flags. Everything after its name goes to the script, including -v and --help . ./my_app first second --name=bob --flag gives cliGetArgs() the positionals first and second and the options name and flag . A script error prints Runtime Error: ... to stderr and exits with code 1. cliExit(n) exits with n . It does not write panic_debug.txt ; that hook belongs to the CLI. Build for other hosts Cross-compiling needs no Rust target on your machine. It needs a CLI that has the other platform's stub embedded, which means a CLI built with the cross-compile Cargo feature. Release CLIs are built that way. Pass the Rust target triple to --target : matchbox --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu my_app.bxs The triples a cross-compile build tries to embed are: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu , i686-unknown-linux-gnu , aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu , armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf x86_64-pc-windows-msvc , aarch64-pc-windows-msvc , x86_64-pc-windows-gnu x86_64-apple-darwin , aarch64-apple-darwin A stub is embedded only if it built. On a Linux build host the Apple stubs are skipped unless they already exist. A CLI without the requested stub stops with: Error: runner stub for target 'aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu' is not embedded That is what the default source build printed for that triple; the host triple ( x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu on the test machine) worked and produced the same executable as --target native . A cross-built executable was not run on its destination in this review, so test each artifact on its destination operating system and architecture. See Building from source for --features cross-compile . Rust interoperability Native Fusion lets a native build expose Rust functions to BoxLang. It requires a Rust toolchain and the MatchBox source tree, and it builds a new executable instead of appending to the stub.

title: Native Fusion example
body: Native Fusion Example Native Fusion lets you write performance-critical functions and stateful objects in Rust and use them directly from BoxLang. Everything is statically linked into a single native binary - no external libraries, no FFI boilerplate at call sites. This example demonstrates both interop styles: Style Rust side BoxLang side Standalone BIF #[matchbox_fn] on a plain function result = fast_fib(10) Native object #[matchbox_class] + #[matchbox_methods] on a struct s = new rust:stats.RunningStats() Project Layout native_fusion/ ├── app.bxs ← BoxLang entry point └── native/ └── stats.rs ← Rust source: BIFs + RunningStats native object MatchBox automatically detects any .rs files inside a native/ directory that lives alongside your entry script and compiles them together with the VM. Building You need a Rust toolchain ( cargo , rustc ) in addition to the matchbox binary. The generated Cargo project depends on the crates/matchbox-vm directory of the MatchBox source tree that built your matchbox binary, so that tree must still exist on disk at its original path. The first build compiles the VM and takes a minute or more. cd docs/examples/native_fusion matchbox --target native app.bxs MatchBox will: Compile native/stats.rs together with the MatchBox VM. Register the exported BIFs ( fast_fib , fast_factorial ) and the RunningStats class. Compile app.bxs to bytecode and embed it. Produce a single app binary. Running ./app Expected output: === Native Fusion Demo === --- Fibonacci (BIF) --- fib(0) = 0 fib(1) = 1 fib(2) = 1 ... fib(10) = 55 --- Factorials (BIF) --- 1! = 1 2! = 2 ... 10! = 3628800 --- RunningStats (native object) --- count : 6 sum : 108 mean : 18 min : 4 max : 42 All results computed in Rust. Writing a Native BIF with #[matchbox_fn] Using the #[matchbox_fn] macro is the recommended way to write BIFs. You write a plain typed Rust function - the macro generates the {name}_wrapper with the correct BIF signature, argument-count validation, and type coercions for you. use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn}; // Write a normal Rust function with typed parameters. // Supported types: f64, i32, bool, String, BxValue (pass-through) #[matchbox_fn] pub fn my_bif(n: f64) -> f64 { n * 2.0 } The macro expands this into two things: Your original my_bif(n: f64) -> f64 function, unchanged. A generated my_bif_wrapper(vm, args) -> Result<BxValue, String> that the VM actually calls. Each .rs file inside native/ must export a register_bifs() function. Register the _wrapper variant (not the original function): use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn, types::{BxNativeFunction, BxValue}}; use std::collections::HashMap; #[matchbox_fn] pub fn my_bif(n: f64) -> f64 { n * 2.0 } pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Register the macro-generated wrapper, not the plain function. map.insert("my_bif".to_string(), my_bif_wrapper as BxNativeFunction); map } The string key ( "my_bif" ) is the name BoxLang uses to call the function: result = my_bif(21) println(result) // 42 Supported Parameter Types Rust type Macro conversion f64 args[i].as_number() i32 args[i].as_int() bool args[i].as_bool() String vm.to_string(args[i]) BxValue passed through as-is Native Objects with #[matchbox_class] and #[matchbox_methods] For stateful interop, expose a Rust struct as a BoxLang native object. use matchbox_vm::{ matchbox_class, matchbox_methods, types::{BxNativeFunction, BxNativeObject, BxValue, BxVM}, }; use std::cell::RefCell; use std::collections::HashMap; use std::rc::Rc; // #[matchbox_class] auto-implements the BxNativeObject trait, // wiring get_property / set_property / call_method to the // dispatcher generated by #[matchbox_methods]. #[matchbox_class] #[derive(Debug)] pub struct Counter { pub value: f64, } // #[matchbox_methods] generates a dispatch_method() router that maps // BoxLang method names (case-insensitive) to the Rust methods below. #[matchbox_methods] impl Counter { pub fn increment(&mut self) -> f64 { self.value += 1.0; self.value } pub fn add(&mut self, n: f64) -> f64 { self.value += n; self.value } pub fn get(&self) -> f64 { self.value } } // Constructor - called when BoxLang evaluates `new rust:mymodule.Counter(0)`. // vm.native_object_new() stores the object on the VM heap and returns an id // wrapped in a BxValue pointer. pub fn create_counter(vm: &mut dyn BxVM, args: &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> { let initial = args.first().map(|v| v.as_number()).unwrap_or(0.0); let obj = Counter { value: initial }; let id = vm.native_object_new(Rc::new(RefCell::new(obj))); Ok(BxValue::new_ptr(id)) } // register_classes() maps "<module>.<ClassName>" to the constructor. // The module name is the filename of this .rs file without the extension. // BoxLang resolves `new rust:mymodule.Counter()` using this key. pub fn register_classes() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("mymodule.Counter".to_string(), create_counter as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang: c = new rust:mymodule.Counter(0) c.increment() c.add(9) println(c.get()) // 10 When to Use Native Fusion You need maximum throughput on a hot path (parsing, compression, crypto, ML). You want to use a Rust crate ( serde , image , reqwest , etc.) from BoxLang. You need direct OS or hardware access. For most application logic, plain BoxLang is sufficient. Reserve Native Fusion for the innermost loops where performance is measured and critical. Limitations Feature Status Available in native builds ✅ Available in WASM builds ❌ --target js with a native/ directory fails to compile in v0.11.0 Multiple .rs files in native/ ✅ Each may export register_bifs() and/or register_classes() Using external Rust crates ✅ Add a Cargo.toml to native/ Mutable self in #[matchbox_methods] ✅ Dispatcher takes &mut self Property access on native objects ⚠️ Override get_property in BxNativeObject manually For the full macro API reference see native-fusion.md .

title: Native Fusion reference
body: Native Fusion: Rust Interop Reference Native Fusion is the mechanism that lets you write Rust functions and classes and expose them as first-class BoxLang Built-In Functions (BIFs) and native objects. Everything is statically linked into your final binary, with no shared libraries, no FFI boilerplate at the BoxLang call site. Native Fusion works with --target native and --target wasi . With --target js and --target wasm the generated build fails to compile in MatchBox 0.11.0. --target esp32 also has a Fusion path that could not be run in this review (no ESP32 toolchain). The Limitations table lists exactly what was run. How It Works Create a native/ directory alongside your .bxs entry script. Write one or more .rs files inside native/ . Each .rs file exports a register_bifs() and/or register_classes() function. Run matchbox --target native app.bxs . Native Fusion detected! Target: native. Building hybrid artifact... ... Native Fusion binary produced: app MatchBox detects native/ , generates a temporary Cargo project that contains the .rs files, the bytecode and the VM, merges all BIF and class registrations, builds it with cargo build --release , and copies the result next to the script. A native build of a one-function example took about 90 seconds on first use and produced a 12,528,504 byte executable that printed 30 for add(10, 20) . The generated project refers to matchbox_vm by the absolute path of the MatchBox checkout that the CLI was compiled from, and the build adds --offline whenever that checkout has a Cargo.lock . Native Fusion therefore needs a Rust toolchain and that source tree, and every crate it uses must already be in the local Cargo cache. It was run with a CLI built from source, not with a downloaded release binary. Macros All interop macros are re-exported from the matchbox_vm crate, so no separate matchbox_macros import is needed: use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn, matchbox_class, matchbox_methods}; #[matchbox_fn] : Expose a Rust function as a BoxLang BIF Annotate a plain Rust function with typed parameters. The macro generates a corresponding {name}_wrapper function that carries the low-level BIF signature expected by the VM ( fn(&mut dyn BxVM, &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> ). The wrapper handles argument-count validation and type coercion automatically. Usage use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_fn, types::{BxNativeFunction}}; use std::collections::HashMap; #[matchbox_fn] pub fn add(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 { a + b } pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Register the generated wrapper, not the original function. map.insert("add".to_string(), add_wrapper as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang: result = add(10, 20) println(result) // 30 Supported Parameter Types Rust parameter type VM conversion applied by the macro f64 args[i].as_number() i32 args[i].as_int() bool args[i].as_bool() String vm.to_string(args[i]) BxValue passed through unchanged The return value is always wrapped as BxValue::new_number(result as f64) . For BIFs that need to return other types (strings, null, objects), write a manual BIF instead (see Manual BIF Signature ). What the Macro Generates // Your function: unchanged: pub fn add(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64 { a + b } // Generated wrapper: pub fn add_wrapper( vm: &mut dyn matchbox_vm::types::BxVM, args: &[matchbox_vm::types::BxValue], ) -> Result<matchbox_vm::types::BxValue, String> { if args.len() != 2 { return Err(format!("add requires 2 arguments, got {}", args.len())); } let a = args[0].as_number(); let b = args[1].as_number(); let result = add(a, b); Ok(matchbox_vm::types::BxValue::new_number(result as f64)) } #[matchbox_class] : Expose a Rust struct as a BoxLang native object Annotate a struct to auto-implement the BxNativeObject trait. The generated implementation delegates get_property , set_property , and call_method to a dispatch_method function that is generated by #[matchbox_methods] . Always pair #[matchbox_class] with a #[matchbox_methods] impl block. Usage use matchbox_vm::{matchbox_class, matchbox_methods, types::{BxValue, BxVM, BxNativeFunction, BxNativeObject}}; use std::collections::HashMap; use std::rc::Rc; use std::cell::RefCell; #[matchbox_class] #[derive(Debug)] pub struct Counter { pub value: f64, } #[matchbox_methods] impl Counter { pub fn increment(&mut self) -> f64 { self.value += 1.0; self.value } pub fn add(&mut self, n: f64) -> f64 { self.value += n; self.value } pub fn get(&self) -> f64 { self.value } } // Constructor: registered separately, not via #[matchbox_fn]. pub fn create_counter(vm: &mut dyn BxVM, args: &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> { let initial = args.first().map(|v| v.as_number()).unwrap_or(0.0); let obj = Counter { value: initial }; let id = vm.native_object_new(Rc::new(RefCell::new(obj))); Ok(BxValue::new_ptr(id)) } pub fn register_classes() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Key format: "<module_filename>.<ClassName>" // This file is native/counter.rs → module name is "counter" map.insert("counter.Counter".to_string(), create_counter as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang (instantiate with new rust:<module>.<Class>(...) ): c = new rust:counter.Counter(0) c.increment() c.add(9) println(c.get()) // 10 #[matchbox_methods] : Generate a method dispatcher for a native class Annotate an impl block to generate a dispatch_method function that routes BoxLang method calls to the correct Rust method by name (case-insensitive). #[matchbox_fn] type-coercion rules apply to each method's parameters. Usage #[matchbox_methods] impl MyStruct { pub fn process(&self, input: f64) -> f64 { input * self.factor } } BoxLang calls obj.process(42) and the dispatcher resolves it to MyStruct::process(&self, 42.0) . What the Macro Generates impl MyStruct { fn dispatch_method( &mut self, vm: &mut dyn BxVM, name: &str, args: &[BxValue], ) -> Result<BxValue, String> { match name.to_lowercase().as_str() { "process" => { if args.len() != 1 { return Err(...); } let input = args[0].as_number(); let result = self.process(input); Ok(BxValue::new_number(result as f64)) } _ => Err(format!("Method {} not found", name)), } } } #[matchbox_module] : Module marker (no-op) A no-op attribute that serves as documentation: apply it to the top-level mod or impl to indicate the file is a Native Fusion module. Currently passes through unchanged. #[matchbox_module] mod my_native_module { ... } Registration Entry Points Every .rs file in native/ may export two entry-point functions. MatchBox calls them both at startup. register_bifs() : standalone functions pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("my_bif".to_string(), my_bif_wrapper as BxNativeFunction); map } BIF names must be unique across all files in native/ . register_classes() : native object constructors pub fn register_classes() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); // Key: "<module>.<ClassName>" where <module> is the filename without .rs map.insert("mymodule.MyClass".to_string(), create_my_class as BxNativeFunction); map } BoxLang uses the key to resolve new rust:mymodule.MyClass(...) . Manual BIF Signature When you need full control (e.g. returning a string, null, or an object pointer), skip #[matchbox_fn] and write the low-level signature directly: use matchbox_vm::types::{BxNativeFunction, BxValue, BxVM}; use std::collections::HashMap; pub fn greet(vm: &mut dyn BxVM, args: &[BxValue]) -> Result<BxValue, String> { if args.is_empty() { return Err("greet: expected one argument".to_string()); } let name = vm.to_string(args[0]); Ok(BxValue::new_string(format!("Hello, {}!", name))) } pub fn register_bifs() -> HashMap<String, BxNativeFunction> { let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("greet".to_string(), greet as BxNativeFunction); map } Project Layout my_app/ ├── app.bxs ← BoxLang entry point └── native/ ├── math.rs ← exports register_bifs() ├── counter.rs ← exports register_bifs() + register_classes() └── crypto.rs ← exports register_classes() Multiple files are supported as long as BIF and class names are unique across all files. Using External Rust Crates A Cargo.toml inside native/ is not read . The CLI generates its own Cargo.toml and copies only the *.rs files from native/ into it, so a dependency listed in native/Cargo.toml is not available. In a test, native/ver.rs that used the semver crate failed with error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate 'semver' in this scope . To use external crates, put the Rust code in a module instead. A module directory that contains matchbox/Cargo.toml is added to the generated project as a path dependency, so its own dependencies are resolved. The crate's src files export register_bifs() and/or register_classes() as above. modules/vermod/ ModuleConfig.bx matchbox/ Cargo.toml (depends on matchbox_vm and semver) src/lib.rs (pub fn register_bifs() ...) With this layout matchbox --target native app.bxs built and the program printed 1 for semver::Version::parse("1.2.3") 's major version. The crate in matchbox/Cargo.toml must name matchbox_vm as a dependency with a path that exists on your machine. Limitations Rows marked "run" were run with MatchBox 0.11.0 on Linux x86_64. Feature Status --target native Works (run). --target wasi Works (run). Output is a WASI module that printed 30 under Node's WASI. --target js Fails to compile (run): the generated code calls Window::console() , but the web-sys dependency enables only the Window feature. --target wasm Fails to compile (run): getrandom reports that wasm32-unknown-unknown needs its wasm_js feature. --target esp32 A Fusion path exists in the source. Not run. Multiple .rs files in native/ Works. Dependencies through native/Cargo.toml No. The file is ignored. Dependencies through a module's matchbox/Cargo.toml Works (run). Return types other than f64 from #[matchbox_fn] Use a manual BIF signature. Mutable self in #[matchbox_methods] The dispatcher takes &mut self . Property access on native objects ( obj.field ) Override get_property in BxNativeObject . See native-builds.md for the complete native build reference and differences-from-boxlang.md for the full list of features not available in MatchBox.

title: Operators
body: Operators Every row below was run on MatchBox 0.11.0. Where BoxLang 1.13 on the JVM behaves differently, the table says so. Arithmetic and strings Operator Meaning Example Result + - * / Arithmetic 10 / 4 2.5 % Remainder, sign follows the left operand -7 % 3 -1 \ Integer division 10 \ 3 3 ^ Power 2 ^ 10 1024 & String concatenation "abc" & 1 abc1 += -= *= /= %= &= Compound assignment x = 10; x %= 3 1 ++ -- Increment and decrement i++ ** and <=> are parse errors. Division by zero throws ExpressionException: Division by zero . + on two numeric strings adds them ( "5" + "6" is 11 ). 1 + "x" returns 1x , while BoxLang throws Can't cast [x] to a Number . Comparison and logic println( 5 == 5 ); println( 5 eq 5 ); println( 5 neq 4 ); println( 5 != 4 ); println( 3 lte 3 ); println( 3 gte 4 ); println( "a" < "b" ); println( 1 is 1 ); println( "abc" contains "B" ); println( "abc" does not contain "x" ); println( true && false || true ); println( true and false ); println( true xor false ); println( 1 eqv 1 ); println( !false ); Output: true true true true true false true true true true true false true true true String comparison ignores case: "a" == "A" is true . === behaves like == , which BoxLang does too. Word operators that are missing Operator MatchBox 0.11.0 BoxLang 1.13 not Parse error: unexpected token in expression: not . Use ! . Works. mod 7 mod 3 inside an expression is a parse error. As a statement, y = 7 mod 3; stores 7 with no error: the mod 3 part is ignored. Use % . 1 ne Parse error. Use neq or != . Not tested. imp , doesnotcontain Parse error. Not tested. ??= Parse error: unexpected token in expression: ? . Write x = x ?: 3 . Also a parse error in the 1.13 build used here. The silent mod case is the dangerous one. Search ported code for mod . Bitwise BoxLang spells bitwise operators with a b prefix. println( 5 b& 3 ); println( 5 b| 3 ); println( 5 b^ 3 ); println( b~ 5 ); println( 1 b<< 4 ); println( 256 b>> 4 ); println( 16 b>>> 2 ); Output: 1 7 6 -6 16 16 4 Both operands must be numbers. castAs and instanceOf castAs takes the type name as a string. Wrap it in parentheses when you combine it with other operators, because the string after castAs swallows what follows. println( ( 5 castAs "string" ) & "!" ); println( ( "3.5" castAs "numeric" ) + 1 ); println( "yes" castAs "boolean" ); println( "a" instanceOf "string" ); println( 1 instanceOf "numeric" ); println( { } instanceOf "struct" ); println( [ ] instanceOf "array" ); println( ( x => x ) instanceOf "function" ); println( 1 instanceOf "string" ); Output: 5! 4.5 true true true true true true false "abc" castAs "numeric" throws BoxCastException: Could not cast object [abc] to type [numeric] . 7.9 castAs "integer" throws a BoxCastException . BoxLang does too. x castAs string without quotes fails. setValue instanceOf "set" is false for a set . Elvis, ternary and safe navigation n = null; println( n ?: "was null" ); println( "" ?: "not used" ); println( 5 > 3 ? "yes" : "no" ); s = { a: { b: 2 } }; println( s?.a?.b ); println( s.missing?.deeper ?: "safe" ); println( isNull( n?.a ) ); Output: was null yes 2 safe true ?: only replaces null. An empty string passes through, so the second line prints an empty line. A ?. guards only the step it is on. n?.a.b with n null throws Member access only supported on structs, instances, JS objects, and native objects . BoxLang returns null. Write n?.a?.b . Statements that fail variables.n++ as a statement throws Fused increment only supported on structs and instances for now . variables.n += 1 , this.n++ and x = variables.n++ work. See known issues . For sets and ranges see sets and destructuring, spread and ranges .

title: Queries and data
body: Queries and data MatchBox has a query type and datasource functions, but they are optional parts of the build and they are not in the browser playground. Examples on this page ran on the CLI, so none have a Run button. Which build has them The query functions ( queryNew , queryAddRow , queryExecute and the rest) are registered only when the VM is built with the bif-datasource cargo feature. Query of queries needs the qoq feature as well. Neither is in the default feature list in the MatchBox Cargo.toml , which is bif-io , bif-jni , bif-crypto , bif-cli , bif-http , jit and server . The CLI used for this page had bif-datasource compiled in and qoq left out. In the browser playground, queryNew fails with Can only call functions. To check your own build, run queryNew( "a" ) and queryExecute( "select 1 as x from q", {}, { dbtype: "query" } ) . The second prints QoQ support is not enabled in this build when qoq is missing. See Building MatchBox for how to enable features. Building and reading a query q = queryNew( "id,name", "integer,varchar", [ [ 1, "Ann" ], [ 2, "Bob" ] ] ); println( q.recordCount ); println( q.name[ 2 ] ); println( serializeJSON( q.name ) ); queryAddRow( q, { id: 3, name: "Cy" } ); println( q.getRow( 3 ).name ); println( serializeJSON( queryColumnData( q, "id" ) ) ); i = 1; while ( i <= q.recordCount ) { println( q.id[ i ] & ":" & q.name[ i ] ); i++; } 2 Bob ["Ann","Bob"] Cy [1,2,3] 1:Ann 2:Bob 3:Cy q.recordCount is the row count and q.columnName returns that column as an array. q.getRow( n ) returns the row as a struct. queryRowData( q, n ) does the same. Also working: queryColumnList , queryRecordCount , queryColumnCount , queryGetCell( q, column, row ) , querySetCell( q, column, value, row ) , queryDeleteRow , queryReverse and queryAddColumn( q, name, array ) . serializeJSON( q ) produces {"columns":["id","name"],"data":[[1.0,"Ann"],...]} , which is a different shape from BoxLang. Numbers in data carry a decimal point. Not working for ( row in q ) fails with Iteration only supported for arrays and structs . Loop over the row numbers as shown. q.columnList is null. Use queryColumnList( q ) . Datasources datasourceRegister( name, config ) registers a connection pool and queryExecute( sql, params, { datasource: name } ) runs SQL on it. In 0.11.0 the only driver is PostgreSQL: datasourceRegister( "main", { driver: "postgres", host: "localhost", port: 5432, database: "app", username: "user", password: "secret" } ); rows = queryExecute( "select id, name from people where id = ?", [ 1 ], { datasource: "main" } ); Any other driver value fails with Unknown datasource driver ... Supported: postgresql . With no server listening, the register call fails with Failed to create PostgreSQL datasource 'main': ... error connecting to server . Calling queryExecute with a name that was never registered fails with Datasource with name [x] not found. Use datasourceRegister() first. Transactions use transactionBegin , transactionCommit and transactionRollback . No live database was available for testing, so the result shape of queryExecute is not documented here. Tree shaking can drop datasource functions With the default CLI settings, datasourceRegister( ... ) fails with Can only call functions. , because tree shaking removes it from the program. Run the script with --no-shaking , or keep the function with --keep datasourceRegister , and it is found. Query of queries Query of queries is queryExecute( "select ... from q", {}, { dbtype: "query" } ) . It needs the qoq feature. Without it the call fails with QoQ support is not enabled in this build . The CLI used for this page was built without qoq , so QoQ results are untested.
headings: Tree shaking can drop datasource functions

title: Running work at the same time
body: Running work at the same time A future stands for a value that is not ready yet. runAsync starts some work and hands you a future straight away. You call get() on it when you need the result. Your first future answer = runAsync( () => 6 * 7 ); println( "started" ); println( answer.get() ); Output: started 42 Several at once Start more than one future, then collect the results. slow = runAsync( () => { sleep( 20 ); return "slow"; } ); fast = runAsync( () => "fast" ); println( fast.get() & " then " & slow.get() ); Output: fast then slow Chaining then runs a function on the result when it arrives, and gives you a new future. result = runAsync( () => 10 ).then( n => n * 2 ); println( result.get() ); Output: 20 Measuring time getTickCount() returns milliseconds, and sleep( ms ) pauses. start = getTickCount(); sleep( 30 ); elapsed = getTickCount() - start; println( elapsed >= 30 ); Output: true In the browser The playground runs on a single thread, so futures take turns rather than running truly in parallel. That is enough to learn the shape of the API. On a native build the same code can use the machine's threads. The playground also stops any run after five seconds, so a script that waits too long ends with an error. Try it Start three futures that each sleep for a different time and return a different word. Print them in the order you started them.
headings: Running work at the same time

title: Scopes
body: Scopes MatchBox does not implement the full BoxLang scope chain. This page lists what each context gives you. Snippets with a Run button ran in the browser playground and on the CLI with the same output. Scripts and functions In a script, a plain assignment creates a variable you can read by its bare name. The variables. prefix does not point at the same storage at the top level of a script. j = 2; println( j ); println( isNull( variables.j ) ); variables.k = 1; println( isNull( k ) ); println( variables.k ); Output: 2 true true 1 Read a value the same way you wrote it: bare name for bare name, variables.k for variables.k . BoxLang treats both spellings as one variable. Inside a function, var and plain assignment create locals that disappear when the function returns: function f() { var local1 = 1; other = 5; return local1 + other; } println( f() ); Output: 6 local.x = 1 does not work. It fails with Member assignment only supported on structs, instances, JS objects, and native objects , and so do request.x = 1 and application.x = 1 . BoxLang accepts all three. These scope names are not defined in 0.11.0, in scripts or in served templates. Arguments Named arguments, defaults and the arguments scope work for declared parameters. function greet( name, greeting = "Hello" ) { return greeting & ", " & name & " (" & arguments.len() & " args)"; } function demo( a ) { return arguments.a & "/" & arguments[ "a" ]; } println( greet( "Ann" ) ); println( greet( greeting = "Hi", name = "Bob" ) ); println( demo( 1 ) ); Output: Hello, Ann (2 args) Hi, Bob (2 args) 1/1 arguments only holds declared parameters. Extra arguments are dropped: function g() { return arguments.len(); } g( 1, 2 ) returns 0. Positional access does not work: function h( a ) { return arguments[ 1 ]; } h( 5 ) returns null. Use arguments.a or arguments[ "a" ] . BoxLang keeps extra arguments ( g( 1, 2 ) gives 2), supports arguments[ 1 ] and hoists function declarations. Functions must be defined before the line that calls them. Calling one that is defined further down fails with Can only call functions. Closures do not capture function variables A closure or arrow function created inside a function cannot see that function's parameters or locals. The name reads as null, and string concatenation then prints the word null . function adder( n ) { return x => x + n; } println( adder( 5 )( 10 ) ); function addAll( n ) { return [ 1, 2 ].map( v => v + n ); } println( serializeJSON( addAll( 10 ) ) ); base = 5; function usesTopLevel() { return x => x + base; } println( usesTopLevel()( 10 ) ); Output: 10null ["1null","2null"] 15 BoxLang prints 15 for the first call. Closures do see top-level variables of the script, as the last call shows. Inside a function, use a for loop instead of a callback that needs the function's own variables: function addAll( n ) { result = []; for ( v in [ 1, 2 ] ) { result.append( v + n ); } return result; } println( serializeJSON( addAll( 10 ) ) ); Output: [11,12] The same bug breaks runAsync callbacks that use a variable of the enclosing function. See async . Classes Inside a class, this.x is the public state and variables.x is private to the instance. See classes . The server scope server exists and accepts assignment in scripts: server.q = 1 works. Web scopes When MatchBox serves templates ( matchbox --serve --webroot . ), these scopes are filled in for each request: Scope Verified behavior url Query string values. ?name=Ann gives url.name . form Posted fields. -d a=5 gives form.a . cookie Request cookies. The server also sets MBX_SESSION_ID . session Persists across requests that send the cookie. A counter in session.visits went from 1 to 2. cgi cgi.request_method returned GET . variables , server Readable and writable. On the plain CLI, assigning to url.x , form.x , cookie.x , session.x or cgi.x fails with the same Member assignment only supported on structs... error, because those scopes only exist in the server. An Application.bx in the web root was not run: its onRequestStart did not write anything when tested. Do not rely on application lifecycle events in 0.11.0. See templates for the tags and the web server example .
headings: Closures do not capture function variables

title: Sets
body: Sets A set holds each value once. Create one with a literal, setNew() , setOf() or toSet() . Everything on this page was run against MatchBox 0.11.0, in the browser playground unless a note says otherwise. Creating a set a = set{ 3, 1, 2, 3 }; println( a.size() ); empty = set{}; println( empty.isEmpty() ); b = setOf( "x", "y", "x" ); println( b.toList( "," ) ); c = [ 5, 5, 6 ].toSet(); println( c.toList( "," ) ); d = setNew( type = "linked", values = [ 3, 1, 2, 3 ] ); println( d.toList( "," ) ); Output: 3 true x,y 5,6 3,1,2 set{} is a literal: the word set followed by braces. setNew() takes type ( default , linked or sorted ) and values . listToSet( "a,b,a" ) and structKeySet( struct ) also return sets. Order Type Behavior in 0.11.0 default and linked Insertion order. sorted Sorted once, when setNew() builds it from values . Values you add() later are appended, not sorted. s = setNew( type = "sorted", values = [ 10, 9, 100 ] ); println( s.toList( "," ) ); s.add( 1 ); println( s.toList( "," ) ); Output: 9,10,100 9,10,100,1 A set is stored as an array that skips duplicates when it is built. isArray( s ) is true , s[ 1 ] reads the first value, println( s ) prints it like an array and serializeJSON( s ) returns an array. s instanceOf "set" is false . Operators and algebra When either operand is a set, + , - , * and ^ do set algebra, and the other operand can be an array. Operator Member function Result a + b a.union( b ) Values in either set. a - b a.difference( b ) Values in a and not in b . a * b a.intersection( b ) Values in both. a ^ b a.symmetricDifference( b ) Values in exactly one. a = setOf( 1, 2, 3 ); b = setOf( 2, 3, 4 ); println( ( a + b ).toList( "," ) ); println( ( a - b ).toList( "," ) ); println( ( a * b ).toList( "," ) ); println( ( a ^ b ).toList( "," ) ); println( a.isSubsetOf( setOf( 1, 2, 3, 4 ) ) ); println( a.isSupersetOf( setOf( 1 ) ) ); println( a.isDisjointFrom( setOf( 9 ) ) ); println( ( a + [ 3, 7 ] ).toList( "," ) ); Output: 1,2,3,4 1 2,3 1,4 true true true 1,2,3,7 Only an array works as the loose right operand. a + "7,8" is string concatenation and gives [1,2]7,8 , and [ 9 ] + a is an array join. Member functions Checked one by one in the playground and the CLI. Group Works Add and remove add , append , addAll , remove , delete , removeAll , retainAll , clear Query contains , has , size , len , length , count , isEmpty , isSubsetOf , isSupersetOf , isDisjointFrom , isCaseSensitive , isSynchronized Algebra union , intersection , difference , symmetricDifference Functional each , map , filter , reduce , every , some , none , find , reject Convert toArray , toList( delimiter ) s = setOf( 1, 2, 3, 4 ); println( s.map( x => x * 10 ).toList( "," ) ); println( s.filter( x => x > 2 ).toList( "," ) ); println( s.reduce( ( total, x ) => total + x, 0 ) ); println( s.every( x => x > 0 ) ); println( s.some( x => x > 3 ) ); println( s.none( x => x > 9 ) ); println( s.find( x => x > 2 ) ); Output: 10,20,30,40 3,4 10 true true true 3 Known issues in 0.11.0 These were reproduced on the CLI built from the 0.11.0 sources. add() , append() and addAll() do not skip duplicates. They behave like array appends, so a set can end up holding the same value twice. union , + and the constructors do deduplicate. Missing member functions: equals , containsAll , any and toString fail with Method ... not found . reject fails in the CLI with BIF arrayreject not found because tree shaking drops the function. It works in the playground and with --no-shaking . sorted does not keep values sorted after creation, as shown above. Workaround for the first one: build with union . s = setOf( 1, 2 ); s.add( 2 ); println( s.size() ); t = setOf( 1, 2 ); t = t.union( setOf( 2 ) ); println( t.size() ); Output: 3 2 The first size() is 3, which is the bug. The second is 2. See also destructuring, spread and ranges and operators .

title: Single-file AWS Lambda
body: Single-File AWS Lambda This example is the smallest MatchBox Lambda shape: Lambda.bx event.json Lambda.bx defines a class with: function run(event, context, response) The runtime passes the raw AWS Lambda event into event , an AWS-style context object into context , and a mutable Lambda proxy response struct into response . The handler here sets its own headers struct, which includes CORS headers, so the runtime's default headers are not added. The AWS Lambda guide describes the full contract, class routing and the Application.bx hooks. Local Invoke From this directory: matchbox lambda invoke Lambda.bx --event event.json event.json is a Function URL style event with name=Lambda in the query string. The response: { "body": "{\"message\":\"Hello from Lambda\",\"path\":\"/\",\"requestId\":\"local-request\"}", "cookies": [], "headers": { "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type, Authorization", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS", "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, "isBase64Encoded": false, "statusCode": 200 } A local invoke reports local-request as the request id. AWS Setup Before deploying, follow the AWS account setup . You need: AWS CLI v2 a configured AWS profile a region an existing Lambda execution role ARN Build the bootstrap The Lambda runtime executable is not part of the CLI. Build it from the MatchBox source tree for the architecture of your function (the default is arm64 ): cargo build --release -p matchbox_lambda_runner --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu The result is target/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/matchbox_lambda_runner . Building for another architecture needs that target installed and a linker for it. Deploy matchbox lambda deploy Lambda.bx \ --function matchbox-single-file-demo \ --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/matchbox-lambda-execution \ --profile matchbox-dev \ --region us-east-1 \ --public \ --bootstrap /path/to/matchbox_lambda_runner Use --public for an unauthenticated Function URL that anyone can invoke. Use --url instead for IAM-authenticated access. Use --arch x86_64 if the bootstrap is an x86_64 build. --memory , --timeout and --out are described in the guide. If deploy succeeds, the command prints the Function URL. Test it with: curl "https://your-url.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/?name=AWS" The body has this shape: { "message": "Hello from AWS", "requestId": "...", "path": "/" }

title: Values and strings
body: Values and strings Variables You create a variable by assigning to it. There is no declaration keyword, and a variable can hold any type. name = "Ada"; age = 36; isAdmin = true; println( name ); println( age + 1 ); println( isAdmin ); Output: Ada 37 true Strings and interpolation Put #expression# inside a double-quoted string to insert a value. The expression can be any code. Use & to join strings. name = "Ada"; age = 36; println( "#name# is #age# years old" ); println( "Next year: #age + 1#" ); println( "Hello, " & name & "!" ); Output: Ada is 36 years old Next year: 37 Hello, Ada! To print a literal # , double it: "Issue ##42" prints Issue #42 . String functions Most string functions work both ways: ucase( text ) or text.ucase() . title = " MatchBox "; println( title.trim() ); println( title.trim().ucase() ); println( title.trim().lcase() ); println( title.trim().len() ); println( title.trim().left( 5 ) ); println( title.trim().reverse() ); println( "hello world".replace( "world", "MatchBox" ) ); println( ucFirst( "hello" ) ); Output: MatchBox MATCHBOX matchbox 8 Match xoBhctaM hello MatchBox Hello Numbers and operators println( 10 / 4 ); println( 10 \ 4 ); println( 10 % 4 ); println( 2 ^ 10 ); println( 3 > 2 ); println( true && !false ); println( 3 > 2 ? "yes" : "no" ); println( "5" + 5 ); Output: 2.5 2 2 1024 true true yes 10 / is normal division, \ divides and drops the remainder, % is the remainder and ^ is a power. Notice that "5" + 5 is 10 : BoxLang converts a numeric string to a number for arithmetic, while & always joins text. Missing values null means "no value". The elvis operator ?: supplies a default when the left side is null. nickname = null; println( nickname ?: "no nickname" ); println( isNull( nickname ) ); Output: no nickname true Try it Make nickname a string and run the sample again. Then write a line that prints your name in capitals, followed by its length.

title: WASI HTTP
body: WASI HTTP --target wasi-http turns a webroot directory into one .wasm component that exports the WASI HTTP incoming handler. The component serves the same files and templates as matchbox --serve , with the webroot embedded in the binary. This is different from --target wasi , which packages a single script that runs once and exits. Build matchbox --target wasi-http --webroot ./site --output site.wasm Flag Default Meaning --webroot <dir> . Directory to package. --output <file> <webroot>.wasm Output file. --webroot and --output are the only flags this target reads. Nothing is listening after the build; the component is run by a host that supports WASI HTTP. The build: Reads boxlang.json from the webroot for rewrites and rewriteFileName . A websocket block is ignored and the build prints a warning. Compiles every .bxm and .bxs file in the webroot. A syntax error stops the build. Embeds every file under the webroot, including boxlang.json , together with the compiled templates. Patches that payload into a prebuilt matchbox_wasi_http_runner component and writes the result. Limits Limit Detail Size The payload must fit in a 4 MiB region of the runner (4 MiB minus 12 bytes). A larger webroot fails with "exceeds the embed capacity". Every file in the directory counts, so keep build output, node_modules and similar out of the webroot. Native code The build fails if the webroot has a native directory, a boxlang_modules/*/native directory, or a .bx , .bxm or .bxs file that contains the text java: or rust: . WebSockets Not supported. Sessions Kept in memory of the running instance. They are not shared between instances and are lost when the instance stops. Behavior The component runs the same engine as the webroot server, so these rules apply unchanged: GET , HEAD and POST are handled; other methods return 405 . .bxm and .bxs files are rendered as templates, and a directory is answered by its index.bxm or index.bxs . Path segments that start with . return 403 . The url , form , cookie , session and cgi scopes are populated as described in Web server . Differences from --serve : Requests are read from the WASI HTTP request, so a POST body with application/x-www-form-urlencoded is available in form . A failure in the engine returns 500 with the error text as text/plain . HEAD responses carry no body. Requirements The CLI builds the runner component when it is not already present. It looks for target/wasm32-wasip2/release/matchbox_wasi_http_runner.wasm inside the MatchBox source tree it was compiled from, and otherwise runs cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2 -p matchbox_wasi_http_runner in that tree. The build therefore needs the source checkout, a Rust toolchain and the target ( rustup target add wasm32-wasip2 ). A CLI downloaded as a release binary cannot find that tree unless the checkout exists at the path it was built from. The component's exported interface is wasi:http/incoming-handler (the proxy world of the wasi crate). Use a host that implements it to run the file.

title: WASM browser Todo app
body: WASM Browser - Todo App A minimal browser Todo application written in BoxLang and compiled to WebAssembly. BoxLang owns the app state and state transitions. The HTML shell wires that state into Alpine using the generated window.MatchBox.State(...) helper. Project Layout wasm_browser/ ├── todo.bxs ← BoxLang source (state + DOM rendering logic) └── index.html ← HTML shell (imports the compiled ES module) How It Works matchbox --target js compiles todo.bxs to an ES module ( todo.js + todo.wasm ). BoxLang owns the state and returns plain snapshot structs for the UI. The generated browser contract owns readiness and module lookup through window.MatchBox . The page owns framework wiring by creating an Alpine store from window.MatchBox.State("todo", ...) . Build You need the matchbox binary and the wasm-bindgen command-line tool on your PATH ( cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli , or set WASM_BINDGEN to its path). wasm-pack is not used. cd docs/examples/wasm_browser matchbox --target js todo.bxs This produces these files alongside your source: todo.js ← ES module wrapper (import this in HTML) todo.wasm ← WebAssembly binary (loaded automatically by todo.js) todo.d.ts ← TypeScript declarations todo_bg.wasm.d.ts ← TypeScript declarations for the wasm exports Run Locally Browsers block WASM loading over file:// for security reasons. Serve the directory with any local HTTP server: # Option A - Node.js (npx, no install required) npx serve . # Option B - Python python3 -m http.server 8080 # Option C - any other static file server Then open the printed URL (usually http://localhost:3000 or http://localhost:8080 ) in your browser. Features Add a task by typing in the input and pressing Enter or clicking Add . Click a task text to toggle it done / undone . Click ✕ to remove a task. Deploy to Production The compiled output ( todo.js , todo.wasm and index.html ) is a fully static bundle. Upload it to any static host: # Vercel vercel deploy # Netlify drag-and-drop # Upload the wasm_browser/ folder to app.netlify.com/drop Ensure your server sets the correct MIME type for .wasm files: Content-Type: application/wasm Most modern hosts (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages) handle this automatically.
