title: WASM container deployment
body: WASM Container Deployment MatchBox can target WASI hosts such as Wasmtime, WasmEdge and WASM-capable container runtimes. This page records what was run against MatchBox 0.11.0. wasm and wasi are two different --target values, and in 0.11.0 neither produces a working module on its own. Known issue: `--target wasm` and `--target wasi` --target wasi fails with WASI stub is missing the BOXLANG_EMBED sentinel . The runner stub has no such sentinel. --target wasm writes <name>.wasm , but the file is the WASI stub with an unframed byte block appended. Node 22 rejects it with unknown section code #0xea . The browser path is --target js and is covered in JavaScript and WebAssembly . The rest of this page describes a verified workaround and the WASI HTTP target. No standalone WASI runtime (Wasmtime, WasmEdge) was available when this page was written. Everything marked as run used the WASI implementation in Node 22. A working WASI module: Native Fusion If a native/ directory exists next to the script, the CLI does not use the runner stub. It generates a small Rust crate with your bytecode inside and compiles it for wasm32-wasip1 . The directory may be empty. my_service/ hello.bxs native/ rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 mkdir -p out matchbox --target wasi hello.bxs --output out/hello.wasm Native Fusion detected! Target: wasi. Building hybrid artifact... ... WASI Fusion binary produced: out/hello.wasm The build took about 50 seconds and wrote 8,669,526 bytes for the three-line hello.bxs from the quick start. The output directory must already exist: the CLI copies the built file there and does not create the directory. Running it under Node's WASI implementation printed the script's output and exited with code 0: import { WASI } from 'node:wasi'; import fs from 'node:fs'; const wasi = new WASI({ version: 'preview1', args: ['hello.wasm'], env: {}, preopens: {}, returnOnExit: true }); const mod = await WebAssembly.compile(fs.readFileSync('out/hello.wasm')); const instance = await WebAssembly.instantiate(mod, wasi.getImportObject()); console.log('exit code', wasi.start(instance)); Hello, world! exit code 0 Requirements and limits of this route: A Rust toolchain with the wasm32-wasip1 target. The MatchBox source tree. The generated crate depends on matchbox_vm by the absolute path of the checkout the CLI was compiled from, and the build runs cargo build --offline against a copy of that checkout's Cargo.lock . It was run with a CLI built from source, not with a downloaded release binary. A Fusion build with native/*.rs files can add Rust functions. A native/Cargo.toml is ignored, see Native Fusion . A Fusion build for WASI with a register_bifs() module ( add(10, 20) ) also compiled and printed 30 under Node's WASI. Running the plain runner stub The WASI runner stub that the CLI embeds is a valid module. After a source build with the wasm32-wasip1 target installed it is at stubs/runner_stub_wasip1.wasm (2,110,700 bytes). It cannot read bytecode appended to itself on WASI, so it falls back to a file named app.bxb in the preopened current directory: matchbox --build hello.bxs --output app.bxb With the same Node script as above but preopens: { '.': '.' } , running the stub printed Hello, world! . With no app.bxb it exits with code 1 and prints No embedded bytecode or app.bxb found . This is how the stub behaves today, not a documented deployment mode. Other WASI hosts Wasmtime, WasmEdge, Docker's WASM runtimes and edge platforms such as Fastly Compute accept WASI modules in general, but none of them were available for testing and none of their commands are given here. Use the module from the Fusion route and follow your host's own documentation. Remember to grant file access to the directory the program needs; the Node example above needed a preopened directory only for the stub's app.bxb fallback. WASI HTTP components --target wasi-http packages a webroot into the matchbox_wasi_http_runner WASI component. It does not take a script: matchbox --target wasi-http --webroot www --output site.wasm WASI HTTP component produced: site.wasm A one-page webroot produced a 6,503,104 byte file. The component was not run, so its HTTP behaviour is untested. The webroot payload may not exceed 4,194,292 bytes. The command needs the server feature and the wasm32-wasip2 Rust target, and it builds matchbox_wasi_http_runner under the source checkout the CLI was compiled from the first time it is used. Limitations of the WASI Fusion module Feature Status Java interop Not available. The WebAssembly builds do not include JNI. DOM and js.* Not available. They need a browser. File access Granted by the host through preopened directories. JIT Not available. Cranelift is not part of the WebAssembly builds.

title: WASM container example
body: WASM Container Example This example shows how to compile a BoxLang script to a raw WebAssembly binary and run it as a serverless workload inside a minimal OCI container - with no OS, no JVM, and no MatchBox installation on the host. The same .wasm binary can also be executed directly by Wasmtime or WasmEdge . Project Layout wasm_container/ ├── service.bxs ← BoxLang source └── Dockerfile ← minimal OCI image (FROM scratch) Step 1 - Prerequisites No special prerequisites are needed. matchbox --target wasi patches your bytecode into a pre-built WASI runner stub that is embedded in the matchbox binary, so no cargo or Rust toolchain is required at compile time. To run the binary outside of Docker you need a WASI runtime such as Wasmtime: # Install Wasmtime (macOS / Linux) - optional, for running without Docker curl https://wasmtime.dev/install.sh -sSf | bash Step 2 - Compile to WASM cd docs/examples/wasm_container matchbox --target wasi service.bxs --target wasi not --target wasm Both targets start from the same WASI runner stub. --target wasi writes the bytecode into a fixed 1 MiB region of the stub, so the compiled script must fit in 1 MiB less 12 bytes. --target wasm instead appends the bytecode as a custom section named boxlang_bytecode ; use --target wasi for this example. For a browser, use --target js (see the browser example ). This produces service.wasm - a self-contained WASI binary embedding the MatchBox VM and your compiled BoxLang bytecode. Step 3 - Run with Wasmtime (no Docker required) If you installed Wasmtime, you can run the binary directly and see output in your terminal immediately - no Docker overhead: wasmtime service.wasm Expected output: === BoxLang WASM Service === --- Dataset Summary --- Values : 10 Sum : 417 Mean : 41.7 Min : 3 Max : 97 Range : 94 --- Fibonacci (first 10 terms) --- term 1: 0 term 2: 1 ... term 10: 34 Service completed successfully. Grant filesystem access if your script reads files: wasmtime --dir=. service.wasm Step 4 - Run with WasmEdge # Install WasmEdge curl -sSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WasmEdge/WasmEdge/master/utils/install.sh | bash # Run wasmedge service.wasm Step 5 - Build a Docker Image # Compile first (patches the prebuilt WASI runner; no cargo build) matchbox --target wasi service.bxs # Build the OCI image, annotating it for the wasi/wasm32 platform. # This must match the --platform flag used at run time. docker buildx build --platform wasi/wasm32 -t matchbox-service . The image is built FROM scratch - it contains only service.wasm . Total image size is the WASM file itself. The runner stub alone is about 2.1 MB in v0.11.0 ( stubs/runner_stub_wasip1.wasm ), so expect a file of at least that size. Why docker buildx build --platform wasi/wasm32 ? Plain docker build tags the image for your host's native platform (e.g. linux/arm64 ). When docker run --platform=wasi/wasm32 is given, Docker looks for an image with a wasi/wasm32 manifest, finds none locally, and tries to pull from Docker Hub - causing a "repository does not exist" error. Building with --platform wasi/wasm32 ensures the manifest matches. Step 6 - Run the Docker Container The containerd-shim-wasmtime always routes the WASM process's stdout through Docker's log driver. It does not stream output to an attached terminal, regardless of flags. The reliable pattern is to run detached and read logs after the container exits: docker run -d --name matchbox-svc \ --runtime=io.containerd.wasmtime.v1 \ --platform=wasi/wasm32 \ matchbox-service docker logs matchbox-svc docker rm matchbox-svc Tip: For live terminal output during development, skip Docker and use wasmtime service.wasm directly - it is simpler and faster. Push to a Registry docker tag matchbox-service ghcr.io/your-org/matchbox-service:latest docker push ghcr.io/your-org/matchbox-service:latest Deploy to Fastly Compute fastly compute pack --wasm service.wasm fastly compute deploy What WASM Containers Are Good For Use case Why WASM containers fit Serverless / FaaS Near-zero cold start, no OS dependencies Edge computing Run BoxLang logic at the network edge Hermetic microservices Strict sandbox, nothing outside the WASM spec CI / batch jobs Tiny image, fast pull, deterministic execution Limitations Feature Status println / stdout ✅ Works via WASI Filesystem access ✅ Requires wasmtime --dir= grant Network (sockets) ⚠️ WASI preview2 / experimental DOM / js.* APIs ❌ Browser context only Java interop ❌ No JNI in WASM Native Fusion Not tested for --target wasi ; see the Native Fusion guide See wasm-container.md for the full deployment reference.

title: Web server
body: Web server MatchBox has two web runtimes. Both are implemented in the matchbox_server crate and run on the same VM as the CLI. Webroot server App server Start with matchbox --serve matchbox_server --app app.bxs Routing The file path in the URL Routes you register in a script Pages .bxm and .bxs templates plus static files Handlers, middleware, event.setView() templates Configuration boxlang.json in the webroot Calls in the script ( app.listen() ) WebSockets Yes, through boxlang.json Yes, through app.enableWebSockets() Example Web server App server , WebSocket counter Webroot server matchbox --serve --webroot ./site --port 8080 Flag Default Meaning --webroot <dir> . Directory to serve. --port <n> 8080 Listen port. --host <addr> 127.0.0.1 Bind address. Use 0.0.0.0 to accept connections from other machines, for example inside a container. matchbox --serve accepts only these three flags and reads boxlang.json from the webroot. The --config <file> flag exists only on the matchbox_server binary, which you build from the MatchBox source tree with cargo build --release -p matchbox_server . On startup the server prints the address, the resolved webroot and whether rewrites are enabled. Files are read on every request, so edits appear without a restart. What gets served Request Result A .bxm or .bxs file Rendered as a template. Response is 200 with Content-Type: text/html and a MBX_SESSION_ID cookie. Any other file Sent as is, with a content type guessed from the extension. A directory index.bxm , then index.bxs , inside it. A missing file 404 Not Found , or the rewrite file when rewrites are on. A path with a segment that starts with . 403 . A path that climbs out of the webroot 403 . A method other than GET , HEAD or POST 405 with allow: GET,HEAD,POST . HEAD returns the headers of the GET response with an empty body. A template that throws returns 500 with the error text. Scopes in templates Scope Contents url Query-string parameters. form Fields of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST body. JSON bodies are not exposed. cookie Request cookies, plus MBX_SESSION_ID . session A struct kept in server memory per MBX_SESSION_ID cookie. cgi request_method , script_name , path_info , server_name , server_port , http_host , content_type , content_length . It is not the process environment. All values are strings. Session values are stored as strings between requests, so a number or struct you assign comes back as its string form on the next request. Sessions have no expiry and are lost when the process stops. To read an environment variable use getSystemSetting( "NAME", "default" ) . There is no env scope. boxlang.json Place boxlang.json in the webroot. All keys are optional. { "rewrites": true, "rewriteFileName": "index.bxm", "websocket": { "uri": "/ws", "listenerClass": "Chat", "listenerState": { "greeting": "hello" }, "handler": "WebSocket.bx" } } Key Default Meaning rewrites false When true , a request whose file does not exist is answered by rewriteFileName instead of a 404. The original path is available as cgi.path_info , and the query string stays in url . This applies to every missing file, including missing images and stylesheets. rewriteFileName index.bxm Front-controller file, relative to the webroot. A value that contains .. or starts with / is replaced by the default. websocket none Enables a WebSocket endpoint. See below. If boxlang.json is not valid JSON, or a websocket block is missing one of uri , listenerClass or listenerState , the whole file is ignored without a warning and the defaults apply. Check the "Rewrites:" line printed at startup. A directory request that finds no index file also does not fall back to the rewrite file. In v0.11.0 it answers 500 with Is a directory (os error 21) . WebSockets in the webroot server The websocket block names a class and the file that defines it. Key Meaning uri Path that accepts WebSocket upgrades. listenerClass Name of the class to instantiate. listenerState JSON object. Its keys are set as instance variables of the listener ( variables.greeting ). The constructor is not called. handler File that defines the class. Default WebSocket.bx . It is looked up case-insensitively in the webroot directory itself, not in subdirectories. class Chat { function onConnect( channel ) { channel.sendJson( { "welcome": variables.greeting, "id": channel.getId() } ); } function onMessage( message, channel ) { channel.broadcastMessage( "echo:" & message ); } function onClose( channel ) {} } If the handler file is missing or does not compile, the server starts without a WebSocket endpoint. An error thrown in onConnect or onMessage is printed on the server's stderr and closes that connection with code 1011. WebSocket channel API The same channel object is passed to listeners in both server modes. Method Purpose sendMessage( text ) , sendText( text ) Send a text frame to this client. sendJson( value ) Serialize value as JSON and send it as text. sendBytes( bytes ) Send a binary frame. broadcastMessage( text ) , broadcastText( text ) Text frame to every connected client, including this one. broadcastJson( value ) , broadcastBytes( bytes ) The same for JSON and binary payloads. close( [code], [reason] ) Close the connection. Default code 1000 . getId() Server-generated UUID of this connection. getPath() Path of the upgrade request, such as /ws . getURL() Full URL of the upgrade request, including the query string. getHTTPHeader( name, [default] ) Header of the upgrade request. Names are matched case-insensitively. Returns null when missing and no default is given. Listener hooks are onConnect( channel ) , onMessage( message, channel ) and onClose( channel ) . message is a string for text frames and bytes for binary frames. The channel has no properties: channel.id is null , use getId() . App server The app server runs one script that builds a routed application with web.server() . It is started with the --app flag of the matchbox_server binary: cargo run -p matchbox_server -- --app app.bxs matchbox app.bxs cannot run such a script: the CLI does not install the web namespace, and web.server() fails with Method server not found on null . In --app mode the --port , --host , --webroot and --config flags are ignored; the address comes from app.listen() . import boxlang.web; app = web.server(); app.get( "/hello/:name", function( event, rc, prc ) { event.renderJson( { "message": "Hello " & rc.name } ); } ); app.listen( 8090 ); The script is compiled once at startup and is not reloaded when the file changes. Its top level runs at startup and then again on every request, in a fresh VM, so variables set at the top of the script do not carry over between requests. Keep shared state in session , a file or a database. Application object Call Purpose app.get/post/put/patch/delete( path, [middleware...], handler ) Register a route. app.use( middleware ) Add middleware that runs for every request. app.group( prefix ) Returns a group with the same methods, a path prefix and its own use() . Groups nest. app.middleware.buildStaticFiles( mount, dir ) Middleware that serves files from dir (relative to the script) under mount . Missing files fall through to routing. app.webhook( builder, handler ) , app.buildWebhook() Signed webhook endpoint. See below. app.enableWebSockets( uri, listener ) Attach a listener object. Its state is snapshotted when you register it. app.listen( port ) or app.listen( { host, port } ) Where to listen. Default 127.0.0.1:8080 . Routes: A path segment that starts with : captures that segment. There are no wildcards or regular expressions. A route matches only when the number of segments is equal. The first registered match wins. Only get , post , put , patch and delete can be registered. Other methods get 404 . An unmatched request returns 404 with the text Not Found . Middleware has the signature function( event, rc, prc, next ) and continues the chain with next.run() . Handlers have the signature function( event, rc, prc ) . [!warning] Known issue in v0.11.0 When the application registers any app.use() middleware, an unmatched URL returns 500 with a "Not Found" error text instead of 404 . Without middleware the 404 is returned normally. Request collections Name Contents rc Query parameters, then form fields, then top-level keys of a JSON body, then route parameters. A later source overwrites an earlier one with the same name. prc Private collection for passing data between middleware and handlers. session Per-session struct, keyed by the MBX_SESSION_ID cookie that the server sets. The store is in memory, round-trips through JSON (only JSON types survive), and has no expiry. JSON bodies are parsed when Content-Type is JSON. The server does not limit the request body size. The event object Method Returns or does getCollection() , getPrivateCollection() , getSession() The rc , prc and session structs. valueExists( key ) , privateValueExists( key ) , sessionExists( key ) Whether the key exists. getValue( key, [default] ) , getPrivateValue( key, [default] ) , getSessionValue( key, [default] ) Read a value. setValue( key, value, [private=false] ) Set a value in rc , or in prc when the third argument is true. paramValue( key, default ) , paramPrivateValue( key, default ) , paramSessionValue( key, default ) Set the value only when the key is missing. setSessionValue is an alias of paramSessionValue . getOnly( keys ) , getExcept( keys ) A struct holding only, or everything but, the named keys of rc . getRouteParams() Struct of the :name captures. getCurrentRoute() The matched pattern, such as /hello/:name . getHTTPMethod() , getRequestMethod() The request method. getPath( [withQuery=true] ) Request path, with the raw query string unless false . getURL( [withQuery=true] ) Full request URL, or only the path when false . getHTTPHeader( name, [default] ) Request header. Names are case-insensitive. getHTTPCookie( name, [default] ) , getCookie Request cookie. isJSON() , isAjax() Whether the request has a JSON content type, or X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest . getHTTPContent( [asJson=false] ) Raw body as a string, or parsed JSON when true . Invalid JSON gives a 400 . setHTTPHeader( name, value ) Add a response header. setHTTPCookie( name, value, [path="/"], [httpOnly=false] ) , setCookie Add a Set-Cookie header. setHTTPStatus( code ) Set the response status. clearSession() , invalidateSession() Empty the session struct. renderText( text ) , renderHTML( html ) , renderJSON( value ) Set the body and content type. renderData( "json" \| "html" \| "text" \| "plain", data ) Same, with the format as an argument. setView( path, [viewArgs] ) , renderTemplate( path, [viewArgs] ) Render a .bxm template (relative to the script) as HTML. The template sees event , rc , prc , session and viewArgs . renderJSON writes numbers as floating point, so 1 is serialized as 1.0 . Errors If a handler throws, the response status comes from the start of the error message: Message contains Status Bad Request: 400 Unauthorized: 401 Conflict: 409 anything else 500 The body is the error text, or {"error": "..."} when the request sends Accept: application/json . Webhooks app.webhook( app.buildWebhook() .path( "/webhooks/stripe" ) .secret( getSystemSetting( "STRIPE_SECRET" ) ) .signatureHeader( "stripe-signature" ) .prefix( "sha256=" ) .timestampHeader( "stripe-timestamp" ) .toleranceSeconds( 300 ) .replayHeader( "stripe-event-id" ) .replayTtlSeconds( 300 ), function( event, rc, prc ) { event.renderText( "ok" ); } ); A webhook is a POST route. The server computes an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body with the secret and compares its lowercase hex form with the signature header, after removing prefix if the header starts with it. A bare hex signature is also accepted. Builder method Rule path , secret , signatureHeader Required. prefix Optional text stripped from the header value. timestampHeader and toleranceSeconds Set both or neither. The header must hold Unix seconds within the tolerance of the server clock. The timestamp is checked, not signed. replayHeader Delivery id header. A repeated id for the same path is rejected with 409 for the TTL. replayTtlSeconds Requires replayHeader . Default 3600 . The replay store is in memory. A missing or wrong signature, a missing or stale timestamp, or a missing delivery id returns 401 . WebSockets in the app server listener = new ClickCounterSocket(); listener.configure(); app.enableWebSockets( "/ws", listener ); The listener and the channel API are the same as in the webroot server, except that the listener is an instance you create and configure yourself. Its state is captured when enableWebSockets() is called and restored inside the WebSocket runtime.

title: Web server example
body: MatchBox web server example This example serves a directory with matchbox --serve . It has BoxLang Markup ( .bxm ) pages, a static CSS file, and the url , form , cookie , session and cgi scopes. The Web server guide covers the server in full. Project structure index.bxm : Home page. Counts visits in the session and prints the time. about.bxm : Prints cgi.server_port . contact.bxm : Reads url.name and shows the session id from the cookie scope. styles.css : A static file, served as text/css . How it works Every .bxm or .bxs file under the webroot is rendered as a template when you request it. Other files are sent as they are. A request for a directory is answered by its index.bxm or index.bxs . Each page render starts with these scopes: url : query-string parameters. form : fields of a URL-encoded POST body. cookie : request cookies, including MBX_SESSION_ID . session : a struct held in server memory for each MBX_SESSION_ID cookie. Values are kept as strings. cgi : request_method , script_name , path_info , server_name , server_port , http_host , content_type and content_length . The server is built on Axum and Tokio and runs the same VM as the matchbox command. Running the example From the docs/examples directory of the MatchBox source tree, or any directory that contains a copy of web_server : matchbox --serve --webroot web_server --port 8080 Open http://localhost:8080 . Visit http://localhost:8080/contact.bxm?name=MatchBox to see URL parameter handling. Reload the home page. The visit count in session.visitCount goes up each time your browser sends the same session cookie. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 unless you pass --host 0.0.0.0 . [!note] Template tags In a .bxm file, #expression# is evaluated only inside <bx:output> . A condition attribute on <bx:if> is evaluated as an expression only when written as condition="#expression#" , and <bx:output> inside <bx:if> ends the page output in v0.11.0. contact.bxm therefore does its branching in a <bx:script> block and prints the result with one <bx:output> .

title: WebSocket counter example
body: MatchBox WebSocket Counter Example This example demonstrates the routed app server plus SocketBox-style websocket listeners. It serves an HTML page at / , opens a websocket connection to /ws , increments a shared counter when the button is clicked, and broadcasts the new count to every connected browser tab. Project Structure app.bxs : Main routed app plus websocket listener registration. views/home.bxm : HTML page with the client-side websocket code. Key Concepts 1. Listener Class Registration WebSockets are enabled with a listener instance: import boxlang.web; listener = new ClickCounterSocket(); listener.configure(); app.enableWebSockets( "/ws", listener ); MatchBox snapshots the listener instance state when you register it, then restores that state inside the websocket runtime. This keeps preconfigured listener objects usable instead of forcing a zero-argument constructor. 2. Listener Lifecycle The listener class uses the familiar SocketBox-style methods: onConnect( channel ) onMessage( message, channel ) onClose( channel ) 3. Channel Helpers The channel object currently supports: sendMessage() / sendText() sendJson() sendBytes() broadcastMessage() / broadcastText() broadcastJson() broadcastBytes() close() getId() , getPath() , getURL() and getHTTPHeader( name, [default] ) , which describe the connection and its upgrade request The Web server guide describes each method. This example uses sendJson() to initialize new connections and broadcastJson() to fan out counter changes. Running the Example The --app flag belongs to the matchbox_server binary, which you build from the MatchBox source tree. From the project root: cargo run -p matchbox_server -- --app docs/examples/websocket_counter/app.bxs Then open: http://localhost:8099/ Open the page in two tabs and click the button in either tab. Both tabs update to the same counter value. The count lives in the listener inside the WebSocket runtime, so it survives page reloads and resets when the server restarts. To attach a listener without a routed app, use the websocket block of boxlang.json in a webroot; see the guide.

title: Welcome to MatchBox
body: Welcome to MatchBox BoxLang is a dynamic language for building applications. It normally runs on the JVM. MatchBox is a second runtime for the same language, written in Rust. It compiles your code to bytecode and runs it on a small virtual machine, which lets BoxLang go places the JVM does not fit: a single native executable, a browser tab, a serverless function, even a microcontroller. You write the same language either way. What changes is where it runs and what you can reach from it. MatchBox complements the JVM runtime, it does not replace it. See what is MatchBox and differences from BoxLang for the details. Your first script Press Run this in your browser under the code. Nothing is installed and nothing is sent to a server: the compiler and the VM run on your device. function greet( name ) { return "Hello, #name#!"; } println( greet( "MatchBox" ) ); Output: Hello, MatchBox! A few things to notice: .bxs is the file extension for a BoxLang script . #name# inside a double-quoted string inserts the value of name . You will see more of this in lesson 3. println writes a line to the console. Try it Change "MatchBox" to your own name and run it again. Then add a second println call that greets someone else. What you will learn Lesson Topic 2 Install MatchBox and run a file on your machine 3 Values, strings and operators 4 Arrays and structs, and how to loop over them 5 Functions, arrow functions and closures 6 Classes and objects 7 Errors and control flow 8 Running work at the same time 9 Building a native executable 10 Where to go next

title: Where to go next
body: Where to go next You can now write and run MatchBox programs and ship them. Here is where each interest leads. Go deeper If you want to... Read Call Rust code from BoxLang Native Fusion Serve HTTP and web pages HTTP and the examples Run on AWS Lambda AWS Lambda Run in a browser or on JavaScript hosts JavaScript and WebAssembly Program a microcontroller ESP32 Understand the speed story JIT See every command and flag CLI reference Compare with BoxLang on the JVM Differences from BoxLang Keep experimenting the playground Things to watch for in 0.11.0 MatchBox is young, and it is honest to say where it is still rough. These all came up while writing this course, and every sample in the lessons avoids them: A function that returns a function using the outer function's own variables does not capture them yet (lesson 5). A constructor needs return this , or new gives you null (lesson 6). variables.n++ as a statement inside a class fails. variables.n += 1 works. Some members you may expect on values are missing, for example keyArray() on a struct and contains() or substring() on a string. The function forms such as structKeyArray( s ) often exist. When you run a file with the CLI, a few array members such as first() and sort( "numeric" ) can fail with BIF ... not found , because unused functions are trimmed from the build. Use the function form ( arraySort( a, "numeric" ) ) or add --no-shaking . The browser playground is not affected. dateFormat uses Java-style masks, so mm means minutes and MM means month. Use MM . Operators spelled as words, such as mod and not , are not supported. Use % and ! . If you hit something else, please open an issue . Keep going You finished the course. Thank you for learning MatchBox. The fastest way to get better now is to build something small and real: a script that reads your own data, a tiny web page, or a command-line tool. Come back to the playground any time you want to test an idea.
